Researchers investigate the B^0_s meson's lifetime using data from ATLAS and CMS at 8 and 13 TeV collision energies. This study also enables researchers to determine the difference between the B^0_s and \bar{B}^0 meson lifetimes as 0.007 picoseconds, which is consistent with but more precise than previous measurements. These outcomes can aid in uncovering processes that violate CP symmetry and other rare occurrences within the Standard Model of particle interactions. Additionally, the tightness of these measurements will make it more difficult to mask potential signs of new physics phenomena, and in certain scenarios, new physics could manifest itself by causing a significant difference (greater than 1.5 times) between the B^0_s and \bar{B}^0 meson lifetimes. Although this distinction remains within the acceptable range predicted by the Standard Model, it is crucial to continue monitoring it closely as more precise measurements become available. This paper explores an approach to addressing uncertainty in discretization methods, specifically for solving stochastic control problems. Our method involves analyzing a modified version of a scheme that accounts for rough data and their impact on solution dynamics. We initially consider a particular scheme and provide an estimate for its rate of convergence. This estimate is expressed in terms of regularity properties of an underlying stochastic differential equation and its solutions. We then apply this approach to a specific optimization problem - managing an asset subject to default - and demonstrate that our method can indeed find optimal control policies. This involves establishing conditions that guarantee the existence of solutions to a related backward stochastic differential equation and verifying that rough estimates of solutions to this equation converge at a specific rate. We also validate the accuracy of our method through numerical simulations, including both static and dynamic feedback controls. These simulations demonstrate the potential benefits of dynamic feedback controls in managing assets with default risk. Lastly, we highlight possible extensions to our approach, including its applicability to other types of stochastic systems and optimization problems. This research is an extension of prior work on rough noise approximation and can be seen as an early step towards approximating solutions of backward stochastic differential equations with rough noise. It also raises important questions about the convergence of approximate solutions under relaxed assumptions. For energies above 4 EeV, we've found a significant dipole component at (1.4±0.3)%, oriented 139±13 degrees and 25±13, which strengthens with energy. We develop a detailed analysis of noncommutative quantum mechanics, focusing on its symplectic geometry. By examining the properties of noncommutative coordinates, we find them to be closely related to specific differential operators within a commutable momentum space. This discovery allows us to convey the symplectic geometry's fundamental characteristics through these operators' symmetries and symmetry properties. In doing so, we are able to accurately describe noncommutative trajectories and compute the associated magnetic field, resulting in a realization of noncommutative harmonic oscillators. Moreover, our framework successfully enables the creation of noncommutative Dirac operators and proves the existence of noncommutative supersymmetric harmonic oscillators. All of this is achieved while adhering to the principle that mathematical theories should be based on geometric, rather than algebraic, concepts. This approach to noncommutative quantum mechanics is fully outlined in a review style, with all results derived from a single, self-consistent foundation. Additionally, our method anticipates a more extensive investigation of noncommutative geometry in the presence of momentum symmetries. Researchers use a technique called tumor infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) testing to examine the effectiveness of the immune system in fighting cancer. To assess this, researchers analyze and computerize sections of tumor tissues to quantify the presence of lymphocytes within the tumor. Several methods are developed to execute this task, including a technique called lymphocyte scoring, which involves manually typing characteristics of the tumor tissues into a computer. In this paper, we propose an alternative, fully automated approach called Lymphocyte Detection and Classification (LDC). This approach consists of two parts: lymphocyte detection, which uses a deep learning technique called U-Net within a module called Lymphocyte Detector; and lymphocyte classification, which uses another deep learning technique called Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) within a module called Lymphocyte Classifier. Both modules receive the input of pre-extracted features from the Lymphocyte Detector module. To prevent the two modules reinforcing each other and contributing no new information, this study implements a technique called multi-task learning with data augmentation. This allows the two modules to share knowledge and enhance the accuracy of the LDC approach. To validate the effectiveness of this approach, it is compared with several methods, including lymphocyte scoring, through a series of experiments. The results show that this approach not only requires no manual typing but also achieves similar or better accuracy when compared with the current state-of-the-art methods. To make this approach accessible to more researchers, this study also releases an open-source code known as OpenLDC in the form of a GitHub repository. In addition to code, this repository includes sample data, a user guide, and a demonstration video to facilitate adoption by other researchers. To further facilitate adoption, this study also invites participation in Lymphocyte Detection Competition (LDC Competition) for researchers to evaluate and compare their own approaches directly with LDC. In this competition, researchers can upload and share their approaches, and the results will be displayed on the LDC Competition website. This approach and the associated code and competition are expected to accelerate the adoption of LDC in various cancer research applications. To mitigate burst errors in high-speed coherent optical communications, we integrate equalization and maximum-likelihood sequence estimation techniques. A new method is proposed, which combines weighted minimum mean squared error equalization and maximum-likelihood sequence estimation. This method's performance is evaluated using a MLSE-WE Equalizer testbed, which showcases significant improvements in data reliability at increased symbol rates. Furthermore, the proposed method is compared to conventional digital equalization techniques, such as maximum a posteriori and zero-forcing methods. Our results demonstrate the MLSE-WE Equalizer's capability to support up to 500 Gb/s net data rate, 17% higher than the baseline system, and feature a reduced error burst size. The method's performance is also found to be insensitive to the types of optical channel impairments, such as chromatic and polarization mode dispersion, and is particularly effective in mitigating burst errors caused by laser phase noise in coherent detection systems employing external cavity mode-locked lasers. The method's efficacy is further highlighted through live trial demonstrations conducted over long-haul optical links. In this study, we propose a novel, efficient algorithm called AutoDilation, which uses evolutionary computation to optimize the dilation pattern of spatial convolution layers in Temporal Convolutional Networks. Unlike traditional methods that require manual tuning of parameters, our algorithm automatically identifies an optimal dilation pattern that minimizes model size and inference latency while maintaining high accuracy. We tested the algorithm with multiple TCN variants and found that it consistently produces high-quality solutions. In particular, we used AutoDilation to enhance two popular TCN architectures, SimpleNet and ResNet, and achieved significant improvements in model size and inference latency (by 1.08x and 1.05x, respectively) without compromising accuracy. All source code and models are openly available on GitHub.

We introduce ALBA, a novel algorithm for calculating first-order correspondents in LE- and LE-inductive logic with the Barcan formula, along with its extension to predicate logic with identity. Our method transforms the input formula into an equivalent HELE formula, then employs Fitting's LE-logic solver to determine the corresponding HELE formula, which is subsequently translated back to the original logic. This approach facilitates computation of corresponding formulas, a crucial step in the development of inductive reasoning systems. Additionally, ALBA enables the derivation of certain inductive rules, specifically the closure rules, which are essential for drawing conclusions within those systems. The algorithm's effectiveness is assured by its design to preserve the inductive properties of the input formulas. The implementation of ALBA is efficient, with a time complexity directly proportional to the number of subformulas within the input formula. This algorithm serves as a key component for the development of inductive reasoning systems that can reason correctly about possible worlds. Furthermore, ALBA introduces a new approach to computing first-order correspondents, which can be applied to other inductive logics that can be expressed as HELE-plus-axioms. The implementation of ALBA is now integrated with the HELE-logic solver, an advanced automated reasoning tool capable of determining whether a formula is a possible consequence of an inductive logic. The source code for ALBA and the HELE-logic solver is freely available under the terms of the Apache 2.0 license. The HELE-logic solver can be accessed via the Metaguru automated reasoning platform at https://metaguru.informatik.uni-freiburg.de/. Recently, a four-valued logic database model has been introduced, leading to an approach for answering queries consistently across multiple databases. This approach uses a set of inclusion axioms and a four-valued logic framework to determine if the answers to a query can be found in the answers to the same query, applied to different databases. By operating within this four-valued logic system, users can distinguish between information that is known to be true, is believed to be true, is known not to be true, and is neither confirmed nor ruled out as true. This distinction enables consistent query answering to be performed not just for sources expressing classical two-valued logic semantics but also for those expressing semantics based on Kelly's three values. This research extends this capability to a four-valued logic framework, solving the consistent query answering problem within this framework by limiting the inclusion axioms to those that do not lead to contradictions. This achievable subset of the axioms' semantic effects can be determined efficiently, thereby making this approach practical even when dealing with very large databases. Additionally, this research introduces an effective way to present the consistent query answering problem to users, allowing them to identify any undesirable axioms that may cause contradictions and thus avoid their semantic effects. This presents users with a clear choice: they can either remove the causing axioms or accept the resulting four-valued logic semantics, which includes values that were previously undistinguishable. This distinction further enhances the effectiveness of this approach in addressing the consistent query answering problem. This research is particularly relevant to the current practices in data management, particularly in the context of Linked Data where data is contributed by different users with varying levels of expertise, access, and intentions. This is also aligned with the current trends in big data analytics, where big data is often described as 'big noise' that needs to be filtered to extract meaningful information from it. This is essentially what this research is set out to achieve, i.e., to develop an approach for filtering out irrelevant information from the answers to a query, thus providing a more effective and efficient way of addressing the consistent query answering problem. This research is primarily focused on an approach based on inclusion axioms within a four-valued logic framework and it is anticipated that this approach will be extended to other types of queries beyond the basic ones it is currently addressing. This will involve exploring other ways to present the consistent query answering problem to users and identifying any desirable or undesirable effects of the inclusion axioms on the query answers. We introduce the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model, a novel extension of the Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (PARX) model. TV-PARX utilizes Gaussian regulatory variables and addresses nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks in rates through time-varying parameters and a proprietary local linear estimation method. A Laplace reconstruction technique is leveraged to maintain efficiency in the face of parameter changes. Our research evaluates the TV-PARX model's performance in relation to state-of-the-art methods for modeling non-stationary Poisson time series. Specifically, TV-PARX is compared to generalized PARX models with time-varying parameters, including the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive (TV-PAR) and Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with seasonal (TV-PARS) models, through both simulated and real-world data scenarios. Results indicate that TV-PARX yields the most accurate predictions across all evaluated scenarios. Software implementing the proposed method is publicly accessible and demonstrated via analysis of a well-known scientific journal. The accompanying code is also shared. The TV-PARX model addresses significant shortcomings of the Poisson ARX model and its derivatives by tackling two major challenges: modeling variable rates and external covariates that influence these rates. The innovative approach to modeling non-stationary Poisson time series through TV-PARX is anticipated to guide future research in this area. The methodology is currently being explored for potential applications in modeling count-based biomedical time series. The authors invite feedback and potential collaboration on this project. Software implementing the proposed method is publicly accessible at https://github.com/alexejandrov/TVPARX and is currently being developed at https://tvparx.apache.org/. Despite significant advancements in robotics, many complex tasks remain difficult to master through traditional trial-and-error learning due to their long horizons and the need for accurate state prediction. To overcome these challenges, the field of robotics is seeing increased interest in learning manipulation tasks directly from raw visual data, using techniques such as self-supervised state inference and reinforcement learning. However, existing approaches to learning manipulation tasks directly from visual data and demonstrations typically require thousands of labeled frames or extensive online exploration. This study introduces a novel framework called Neural Descriptor Fields that allows for the efficient learning of manipulation tasks from very limited demonstrations, leveraging the capability to perform unsupervised object detection and state prediction on RGB images. By formulating tasks as dynamic relationships between a fixed set of objects in a bounded workspace and developing a method to automatically generate critical states through offline reinforcement learning, we have demonstrated the ability to learn multiple manipulation tasks with varying target positions, orientations, and object configurations from just a handful of visual demonstrations. Compared to other direct learning methods, our framework achieves comparable performance with as little as 1/50th the number of training examples needed. Moreover, our work showcases the first instance of a neural network to naturally develop a level of robustness to minor changes in its training data, achieving successful adaptations with as little as 10 new training frames per task variation. Moreover, our work has a clear connection to the field of cognitive development and could serve as a starting point for studying how children quickly acquire a broad range of manipulation skills across various objects and tasks throughout their early life. With numerous practical applications, our framework's potential to efficiently learn a wide array of manipulation tasks from minimal visual demonstrations paves the way for its use in actual robotic platforms. To facilitate further research, we have made all code, data, and models publicly available. Measuring multiple first-generation chemical abundance patterns, researchers found Tononzintla 2's metal content and abundance dispersion to be exceptionally high, surpassing most other metal-rich, multiple-population Galactic clusters. This study examines the underlying structure of the dependency graph in the Formal Archive of Certified Proofs (FACT). A sample of 500 FACT proofs from the PRA archive was analyzed to examine the distribution of in-degree and out-degree among the nodes of the dependency graph, as well as the characteristics of the graph's overall topology. The results show that the dependency graph exhibits characteristics of a scale-free distribution in both a small-world network and a highly connected, grid-like network. Specifically, a small subset of highly connected nodes was identified, with the majority of nodes having minimal connections. This topological pattern was found across multiple degree distributions and was consistent with other formal proof archives, including one derived from the Isabelle archive of 1000 certified proofs. A notable anomaly was found in the distribution of out-degree among the FACT graph nodes, with an exceptionally high level of connectivity at a specific range. Additionally, the results indicated that the FACT graph exhibits a high level of clustering and non-randomness. To place the FACT graph's characteristics into perspective, the results were compared to those obtained from a similar analysis of a randomly selected sample of 500 FACT proofs. The implications of the findings for the development of visual dependency graphs within formal archives are also considered. While conducting this research, a novel method for visualizing the dependency graph was developed, featuring an interactive interface that enables users to explore different aspects of the graph's topology. The effectiveness of this approach was validated through user feedback, demonstrating that visual dependency graphs can effectively facilitate users in navigating and understanding the underlying structure of formal proofs. The methodology employed in this research is universally applicable to any certified proof domain and has significant ramifications for the way people interact with formal proofs, particularly in relation to their underlying topology. Furthermore, this research has a broader significance, given its potential to contribute to existing theories related to the topology of formal proof domains. To facilitate replication and build upon this research, an open-source tool has been developed, along with a publicly accessible FACT graph derived from a sample of 500 PRA archive proofs. Alongside this, a series of novel methods for analyzing graph topology have been created and integrated into an open-source package, along with a proposed distribution model that is unique to FACT graphs and certified proof domains generally. Lastly, several concrete suggestions are put forward to advance both the development of visual dependency graphs and the underlying topology of certified proof domains, centered on the concept of enabling collaborative modification of certified proofs. Ultimately, this research seeks to position certified proofs as more accessible tools

These calculations were performed for both $N=2$ and $N=4$ in the context of the pure Yang-Mills theory and revealed significant discrepancies in the value of $|z_c|$ when $N$ is increased from $2$ to $4$. Furthermore, our study indicates that the critical time $t_c$ is directly proportional to $N$ when $N$ is greater than or equal to $2$. We have subsequently derived renormalized field strength operators utilizing the impact of massless fermions, which preserve the symmetry properties of the pure Yang-Mills theory. We have also determined the anomalous dimensions of these operators to the NNLO. All our calculations were carried out in the fundamental representation and at the precise fixed point of the Yang-Mills theory in $2+1$ dimensions. We have subsequently determined the spectral functions $\rho(\omega)$ at various scales, which exhibit scale-invariant behavior. We have found that the normalized two-point correlation functions $G(t, T=\Lambda^{-1})$ follow a logarithmic time dependence. We have determined the coefficients $z_{\Lambda}$ and $z_c$ for both $N=2$ and $N=4$, which enable the conversion of physical lengths to the latent time parameter. We have discovered that the latent time representation of $\rho(\omega)$ reveals distinct spectral peaks at low energy for both $N=2$ and $N=4$. In contrast, the latent time representation of $G(t, T=\Lambda^{-1})$ shows notable discrepancies between $N=2$ and $N=4$, displaying an abrupt change from a logarithmic to an exponential time dependence at $N=4$. All our findings can be interpreted within the context of a phase transition from a confined to a deconfined phase when the Yang-Mills theory transitions from $N=2$ to $N=4$. This transition is marked by a critical temperature that is directly proportional to $N$ when $N$ is greater than or equal to $2$. In this study, we investigate the $	ext{Z}_2$-synchronization problem, a well-known representative of approximate message passing thresholds, to bridge the gap between AMP and the Bethe free energy (BFE). Specifically, we find that at high temperatures, the BFE converges to the TFE, and both exhibit the same phase transition behavior as predicted by AMP. Moreover, we establish that the convergence of BFE to TFE occurs before the spin-glass transition and that both can be used to determine the AMP threshold. Our findings provide insights into the relationship between the dynamics of AMP and the statistical mechanics of the underlying system and enable the application of statistical physics methods to analyze and improve the performance of AMP. By extending this approach to other AMP algorithms and contexts, we may gain a deeper understanding of the fundamental limitations and capabilities of AMP. As a practical aspect, our results make it possible to compute the AMP threshold more accurately without performing actual AMP simulations. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method by deriving a precise threshold for the $ext{Z}_2$-synchronization problem, with a threshold of approximately 1.8348, and suspect that this technique may be applicable to other AMP algorithms and systems. We anticipate that this new framework will become an important tool for analyzing and understanding the collective behavior of interacting discrete variables and the corresponding AMP algorithms. As a byproduct of this research, we develop an iterative algorithm for computing the BFE that outperforms existing methods in terms of convergence speed and accuracy, especially for systems characterized by strong loops and near-saturated messages. This new algorithm relies on a sophisticated relaxation method that incorporates an extrapolation technique to enhance performance. As demonstrated by our results, this new algorithm converges to the BFE before the spin-glass transition and can be used to determine the AMP threshold. As shown by our results, this modification induces a spin-glass transition within the corresponding sub-system, even when the entire system does not exhibit a spin-glass transition. The proof of local orbital linearization theorems employs a combination of the blowing-up method and a version of the slice theorem. Specifically, this proof utilizes a sequential strategy, involving sequential applications of the blowing-up and slice theorems to achieve a desired outcome. The initial stage of this process is concerned with proving a simplified local linearization theorem. Within this context,'simplified' signifies that the underlying Lie group in question is noncompact. The application of this simplified theorem relies on an argument by induction. This argument starts with an anchor point, obtained via the blowing-up method. The anchor point serves as a foundational case for an inductive process, aimed at achieving an intermediate outcome known as a'semi-standard' outcome. The semi-standard outcome represents an intermediate stage of refinement, where the action of the Lie group is still somewhat distorted. To reach this outcome from the anchor point, the action of the Lie group is further refined through an application of the slice theorem. The resulting semi-standard outcome can then be used as a starting point for further applications of the slice theorem, aimed at achieving additional levels of refinement. These additional levels of refinement are concerned with addressing more complex algebraic properties associated with the action of the Lie group. Ultimately, these applications of the slice theorem, starting from the semi-standard outcome, will yield the desired outcome of the linearization theorem. The final stage of this process is concerned with establishing an appropriate version of the slice theorem, known as the'standard' slice theorem. This standard slice theorem is the most refined version of the slice theorem, where the action of the Lie group is distorted as little as possible. The application of this standard slice theorem is in turn concerned with achieving an 'almost-standard' outcome, which is the desired outcome of the linearization theorem. The distinction between'semi-standard' and 'almost-standard' outcomes is concerned with whether the algebraic properties associated with the action of the Lie group have been completely addressed. The angular part of atomic orbitals is no longer a solitary concept, but rather a fundamental component that arises from the angular part of atomic one-body density matrices. These density matrices are derived from atomic one-electron momentum space wave functions, which can be obtained through a linear combination of atomic energy eigenstates or directly from atomic momentum space spectra. In this paper, we introduce an angular complementary perturbation neural network (eCPNN) design that utilizes neural network functions to model the angular part of atomic one-body density matrices and derived potential functions, which in turn can be utilized to explain atomic Compton profiles. The eCPNN model incorporates an external reference potential and complementary perturbation philosophy to only focus on differences from a simplified model, which in this case is the atomic Thomas-Fermi model. The training of the eCPNN leads to multiple potential functions that describe the spatial correlations among electrons with varying complementary perturbation strengths. These potential functions and atomic one-body density matrices can be used to explain atomic Compton profiles and provide more in-depth analysis of the electronic structure of atoms. Several examples are given to illustrate the capability of the eCPNN to accurately reproduce experimental and theoretical Compton profiles collected across a full 2π solid angle for various atomic energy levels. The results from the eCPNN models also correlate with the experimental total atomic Compton profile cross sections, which are found to be in agreement with calculations from both simple models and actual measurements. The output from the eCPNN models has the potential to contribute to the deconvolution process involved in analyzing atomic Compton profile spectra, which is essential for understanding the internal structure of atoms through direct measurement of atomic Compton profiles. Moreover, this approach can also be applied to other systems, such as ions and molecules, that have complex electronic structures, especially those with insufficiently understood low-lying energy levels. In such cases, this method could provide a useful tool for interpreting experimental Compton profile data and determining the internal structure of these systems. In conclusion, the eCPNN model has successfully demonstrated its capability to accurately reproduce a wide range of experimental and theoretical Compton profiles and has provided new insights into the underlying causes behind these profiles. In doing so, the eCPNN model has shown that atomic Compton profiles are influenced by various factors including spin states, reference potentials, and the methodology used to focus on specific portions of the atomic one-body density matrices. Wide-field photometry's high spatial resolution and wide field of view make it an interesting method for estimating vertical aerosol optical depth (VAOD). VAOD can be determined independently of absolute calibration by analyzing the variation in aerosol optical depth across the sky. This approach is based on the empirical plane-wave method, which correlates VAOD with the difference in optical depth measured simultaneously at two points on the sky. These two points are located at angles of 30 degrees from the optical axis. In order to apply this method, the empirical relationship between VAOD and the difference in optical depth must be established through observations of the aerosol content in the atmosphere. In the past, the necessary calibration observations were obtained using photometric and spectroscopic methods to determine the difference in optical depth. In the context of the VPS-1 telescope, the necessary calibration observations are obtained using three wide-field photometers. The software used to collect and process the data, the calibration procedure, and the methods used to determine the VAOD are discussed in this paper. The VAOD values obtained with the VPS-1 telescope show good agreement with those obtained from solar spectral measurements made with the MAIA satellite's EPPD1 instrument. The values obtained with the VPS-1 telescope show good agreement with those obtained from satellite measurements. In complex real-world scenarios, an object's presence can be inferred from various projections onto multiple surfaces. This paper reframes this as an object pose problem, where the goal is to find a coherent set of projections that can explain the partially hidden object and its relationships to given 3D shapes. To achieve this, we propose a method called Projective Grouping Network (PGN), which estimates multiple projections and organizes them into a hierarchical structure based on spatial connections. This approach allows for accurate pose detection, even when an object is partially concealed behind other objects or incomplete shapes. Our method is efficient because it uses a hierarchical organization to focus on key projections and their relationships. To train the model, we created a dataset called Real-time Scene Understanding Dataset (RSD) that includes animated videos and corresponding pose annotations. Our experiments show that our approach compares favorably to other state-of-the-art methods on this dataset and demonstrates robust performance on various scenes. The code and dataset are available online. This research is part of our effort to create a scene understanding system that can efficiently process complex, real-world environments by identifying and grouping objects based on their distances and relationships. While our current work focuses on recognizing and organizing 3D shapes within a scene, our long-term goal includes incorporating additional elements, such as texture and color, to develop a more comprehensive and practical scene understanding system. This approach will enable us to create a functional scene-activated grasping system, a key capability for autonomous machines interacting with their surroundings. To this end, we are exploring a multi-stage approach, starting with coarse pose detection and then refining the object's shape, texture, and position for successful grasping. This paper represents an initial step in this direction, with our ultimate goal of establishing a foundation for autonomous machines that can efficiently understand and interact with their surroundings. The peridynamic theory's kernel function plays a crucial role in identifying cracks within materials. This study examines the characteristics of kernel functions, including their symmetry properties and the role they play in determining the non-local damage accumulation. By reorganizing the theory into a standard boundary value problem, our findings also reveal that the point of highest stress concentration can be located within the material. This stress peak's location is a key indicator for determining whether a crack exists within the material. In addition, stress concentrations occur at the material's boundary when a crack is present. Our research introduces an alternative approach to determining cracks, one that does not rely on the material's stress concentrations. Instead, we propose identifying cracks based on the accumulation of damage throughout the material, rather than solely within the stress concentration region. This new approach to crack identification is then applied to a specific numerical problem and solved for multiple types of material configurations. Our results demonstrate that our proposed method of identifying cracks through damage accumulation yields more accurate solutions than the original method. Furthermore, stress concentrations are no longer necessary for determining cracks, and our method is capable of handling a broader range of materials, including those with stress concentrations at their boundaries. In such cases, our method produces the same results as the original method. In conclusion, our research on kernel functions, stress concentrations, and crack identification within materials lays the groundwork for further investigation into the role of damage accumulation throughout the material, rather than within stress concentration regions. This, in turn, may lead to a deeper understanding of how stress concentrations form within materials and how they relate to crack identification. Ultimately, our proposed method of identifying cracks through damage accumulation, rather than stress concentrations, may also have practical applications in guiding the design of materials and systems prone to cracking issues. In particular, our approach could be employed within numerical simulation frameworks that interact with engineers in real-time, helping to refine the design based on up-to-date crack identification results within the material, even as the system operates and is modified over time. Such design tools, powered by our method, might be particularly useful in industries like construction, aerospace, and biomedical engineering, among others. In these sectors, real-time access to accurate crack identification within materials could become a valuable feature for designing safe, durable systems and products. In addition, our research introduces micromanual methods for determining cracks within materials, one such method being the stress peak's location, and shows that these methods can be employed within the context of gradient theories of the simple material type. The Graphical Lasso method, a popular approach for estimating a network's inverse covariance structure from independent and identically distributed data, is now a well-established technique. The creators propose a sophisticated variation of Graphical Lasso known as Generalized Graphical Lasso, which incorporates an advanced placement strategy for latent variables to expand the framework's applicability and usefulness. This generalized version includes hidden variables that are connected to each other and to observable variables, which are located at the framework's periphery. A novel placement strategy is devised that places the parameters for central latent variables on one side of the partial positive definite matrix and estimates the network's inverse covariance structure through a Graphical Lasso-style optimization. The creators demonstrate the benefits of this generalized variation through simulations and a real-world application, demonstrating that it outperforms multiple competing methods. Moreover, they provide one of the most sophisticated Python implementations of Generalized Graphical Lasso, along with source code. This implementation can be used within scikit-learn and supports a variety of convex constraints, which can be used to estimate multiple separate networks from the same data set by employing Generalized Graphical Lasso's strategic placement of variables. This strategy can be viewed as a key methodological innovation involving Gaussian graphical models and it can be used as a highly effective technique for avoiding the overfitting of models through data partitioning techniques. The creators make the software that is based on this generalization of Graphical Lasso available over GitHub at https://github.com/monroeb/GeneralizedGraphicalLasso. The creators also created an example dataset based on the one used in Smola et al. (2005), along with related results, which can be viewed on the creators' research website at https://www.bu.edu/tao/20190324_baranowski/. The creators welcome feedback and professional discussions based on this generalization of Graphical Lasso. This study investigates how numerical techniques influence the accuracy and computational speed of simulations for the alanine dipeptide, a crucial test system. We examine multiple methods, including single-step integrators like the Verlet algorithm and linearized algorithms like Newton-SOR, with varying degrees of constraint treatment, and a high-performance linear solver, Newton-Krylov. Our findings reveal that while the total energy remains stable across methods, its accuracy varies significantly. Notably, we observed an unexpected inaccuracy in the total energy using the Verlet algorithm, likely attributed to conservative errors. Conversely, the linearized algorithms exhibited lower inaccuracy, with Newton-SOR showing the smallest deviation. Furthermore, we found that the computational efficiency of these methods differs substantially, with the Verlet algorithm being the fastest, followed by Newton-Krylov, and linearized algorithms occupying the middle ground. Our results also highlight the importance of accurate propagation and efficient computation in simulations, and we provide insights into developing improved numerical methods for biomolecular simulations. Additionally, we provide implementations of the methods tested in this study as highly performant, tightly integrated modules within the Amber toolkit. This research aims to stimulate dialogue among experts in the field and encourage the creation of specialized numerical frameworks that can match the performance of traditional force fields like AMBER. This initiative is reflected in the recently developed Amber18 framework, which features several numerical methods, including Newton-Krylov, and showcases the potential for bespoke numerical solvers to elevate the overall performance of biomolecular simulations. This study is a part of a larger project centered on the development of highly performant numerical methods for biomolecular simulations, with a focus on solving the alanine dipeptide challenge. This project is an open research effort, and all methods tested in this study are available as highly optimized modules within the Amber18 toolkit. This development aims to spark dialogue among experts in the field and encourage the creation of customized numerical frameworks that can provide exceptional performance, matching that of traditional force fields like AMBER, and has inspired the creation of Amber18. Researchers have discovered gravitationally wave signals originating from merging black hole and neutron star systems using the LIGO detector. These discoveries have sparked interest in studying binary black hole and neutron star systems within their surrounding accretion disks, particularly in dense star clusters. Such studies are complicated by the high computational requirements but recent advances in computational power have made it possible to run large-scale simulations involving multiple interacting bodies. This study employs such powerful computers to run a series of binary black hole simulations within dense star clusters by incorporating the effects of gravitational waves and their interactions with surrounding matter. The researchers focused on initially fast-orbiting binary black holes with a high likelihood of producing gravitational waves in the frequency range detectable by LIGO. The simulations revealed a significant impact of the accretion disk on the binary black holes, with the disk's viscosity playing a crucial role in accelerating the stars around it. As a result, the binary black holes experienced an additional slowing down due to gravitational interactions with the accelerated stars, leading to a broader orbital period distribution than previously predicted. Interestingly, this effect increased the likelihood of detecting these binary black holes with LIGO, especially in smaller clusters, by as much as a factor of five due to their increased probability of producing gravitational waves within the desired frequency range. Furthermore, the simulations showed that LIGO could detect these binary black holes at a greater distance, up to 0.32 parsecs, which would significantly increase the detector's detection capacity. Additionally, the researchers found that the probability of observing two binary black holes with producing gravitational waves within the same LIGO detection window increased by more than five times due to their broader distribution of orbital periods, making it possible to detect multiple gravitational wave signals originating from the same binary black hole system within a relatively short period of time, i.e., within 20 days. The study's findings demonstrated the capability of LIGO to detect binary black holes that produce gravitational waves within the desired frequency range, even in dense star clusters, and highlighted the potential for discovering multiple gravitational waves originating from the same binary black hole system, a phenomenon that could provide valuable insights into the behavior of these cosmic systems. We have already established the correctness of our implementation by verifying that it meets the requirements for exponential stability. Here, we delve into a modified version of the system, characterized by unstable orbits on the edges without elasticity, and demonstrate that the original system exhibits asymptotic stability. We have developed a novel method to determine the exponential stability of closed orbits on graph domains. This method is grounded in the concept of reduced dimensionality, and is distinct from earlier approaches that relied on the diagonalizability of the reduced system. We have successfully applied this method to show the exponential stability of two specific systems: one defined on a star-shaped graph with non-elastic edges, and another on a weighted star-shaped graph. Both of these systems encompass dynamic systems on graph domains. We have also established the condition for exponential stability along the central node of a general star-shaped graph. Lastly, we have validated our method by comparing it to numerical simulations. This comparison has been extended to systems with closed orbits of both quadratic and cubic nature. Lastly, we have formally defined the concept of uniform exponential stability for closed orbits on graph domains and successfully applied this definition to systems from the literature. This study delves into the acoustic characteristics of a novel adhesive called 
Stycast 1090SI, considering both its isolated and adhered states to a widely
used acoustic material, PMMA. Researchers examined the impedance and attenuation
properties of Stycast 1090SI in comparison to PMMA, using a combination of 
ultrasound and X-ray micro-computer tomography on multiple samples. Two major
findings emerged - that the adhesive's impedance matches that of PMMA and that 
its attenuation pattern resembles that of PMMA, with a notable exception being 
air bubbles within the adhesive layer. Additionally, researchers monitored 
over time the changes in acoustic characteristics of PMMA when bonded with a thin 
layer of Stycast 1090SI, observing little alteration, and also investigated 
the impact of incorporating small glass beads into the adhesive, discovering 
they significantly reduce the adhesive's impedance and attenuation. Models 
derived from these experiments are also presented, along with potential applied 
scenarios for this type of adhesive in acoustic phased arrays and tissue-mimicking 
phantoms. Researchers believe their results will contribute meaningfully to the 
development and testing of medical ultrasonic technologies.

This research extends traditional concepts of node importance from single-layer networks to multilayer networks, with specific focus on applications involving traffic monitoring. A novel framework is introduced, where inter-layer constraints are accounted for to calculate weighted degree centrality, with initial testing showing its effectiveness on real-world data. The framework's performance is evaluated under varying conditions of noise in traffic data, with both centralized and decentralized algorithms proposed for implementation on large scales. Overall, this study provides a foundation for further research on multilayer network analysis and its potential uses in traffic monitoring and related fields. Due to its general applicability, the method can be adapted for other domains with similar network structures. The code developed is openly accessible online. Despite its potential, the method has not been fully tested on very large datasets or real-world, life-changing applications. We employed full-scale tight-binding modeling and lattice parameters from first-principle calculations to examine the electronic properties of cubanite. Our techniques revealed that cubanite's distinct properties, including stable charges and ferromagnetic ordering, can be explained by its unique electron structure, which is a result of mixed valence and the presence of an orbital triequivocity state. These features result from localized $5d$ orbital interactions and result in the presence of a charge gap and a heavy fermion state at the Fermi level. Mott-Hubbard charge gaps were ruled out based on our analysis of the correlation between bond lengths and charge valence. Additionally, our analysis of the crystal field and spin-hammer and spin-orbit interactions confirmed the presence of a heavy fermion state, and suggested that it may be responsible for the material's ferromagnetic behavior. Our study provides a theoretical framework that can be applied to other mixed-valence compounds, and highlights the potential of cubanite as a suitable platform for studying heavy fermion physics. Our findings are consistent with experimental data, and contribute to a deeper understanding of the material's magnetic properties and chemical stability.

Inventive Ventilator Reconfiguration for Single-Unit Operation: A Mathematical Approach A novel method of converting a ventilator for individual patient ventilation is presented, enabling a single ventilator to serve multiple patients with customized tidal volumes using a specific ventilator setting. Initially, we developed a mathematical model to determine the optimal ventilator setting for a given tidal volume in both volume-controlled and pressure-controlled modes. Now, we're investigating the opposite problem – how to find the optimal tidal volume for a specific ventilator setting. This problem has practical applications, such as patients being ventilated using a shared ventilator with adjustable settings to match their breathing needs. To address this problem, we examined the ventilator's operating curve and identified key parameters that influence tidal volume. A mathematical analysis reveals that these parameters follow a specific spatial arrangement, indicating that the ventilator's operating state is defined by a point on a curve that relates to the shape of the patient's breathing curve. However, this relationship is not causal, and further research is needed to fully understand the ventilator's dynamics. In the context of shared ventilation, we propose a method using the ventilator's operating curve to estimate the optimal tidal volume for a given setting, and this approach could also be applied to other medical devices that involve interacting with biological systems. While our analysis focuses on a specific type of ventilator, the method is versatile and can be adapted to any device with a similar operating characteristic. In the context of the current COVID-19 pandemic, this work has implications for using existing ventilators to treat more patients with COVID-19 patients' breathing characteristics. Recently, attention-based methods have gained popularity in medical image segmentation due to their ability to focus on relevant image areas. However, these models often face challenges with tumor initialization and visibility variability. To address these issues, this study proposes Dilated Dense Attention Unet, a model that combines dense attention with spatial dilation. The model leverages attention mechanisms across multiple scales and spatial regions, prioritizing relevant image areas over others. It is particularly effective in handling partial tumor visibility and can efficiently handle esophageal tumor segmentation on CT scans, as demonstrated by its performance on the ESOP-1 dataset. The evaluation shows a high Dice similarity coefficient of 0.8751 along with excellent initialization and visibility variability results, showcasing its potential for clinical applications. Moreover, this study emphasizes the benefits of dense attention in medical image segmentation and suggests it as a viable alternative to conventional attention-based methods. The code and models developed as part of this research are available online for further exploration and application in other medical image segmentation contexts.

Real-time formation evaluation in real-time mode requires highly efficient formation evaluation algorithms. Due to the complex nature of radial basis function interpolation, traditional methods like explicit formulae are not suitable for real-time applications. This paper proposes an innovative approach, LM-EnRML, which utilizes an interior method and an efficient learning technique to create a highly efficient and precise interpolation method for real-time formation evaluation. This method demonstrates over 50 times faster computation speed compared to an industry-standard method and shows no noticeable differences in accuracy. Additionally, LM-EnRML can handle large well logs with minimal memory usage, making it an ideal solution for modern high-resolution well logs. Furthermore, this paper explores enhanced learning techniques, such as gradient descent, as a means to further improve computation speed while maintaining accuracy. The results of this research make it an excellent candidate for future formation evaluation applications that require even faster computation speeds. The source code for this paper is publicly available online. 

Also, this paper's research is relevant to various other applications that involve interpolating large datasets with a non-linear method, such as power-law decay. The speedup achieved by LM-EnRML can benefit other research and industries that need to quickly interpolate large datasets. 

To achieve these efficient computation speeds, LM-EnRML leverages an interior method with an efficient learning technique that utilizes mean squared errors to converge quickly. The method begins with an initial guess at the interpolation points, then iteratively refines it until it reaches the optimal solution. This approach allows LM-EnRML to handle large well logs with minimal memory usage. 

While the results of this paper demonstrate no noticeable accuracy differences with an industry-standard method, the research also explores the potential for further improving computation speeds using additional learning techniques, such as training the method with actual well log data rather than a simulated dataset. The potential for these methods to be applied to other datasets that involve large-scale, non-linear interpolation is also highlighted. The publicly available code for this research includes a means to measure the accuracy and computation speed of LM-EnRML, as well as its memory usage, for any given dataset. This code can be used by other researchers as a starting point for adapting LM-EnRML to other applications.

This study seeks to explore the potential performance gains of named entity recognition (NER) by incorporating corpus-level knowledge into model training. To achieve this, we propose using a multi-task learning approach, where NER is trained on top of already existing semantic tasks such as part-of-speech tagging, noun chunking, NER, NER with limited annotations, and corpus-level tasks like language modeling. We conducted a comprehensive experiment involving 17 NER tasks from the CoNLL-2002, CoNLL-2003, and i2b2 datasets on English and Chinese datasets. Our findings demonstrate that, when training from scratch on very small annotation sets, a well-chosen corpus-level task can raise NER performance by a significant 1.5-2.5% F-score on English and 1.2-2.4% on Chinese. A novel approach called Localization via Compressive Sensing (LCS) has shown promise, employing compressed sensor readings to identify node positions. Although previous studies had explored various compression techniques and sensing protocols, the ideal performance of LCS remained uninvestigated. This study tackles this limitation by creating a range-free LCS framework and implementing ideal simulations to evaluate its performance. Specifically, it investigates the ideal accuracy of its algorithm and confirms its scalability by analyzing the ideal performance at both small and large dataset sizes. While several evaluation metrics for single-language tasks refine results and ensure consistency, there is a lack of standardized evaluation metrics for multilingual tasks. To validate the E-ZMEP protocol, we conduct various experiments involving leading multilingual models and datasets, with notable findings including the notable performance disparities between models when evaluating tasks in languages that have been previously encountered versus those that have not. Our work offers a comprehensive framework for evaluating the multilingual capabilities of NLP models and provides significant insights into their effectiveness and efficiency. The growing popularity of computer vision tools like captioning, retrieved-by-sentence, and object detection makes them a crucial component for mobile applications. These powerful tools are now accessible to a wider audience through mobile webpages, allowing for seamless, visually-driven user interfaces. However, one significant drawback of mobile browsing is the difficulty users face when navigating through search results due to confusing interface layouts, making it hard for visually impaired users to access information easily. 

To address this challenge, we propose MobileScannable, an innovative approach that leverages computer vision to describe search results, enabling visually impaired users to navigate search results more efficiently and accurately. By employing a deep learning algorithm known as spatial fusion-based stream, mobile web developers can train models to generate human-like descriptions of webpages based on their layout, content, and ability to recognize interactive elements such as buttons and navigation bars. 

A user study consisting of 30 visually impaired participants revealed a notable improvement in user performance and overall satisfaction when using MobileScannable, particularly in locating specific buttons and navigating through search results. Notably, our research demonstrates the potential for computer vision tools to enhance accessibility features on mobile devices, showcasing a unique solution that can be integrated with existing screen readers to provide a more comprehensive accessibility solution. The development of MobileScannable also contributes to the advancement of visual-to-text generation, a relatively underexplored field with numerous possibilities for future innovation. 

To facilitate the community's access to this research, we are releasing the dataset and model associated with MobileScannable, allowing for the comparison of our approach against other captioning methods in this domain. Our study serves as a foundation for the development of more advanced computer vision tools and accessibility solutions, with opportunities for collaboration and further exploration along this path. 

Lastly, we would like to emphasize that to achieve meaningful improvements in accessibility, more robust and practical guidelines are necessary to ensure that visual elements serve a purpose beyond mere aesthetics, prioritizing the needs of both users and developers.

To accurately calculate the energy loss functions of TaO by using the dielectric function of Ta, with consideration of local field effects and spin-orbit coupling, a robust method is needed to efficiently determine dielectric function components. This method involves using the Feynman linear response technique for its ability to incorporate influential factors like local field effects and spin-orbit coupling. Although this method can account for collective behavior in electrons, it requires a significant computational time. To make it more practical for computational simulations, the Feynman linear response method needs to be modified by utilizing the Boltzmann equation and relaxing the assumption of a steady state. This modification, known as the time-dependent linear response method, is based on the assumption that the system starts from a state of equilibrium and allows the calculation of time-dependent dielectric function components. As a result, this method can be used to simulate the temporal evolution of electrons in materials experiencing optical excitations. In this paper, we describe this method in detail and demonstrate its efficiency by applying it to the computation of energy loss functions of TaO. For comparison, the results are also presented alongside the outcomes of other computational methods commonly employed for such computations. Finally, a discussion is held on how the shape and position of spectral loss features correlate with experimental data obtained via electron energy loss spectroscopy. Additionally, the importance of considering local field effects and spin-orbit coupling in the computation of energy loss functions is highlighted through comparisons with simplified models that disregard these factors. To further validate this method, a comparison is made with ab initio results obtained via the random phase approximation within the time-dependent density functional theory. It is found that, for TaO, considerations of local field effects are essential while spin-orbit coupling can be considered less significant. On the other hand, the failure to consider local field effects leads to incorrect interpretation of experimental data obtained via electron energy loss spectroscopy. The phenomenon known as "The Big Sort" suggests that in highly partisan areas, extremes are given a freer rein to spread their views. This notion is explored in the context of online misinformation spread among users in geographically segregated regions, indicating that extremes are given greater opportunity to disseminate false information and profit from it. Additionally, an examination of public figures who spread misinformation reveals that these individuals are often given more leverage to spread false information and profit from it in highly partisan areas. Furthermore, research shows that users in areas given to extremes have a higher tendency to spread the very same misinformation and profit from it, suggesting a form of online contagion. This phenomenon is found to be at least partially attributable to the greater exposure users in areas given to extremes have to false information, as well as the social norms that emerge in these areas, normalizing the dissemination of misinformation. Lastly, policy interventions and potential solutions to mitigate the spread of online misinformation in these areas are proposed. These solutions include limiting the dissemination of false information by influential users and promoting media literacy. A possible empirical strategy to test these findings is also outlined. This research provides a initial framework for examining the interplay between geographical segregation and the spread of online misinformation, and can be further developed through empirical testing and theoretical advancements. To explore the underlying concepts of speech during teaching, we designed an experiment where participants were asked to teach fellow students a series of simple tasks using only speech, with the learners' primary source of information being the audio recordings of the teachers. We gathered a diverse group of 30 teaching pairs and analyzed the speech recordings from both the teachers and the learners. Our research revealed that the concepts conveyed through speech during teaching are influenced by various factors such as the type of demonstration, type of audio instructions, type of subtasks, and errors made during the process. Additionally, we discovered significant differences in the clusters of these concepts based on the demonstration method (visual or kinesthetic) and the presence of errors. Moreover, we found notable variations in the clusters of these concepts during tasks that require physical manipulation versus those that are more abstract. Our research also demonstrated that using audio instructions generates new concepts related to sound and tone. Furthermore, we observed distinct patterns in the clusters of these concepts during subsequent subtasks, indicating that the learner's understanding evolves over time. To facilitate future research, we are releasing the dataset and the experimental design associated with our study. This dataset offers a valuable resource for investigating the complex dynamics of speech during teaching and can contribute to the development of more effective artificial teaching methods. This research introduces an original algorithm to generate ordered trees of any degree, either specified individually or in the form of a general degree distribution. The algorithm we developed efficiently and accurately creates ordered trees to match given outdegree patterns. Unlike prior methods, our algorithm does not limit outdegrees to zero or assume a specific degree distribution, making it a more versatile tool for generating ordered trees. We demonstrate the benefits of this approach by applying it to a critical problem of ranking query results for a particular type of database configuration. Our solution employs the novel algorithm to generate low-ARO trees, a specific type of ordered tree. Additionally, we show how to extend our ranking technique to support multiple query types being ranked together. This is achieved by constructing a general degree distribution from individual outdegrees and generating corresponding low-ARO trees. Several concrete examples illustrate the algorithm's performance and flexibility. A software implementation of the algorithm is now available online. 

Keywords: ordered trees, algorithm, degree distribution, specification, generation, low-ARO trees, database, query ranking, ARO property.

Specifically, these equations play a crucial role in calculating the optimal surface configurations that minimize the constraint-defined volume within given volume boundaries, where the surface is subject to influence by an external force. Notably, both of these 'Chaplygin-type' problems can be solved through the application of Euler-Arnold equations, and the corresponding Hamilton-Arnold equations govern the dynamics of these surface configurations. According to General Relativity, a massive, quiet object should create detectable gravitational waves in the surrounding space. Unaware of this phenomenon until recently, scientists can now utilize gravitational microlensing to search for hidden masses. Employing the enRoute dataset from the Micro-Lensing Observation Experiment (MOLE-2), along with additional data from the Moon and a dataset from the Planet Finder, researchers established a sensitive detection range of approximately 13,000 light-years (8,000 parsecs) for detecting an unseen Earth-mass object over 90% of the sky. Under more constrained viewing conditions, the detection range shrinks to 8,000 light-years (4,800 parsecs). This study demonstrates the potential of microlensing to identify dark matter components consisting of compact objects, and given future advancements in observational technology, a search radius of up to 20,000 light-years (12,000 parsecs) will become feasible. Furthermore, researchers propose several methods to enhance the sensitivity of such searches, including the use of space-based observations and the analysis of high-magnification events, which could lead to significant breakthroughs in the investigation of massive compact objects and dark matter in our galaxy. Until such observations become available, researchers believe that a thorough search for hidden masses in the Milky Way will remain an interesting and rewarding area of study. The established sensitivity to a 1 Earth-mass object at 13,000 light-years (8,000 parsecs) over 90% of the sky allows for some inferences about possible dark matter components in our galaxy, consisting of objects similar in mass to the Earth. According to this study, our galaxy's dark matter component consisting of compact objects with a mass two orders of magnitude greater than the Earth-mass object detected in VVV8835 would be in the range of 10^10 to 10^11 Earth-mass objects. Given that such objects would generate gravitational waves with characteristics similar to those of binary black hole mergers, researchers believe that the study of gravitational waves will be capable of identifying up to 10^10 Earth-mass objects in our galaxy by the end of the next decade. Additionally, with the use of data from various gravitational wave detectors, such as LIGO, VIRGO, and the planned DECIGO, scientists may discover as much as 50% of these objects through a global network search by the end of the next decade, significantly expanding the initial findings presented in this study by a factor of over 100. Furthermore, this proposal goes beyond conventional bilingual translation memory methods by expanding the scope to multiple languages. Experimental results indicate significant improvements over baseline models and even outperform some data-Augmented machine translation methods on various low-resource settings and the Semeval-2012 task 3.1. Moreover, an in-depth analysis into the quantitative and qualitative aspects of the produced translations reveals the actual translation benefits derived from the cross-lingual memory retriever. This paper investigates the Yamabe flow with initial data under certain non-concentration estimates and establishes the existence of weak solutions with bounded energy through an approach utilizing the Strichartz estimate. Additionally, the paper explores obstructions to developing singularities in solutions of the Yamabe flow on Riemannian manifolds with a negative Ricci curvature. A key aspect of the analysis involves demonstrating the existence of solutions that evolve into flat hyperbolic planes in the optimal regularity class, given specific initial conditions – in particular, this is shown for initial data consisting of a pair of expanding solitons under certain concentration and alignment assumptions. The study further reveals that such solutions on the optimal regularity space develop singularities in a finite time, with a rate dictated by a non-degenerate equation of motion for their centers. The primary obstacle in finetuning models for a new task after initial training is dealing with rare demonstration samples. To overcome this limitation, we develop a method that incorporates element-wise differences and categorical representations to create a novel metric learning framework called Contrastive Learning of Sub-paths (CLSP). In CLSP, we leverage pre-trained models and modify their outputs to generate embedding vectors for input samples and category labels. These generated vectors are processed by applying a grid pattern to the embedding space, allowing us to craft a meaningful contrastive loss function. We show that our proposed framework surpasses existing methods like support vector machines and Prototypical Networks even with just one shot per class and demonstrate its practical applications by successfully adapting a language model to improve dialog understanding and sentiment analysis on the SuperGLUE benchmark, achieving exceptional results on the low-shot learning Porter Dataset, and successfully adapting a medical diagnosis model known as BioMedNLP for low-shot medical diagnosis. These outstanding results prove that our proposed method is an exceptionally powerful tool for a model to adapt to new tasks with limited demonstration samples. However, when we increase the number of demonstration samples, our method no longer has a significant advantage over other methods. Additionally, we find that the initial training of models has a more significant impact on their performance in low-shot learning than previously thought, with pre-trained models that have not been fine-tuned on a large dataset like the Generalizated Corpus of Common Sense (GCC) performing much better than those that have been fine-tuned on the same dataset, despite both models being equally suitable for our CLSP. Moreover, we discover that the benefit of using the contrastive loss function in our proposed framework is most apparent in demonstration samples that are similar to the initial training dataset but differ from the actual test dataset, with our method producing models that are 15% more effective in adapting to new demonstration samples that are similar to the training dataset but differ from the actual test dataset. Despite the effectiveness of these models, extracting specific, individualized preferences remains a significant challenge. To tackle this, we propose the Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module, a innovative module designed for learning preferences within a multi-task framework. This module allows the extraction of specific preferences from general aspects and has been successfully applied to two popular applications: collaborative recommendation and dialogue response generation. In the former, GAPE was incorporated into an existing model, and the resulting system achieved superior performance in recommending diverse and personalized items. In the latter, GAPE was used to develop a neural knowledge diagram, which enabled accurate and precise delivery of precise information. Experimental results validate the feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed GAPE module in learning individualized preferences. The effectiveness of machine learning models in processing MRI scans relies heavily on the quality of their training data. Yet, real-world applications often involve evaluating these models on unseen MRI images, which necessitates some degree of tolerance to varying training datasets. In this study, we explored the impact of different training datasets on the performance of models, evaluating their robustness to new, untested MRI data. We used three distinct datasets - BrainMRI, CancerDetection, and Skull-Brain Segmentation - consisting of publicly accessible MRI datasets, which were utilized to train and test several popular deep learning models, including U-Net, FC-Network, and ResNet. Our research revealed significant performance disparities between models trained on their own datasets and those trained on other datasets, with an average difference of 13.45% in classification accuracy and 24.75% in regression score. Nonetheless, our findings also indicated some models' ability to adapt to new, unseen MRI data to some extent, with a maximum increase in BrainMRI Brain score of 26.29% when evaluated on data outside their training dataset. This phenomenon was observed to be model-dependent, with some models exhibiting greater robustness than others. We hypothesized that this model variability might stem from their differing design features, including parallel depth and non-linear activation functions, which facilitate adaptation to new MRI data to some degree, even if only statistically significant. Our research offers a comprehensive evaluation of the performance of various machine learning models when faced with new, unseen MRI data, as well as the potential for them to be used in real-world applications involving unknown MRI images. Additionally, we made the training and testing datasets, along with the associated code, freely available for use by other researchers in the field. This resource is poised to help researchers make more informed decisions when selecting models for specific MRI tasks and might ultimately contribute to the development of more robust models capable of adapting to new MRI data. This, in turn, could pave the way for the widespread adoption of machine learning models in high-stakes medical applications, fueled in part by the potential for them to be trained on existing datasets rather than being retrained from scratch for each new task. This approach could also be extended to other machine learning models and datasets, giving them a greater capacity to adapt to new, unseen data, which could be crucial in other fields as well. This paper introduces a framework that broadens the scope of network-based multi-agent optimization problems, addressing issues of incomplete and biased data within dynamic network systems. Based on time series data and historical network information, the proposed method determines optimal target values for network nodes, even when faced with missing or inaccurate data. The approach is designed for flexible application to various optimization objectives and network types. Theoretical convergence and stability of the method are proven, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through simulation examples involving different types of networks and data characteristics. The algorithm is also tested on real-world traffic data from the city of Pavia, Italy. The source code is available online at a corresponding repository. 

Keywords: Network optimization, time series analysis, dynamic systems, multi-agent systems, optimization algorithms, traffic management.

Although some studies have examined memory management techniques, little research has been done on file systems tailored to numinous memory management.  Our work involves developing a file system called NOVA-relaxed for NVMM and testing its performance on various applications.  To evaluate its effectiveness, we created a benchmark consisting of five benchmarks, including a new Java benchmark, and observed significant improvements in application performance when using NOVA-relaxed with Optane DC PMMs, particularly for small, persistent writes.  Our results demonstrate that NOVA-relaxed can achieve a 5-30 times speedup and reduce the processor utilization by 15-60% compared to the original ISO-Relaxed.  Our data also shows that NOVA-relaxed can minimize memory contamination caused by small persistent writes, lowering memory contamination by 20-80%.  Our research confirms that a well-designed file system can produce notable gains in application performance and memory reliability. As social learning theories, both the Motivation Dynamics (MDD) model and the DeGroot learning model have been influential in studying how individuals form opinions through interactions from a single common source. This study takes the MDD model into a multi-agent realm and incorporates a novel variant of the best-response function to examine its application to a prolonged rendezvous problem. In this environment, agents move dynamically, sharing their current positions and updating their aspirations in a way that ensures mutual approach. The model's multi-agent variant reveals that even with asymmetric, non-transitive preferences and incomplete information about other agents' preferences, derived equilibrium play can lead to the efficient discovery of a mutually acceptable action, thereby solving the rendezvous problem. Furthermore, our results also demonstrate that the introduction of biased learning among agents can promote swift convergence to their desired destination. In addition, our results provide a critical test for the consistency of the recent multi-agent learning in networks model. For the classical finite Coxeter group Bn, we examine the exchange laws pertaining to its generalized standard elements, which we can express in terms of the Coxeter length and descent configuration. We establish a clear, recursive framework for identifying the exchange laws, and demonstrate that the overall structure is governed by a simple, yet fundamental principle. We also develop a direct method for determining the exchange laws based on the extra edge present in the generalized standard elements of type Bn. We are able to derive explicit descriptions and patterns for specific subgroups within Bn, particularly those related to the symmetric group Sn and the dihedral group Dn+1, and provide a thorough analysis of the standard elements and their associated structures. Moreover, we introduce a new notion of weak ascent positions and a corresponding weak descent set, which we found to be closely linked to the generalized standard elements of type Bn. We are also able to establish a direct connection between the weak descent set of a permutation and its Coxeter length, and provide a clear, concise classification of the permutations with minimal weak descent point. This groundbreaking work is a significant extension of earlier research on the standardized elements of finite Coxeter groups, and its innovative concepts and techniques will surely pave the way for further advancements in this field. We are confident that the sophisticated, yet elegantly simple frameworks derived from this investigation will prove invaluable in future explorations of Coxeter groups and their extensive applications.
