In order to create precise and varied entity representations for recommendations, we propose a novel framework that combines both structural and contextual aspects. This framework uses a method that we call "Unified MultiAspect Entity Learning" which incorporates multiple facets of entity information and develops customized representation learning techniques for different types of entities. By applying this approach, we designed and executed two specific recommendation tasks with outstanding results. Firstly, we developed an integrated solution for both personalized search and recommendation, using our entity representation learning method to achieve top-ranked performance on the MSLP dataset. Secondly, we created individual models addressing specific entity representation challenges on the ALiME dataset, focusing on tail entities and incorporating customer feedback. These models demonstrated exceptional entity retrieval capacity in our experiments. Overall, our proposed framework yields high-quality, diverse entity representations, ready for direct use in recommendation and search applications. This leads to better entity recommendations and search results, with both quality and diversity being critically important factors. Additionally, our approach offers more flexible and efficient entity learning, eliminating the need for additional retrieval methods in search applications. Moreover, our method achieves enhanced entity representations with both richer semantics and better generalization, particularly for low-frequency entities. This is accomplished through the use of a customized loss function, semi-supervised learning, and a highly effective sampling technique. Lastly, our approach provides a higher degree of interoperability and compatibility with existing recommendation architectures, enabling a seamless integration of our entity representations into existing applications. This is showcased through our successful deployment of this framework in a real-world e-commerce application. This application, which we call "Personalized Recommendation Portal", has been successfully deployed on the Alibaba Group's frontend website and has been adopted by over 1 billion users globally. This portal has led to notable increases in both recommendation click-through rates and customer satisfaction. Additionally, our approach has been adopted by multiple other Alibaba Group applications, also yielding significant gains. This success has motivated our ongoing research in Unified MultiAspect Entity Learning, which we believe has immense potential to create a new generation of high-quality, customizable entity representations, ready for direct use in recommendation and search applications. This potential is backed by our promising results, which we are sharing with the research community in an open-ended framework, inviting further innovations and improvements. This framework is now available on GitHub at https://alibabaingroup.github.io/UMELE.html. To address delays in kidney transplantation, we're proposing a novel framework that adapts the Multi-Armed Bandit theory to consider an unwanted state - incompatibility. In this approach, best arm identification is redefined as selecting the most compatible kidney for a given patient. Our framework leverages both discounted rewards and switching costs to create dynamic best arm identification algorithms. To evaluate these algorithms, we develop a simulation based on real-world transplantation data. Interestingly, our results show that simply accounting for incompatibility as a state variable significantly enhances decision-making efficiency. Moreover, we find that complex transition dynamics and state-dependent costs have minimal impact on the transverse temporal efficiency gains. Moreover, our findings indicate that sophisticated algorithms consistently converge to optimal performance over time. Finally, we explore the practical implications of our findings for improving the kidney transplantation matching process. Our framework is highly versatile and can be applied to other compatibility-driven problems. To facilitate replication and advancement of our work, we're making both our framework and data set openly available. By addressing the incompatibility challenge, we believe our approach holds significant potential to accelerate life-saving transplantations. Alongside our methodological contributions, we're also introducing two new concepts - time-wise and efficient optimal policies - that have value beyond our specific application to kidney transplantation. Ultimately, our goal is to empower data-driven transplantation policies that minimize delays and boost transplant success rates. To achieve this, we'll continue to build on our framework and explore more innovative algorithms. By doing so, we aim to make a lasting, life-changing impact on transplantation practices worldwide. Our code is available online at https://github.com/ahmedossamhan/Kidney-Transplant-Bandit. We employ the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization formula to analyze a one-dimensional interacting Dirac model. By showing the equivalence of these two methods, we derive a mean-field approximation for the interacting Dirac model using a self-dual variable. This self-dual approach allows us to investigate different mean-field theories, including ferromagnetic, broadening, and interaction mean-field theories. By translating the one-dimensional interacting Dirac model into a spin-less fermion model with an external magnetic field, we can solve the self-dual equation exactly. This exact solution represents a major step in demonstrating the stability of Nambu fermion condensates mentioned in earlier studies. Furthermore, we establish that the interaction mean-field theory is capable of describing a phase transition from a normal to a Nambu condensate state. This theoretical framework can also be applied to other one-dimensional interacting models, such as the interacting Majorana Fermi oil model. By examining the interplay between different symmetries in one-dimensional interacting systems, we propose novel types of mean-field transition phenomena. Additionally, we propose a new classification of one-dimensional interacting systems based on their symmetry properties and discuss the feasibility of realizing these models experimentally. Some of the proposed models can be related to actual experiments, such as an experiment involving carbon nanotubes. We anticipate that our analysis will contribute to a deeper understanding of one-dimensional interacting systems involving Majorana fermions and neutral fermion systems. An analysis of top quark spin asymmetry in events featuring two leptons and missing energy is presented, based on proton-proton collisions at 8 TeV and 13 TeV. Events are excluded that display an exclusive hadronic pattern, characterized by an isolated photon, three hadrons, and missing energy. Events that pass these criteria are simulated using different scenarios and their spin asymmetries are calculated. As a control, events that fail these criteria but contain a misidentified anti-lepton are also simulated and their asymmetries are calculated to account for background. As a result, events that pass the criteria and those that fail it but contain a misidentified anti-lepton are subtracted to obtain the final asymmetry value. The measured asymmetry at 8 TeV is 0.24 ± 0.08, which is compatible with the standard model prediction of 0.44. An analogous analysis is carried out at 13 TeV, however it reveals a discrepancy of 1.5σ with the standard model prediction. This analysis utilizes approximately 19 inverse femtobarns of data at 8 TeV and 35 inverse femtobarns at 13 TeV.

We investigated the temperature dependence of LaNiO$_3$ relaxing components in (LaNiO$_3$)/((LaNiO$_3$)/LaAlO$_3$) superlattices using impedance and dielectric relaxation measurements. The results showed a varying relaxing component across different LaNiO$_3$ thicknesses, with an underlying symmetry revealed by in-plane resistivity and relaxation time measurements. A theoretical model was then employed to analyze the data and the results indicated that the surface conductive channel's thickness can be modified by changing LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness. The model also facilitated the extraction of bulk and surface relaxation times from experimental data, with the latter displaying a notable temperature dependence. Our findings provide insights into the transport mechanisms of LaNiO$_3$ and may have implications for understanding the electronic phenomena in other perovskite oxides. Additionally, our results highlight the potential uses of (LaNiO$_3$)/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices as model systems for investigating two-dimensional transport physics.

Yet, despite significant progress in recent years, we remain limited in our understanding of how humans develop the ability to share thoughts and maintain conversations. Our approach involves leveraging the existing cognitive architectures that underpin theory of mind and incorporating a set of foundational knowledge that can facilitate logical connections between concepts, including both the lexical and lexical-free forms. We introduce MG-GLAM, a novel code utilizing the Tree-PM method that efficiently handles N-body simulations on a massive scale. MG-GLAM is based on the Gadget code's legacy version and builds upon the code's previous iteration, MG-AMR. While maintaining the same performance boost from multi-level methods, MG-GLAM further increases computational speed by 10-fold and reduces memory consumption by 20%, primarily by optimizing mesh refinement strategies and simplifying code architecture. Recent research lies at the forefront of analyzing coupled dynamical systems, specifically those with multiple coexisting synchronized clusters. A central focus lies on developing tools to identify these clusters from a state vector, even when the system's structure is unknown. By applying a new method based on robust principal component analysis (RPCA), we can derive a method to determine the number of synchronized clusters by analyzing the rpca results and the eigenstructure of a robust covariance matrix. Specifically, the number of clusters can be determined as the difference between the number of non-zero eigenvalues obtained from rpca and those derived from an optimized total-least-squares method. We validate this new method on three examples: a system of coupled Mathieu equations with distinct and close clusters, a system of coupled Duffing equations with very close clusters, and a system of coupled harmonic oscillators with distinct and close clusters, using both numerical state vectors and actual experimental data. The new method is compared to two alternative methods on these examples. The designed tool is also useful for improving the performance of other cluster identification methods by filtering out unwanted cluster components. The benefits of this method are demonstrated on all three numerical examples. Moreover, we explore the relationship between the robust covariance matrix and the rpca results, and provide guidelines for adjusting rpca parameters. The designed method is implemented in a publicly accessible MATLAB toolbox. In this study, two-dimensional periodic networks with specific geometries are examined: a triadic lattice and a diamond lattice are both broken down into their fundamental components, with individual nodes representing local random walks in their respective lattices. Our research focuses on the dynamics of nearest-neighbor dimers within these lattices, exploring how their movement patterns differ from complete neighbor coverage. Our findings show that dimers follow a non-stationary self-avoiding walk on the triadic lattice and a stationary self-avoiding walk on the diamond lattice, with our results providing discrete-time formulas for the triadic and diamond lattices that differ from continuous-time formulas. These discrete-time formulas offer an alternative to established continuous-time formulas used in similar studies. Moreover, our results include an analysis of the triadic lattice with a larger Q-matrix and a diamond lattice with complete neighbor coverage. This research aims to contribute to a better comprehension of how the geometry of periodic networks influences the behavior of fundamental random walk components, with possible applications in modeling discrete-time processes on these networks. Additionally, our results may lead to a greater understanding of discrete-time random walks within these networks, with possible extensions to continuous-time random walks. This study also lays the groundwork for more in-depth analysis of discrete-time random walks on these networks, with possible connections to continuous-time random walks. If ultralight dark matter is coupled to neutrinos, it is probable that the interaction influenced the neutrino population in the early universe. As a result of this interaction, a portion of the dark matter could have been transferred to neutrinos, potentially affecting the cosmic lepton asymmetry. Since the neutrino sector's flavor differences arise from the interplay of their masses and a single collective phenomenon, the same factors that influence the neutrino collective behavior also impact the dark matter-neutrino system. Consequently, in the early universe, when the neutrino system experienced significant fluctuations in the bulk neutrino oscillations phenomenon, a substantial amount of dark matter could have been transferred to neutrinos, leading to a more complex cosmic neutrino chemistry and potentially affecting the primordial abundance of light elements like helium and lithium. Furthermore, in the present day, this interaction could result in a continuous monochromatic neutrino spectrum and a corresponding dark matter spectrum, leading to distinctive signatures in future neutrino and dark matter experiments. The effects of this interaction on the cosmic evolution could also result in a detectable imprint in the cosmic microwave background and large-scale structure, and in some scenarios, it could explain the observed small-scale structure. The most compelling scenario is realized when the dark matter mass is around $10^{-3}$eV, its coupling to neutrinos is approximately $10^{-14}$ per unit, and the present-day dark matter density is comprised of both the transferred and initial components. If true, this would provide a long-sought explanation for the cosmological neutrino mass scale observed in certain long-baseline neutrino experiments, and it could also offer a major breakthrough in our understanding of the dark matter and neutrino sectors. The most consequential consequence of coupling dark matter to neutrinos is the possibility that a portion of the dark matter in the universe could be composed of neutrinos, a factor that should be accounted for when interpreting future neutrino experiments and determine the total dark matter density, particularly when searching for dark matter annihilation or decay in neutrino detectors. Ultimately, this theory has not been entirely ruled out by existing constraints, and it is worth exploring further in order to determine its validity. The parameters that characterize this scenario can be probed with on-going and future experiments, such as: neutrino experiments (e.g. KBT and T2K); direct and indirect dark matter detection experiments (e.g. XENON1T and AMANDA); and experiments searching for dark matter decay (e.g. ADMX and SABRE).

Recently, Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) have gained significant interest as a powerful tool for designing distributed systems. However, as systems scale horizontally using microservices architecture, ensuring correctness and fault tolerance requires a comprehensive framework that can accommodate multiple data types and protocols. Unfortunately, existing custom solutions for combining multiple CRDTs often lead to fragmented knowledge and difficulties in understanding individual components. This paper introduces a modular, design-focused approach that categorizes Replicated Data Types (RDTS) into abstract modules, allowing developers to create custom combined CRDTs through structured composition. We apply this framework to devise three concrete combined CRDTs, including one renowned example, and make the framework's functionality verifiable via existing formal specifications. Moreover, our approach facilitates automated generation of specifications and protocol descriptions, making it easier to identify individual component behaviors and debug the system during development. By leveraging this framework's design-friendly interface, even a single engineer can design and test integrated CRDTs, contributing valuable expertise along the way. This approach was successfully implemented in the Scala programming language and is freely accessible at https://github.com/paragon-ic/rdt-combiner. Despite its practical utility, this research primarily addresses theoretical aspects of combined CRDTs and is compatible with existing formal specifications and proofs. Its innovative design-focused methodology is expected to pave the way for broader acceptance of CRDTs in industry settings. We also introduce a new, widely used example of a combined CRDT, referred to as 'CounterSet', which is derived from a well-known existing protocol and is suitable for horizontal scalability applications. CounterSet is available at https://github.com/paragon-ic/rdt-combiner/issues/1 and can be utilized as a best-practice example. To understand how protein sequences influence the appearance of phenotype-related single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), we used a method called proteinoetic mapping. This approach is based on the assumption that SNPs affect protein function through various mechanisms, including changes to protein structure, post-translational modification sites, and the ability to interact with other proteins or ligands. We used data from the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project and the Universal Protein Resource (Uniprot) to analyze 46 different human traits and found that, on average, about 50% of associated SNPs had some link to the protein sequence. However, the impact of these proteins varied greatly across different traits, with some proteins showing little effect and others with a significant influence. In addition, we found that most of these influenced proteins were linked to membrane-bound complexes and involved in signal transduction and transport. We also identified specific genes whose functions could be understood using our method and were related to important human diseases such as cancer, HIV, and SARS-CoV-2. Furthermore, we found that some of these genes had been difficult to study using other methods. By applying machine learning to our data, we were able to create a predictive model that could accurately determine the impact of proteins on the appearance of phenotype-related SNPs. We made our method and data publicly available in the Proteinoetic Mapping Portal. With this approach, researchers can now better understand the link between protein sequences, the proteins themselves, and the appearance of phenotype-related SNPs. By doing so, it may become possible to analyze the complex relationships between genotype, protein function, and phenotype more effectively. Researchers utilize radial velocity measurements to study wide binary star systems by analyzing the motion of the individual components. However, measuring the one-dimensional velocity dispersion, or the distribution of velocity within a system, is more complicated and typically requires a three-dimensional analysis. A newly proposed method develops a statistical approach to accurately determine velocity dispersion from a limited set of line velocities. This method's performance is evaluated on a simulated dataset consisting of 1000 wide binary systems with known velocity dispersion values. The simulations include various velocity distributions, line strength variations, and different observation lengths. The results show that the new approach yields superior outcomes compared to existing methods, especially when analyzing short observation periods. The most significant improvement comes from line velocities, which significantly enhances the accuracy of velocity dispersion measurements. The best-fitting velocity dispersion values correlate strongly with the true values, exhibiting a high R2 coefficient of 0.998. The new method also demonstrates robustness in dealing with data limitations, velocity field asymmetries, and binary system mass variations. Ultimately, this innovative technique has the potential to raise detection limits for one-dimensional velocity dispersion in wide binary systems from several kilometers per second to several tens of kilometers per second. This advancement is expected to expand the scope of this type of research. The model is now available for public use, providing a useful tool for studying wide binary systems and facilitating the interpretation of ongoing and future radial velocity survey data. The new algorithm is also capable of modeling multiple wide binary systems simultaneously, making it suitable for analysis of binary systems with interacting components. The algorithm is comprised of three key parts, including a line profile model, a binary system model, and a velocity distribution model. The line profile model incorporates various line strengths, effective temperature, and line velocity, while the binary system model accounts for the position of the component stars, their mass ratio, and the viewing angle. The velocity distribution model is based on the phase-space density of the broad distribution function, which is derived from an empirical flow-corrected distribution function. The algorithm is tested on existing public wide binary system data, and it is shown that it is capable of recovering the original parameters when simulated velocity spectra are analyzed. The algorithm can be employed to study binary systems with interacting components, and it is one potential method for distinguishing real binary systems from false positives in large radial velocity survey datasets. The code is included in the package's repository on GitHub, and it is available for public use. However, it is essential to note that the algorithm's performance may decline when analyzing systems with large velocity gradients or stellar interactions

The relationship between the polarization of low-frequency radio waves and the polarization properties of plasmas in the interplanetary medium near Earth has been investigated. Researchers analyzed data from various radio experiments, including broadband radio waves and extreme polarization radio waves, collected between 2000 and 2016. Their findings show a strong connection between the curvature of the radio waves and their polarization properties. Specifically, they found that the curvature of the waves is influenced by the strength of magnetic fields in the interplanetary medium, and that the polarization of the waves is affected by the curvature and strength of the fields. Further analysis indicated that the polarization of low-frequency radio waves is linked to the median fractional polarization of radio sources, and that this median fractional polarization increases with the strength of magnetic fields in the interplanetary medium. Notably, the researchers found that the polarization of low-frequency radio waves is highly correlated with the median fractional polarization of radio sources, and that this median fractional polarization of radio sources is linked to the strength of magnetic fields in the interplanetary medium, and thus to the level of solar wind turbulence, and ultimately to the strength of magnetic fields in the interplanetary medium, and thus to the curvature of the radio waves. This finding suggests that the polarization of low-frequency radio waves can be an indicator of the condition of the interplanetary medium. In graph theory, splitting vertices is a local transformation where a non-trivial vertex is replaced by two adjacent vertices and the edges connected to the original vertex are redirected to these new vertices. We investigate the application of this transformation to achieve planar drawings of bipartite graphs. Specifically, we analyze the minimum number of vertex splittings required to planarize an embedded bipartite graph, and we explore the implications of combining vertex splittings with edge splittings, a different type of transformation that shifts edges between adjacent vertices. We show that splitting vertices and edges in either order requires exactly n-1 splittings, where n represents the number of non-trivial vertices, under the assumption that the initial embedding is non-trivial. Furthermore, we demonstrate that using vertex splittings alone becomes essentially equivalent to using edge splittings alone for minimizing the number of planarizations, provided that the target graph has a specific property. Finally, we conjecture that a simpler procedure, successively splitting edges between adjacent vertices, achieves the optimal number of edge splittings for any bipartite graph, regardless of whether the graph is embedded or not. This conjecture is confirmed for certain special cases, including complete bipartite graphs and certain families of graphs characterized by specific structural properties. The proposed research provides a theoretical framework for understanding the application of splitting vertices and edges in graph planarization, a topic of ongoing practical relevance in graph visualization. The results described herein represent significant advances in our understanding of splitting vertices, a technique already shown to be useful in graph visualization, and they offer valuable new contributions to the broader study of graph planarity. To understand the influence of calibration on models dealing with data imbalance, we first analyze the relationships between classification accuracy, confusion, and real-valued scores.  Based on these findings, we develop a theoretical framework explaining how data imbalance affects the performance of models and is mitigated by calibration.  To support this theoretical framework, we conduct experiments involving multiple models, calibration methods, scenarios with class imbalance, and a comprehensive evaluation protocol.  The code for our evaluation protocol and theoretical framework is openly available online.  By leveraging our evaluation protocol and the insights provided by our analysis, we offer practical guidelines for selecting the best calibration method to address data imbalance issues.  Our experiments demonstrate that, depending on the nature of the data distribution, some calibration methods can either positively or negatively impact the performance of models, even when the data is not inherently balanced.  We show that temperature scaling and sigmoid calibration can be beneficial in specific scenarios, whereas lateral regularization and maximum a posteriori estimation can be beneficial in other scenarios.  We also found that the performance of models can benefit from these calibration methods, even when the data is seemingly well-balanced.  We believe that our evaluation protocol and the code related to our experiments will be useful for researchers evaluating the effectiveness of calibration methods in future studies.  We also propose a new metric, called confusion reduction, to evaluate the impact of calibration on the imbalance issue. Building upon his work, we have achieved a significant advancement by demonstrating that any knot diagram can be converted to a trefoil knot diagram utilizing only diagonal passes, which in turn can be untangled into a straight line using an advanced algorithm. Furthermore, we have found that combining diagonal passes with other types of moves enables the untangling of any knotted structure, which can be expressed as a trefoil knot diagram multiplied by an arbitrary number of crossings. This finding enables the application of Ooura's method to various knotted objects, which can be represented as torus knots on a three-dimensional sphere. This includes, for instance, knots located within proteins, which are represented as a three-dimensional sphere crossed with the real line. By utilizing this method, we have successfully untangled several complex knots found within proteins. In particular, we have found that the 'Grossman dimer' protein, which contains two intertwined trefoil knots, can be untangled into a straight line consisting of two separate polypeptide chains. Additionally, we have shown that any knotted substructure within proteins can be untangled into a straight line due to their ability to be converted into trefoil knots via diagonal passes, which can then be untangled into a straight line using an advanced algorithm. In systems that involve competing agents, where each agent has its own task to complete and can make a choice that affects the success of other agents, the agents must balance their self-interest with a degree of cooperation. The prevalence of automation in these critical systems highlights the need for a systematic approach to analyzing and guiding decision-making. The current study transforms decision-making into a stochastic control problem and addresses computational limitations by developing an approximate reinforcement learning solution using linear quadratic state-dependent controllers. The framework is versatile and can be applied to various scenarios, including those with diverse task distributions, and is evaluated using both simulation and real-world data, showing its ability to adapt quickly and efficiently. The advantages of this method are highlighted through comparison with both traditional decision-making approaches and alternative learning techniques. The study also provides the source code for an agent that demonstrates its effectiveness in a well-known competition scenario, known as the multi-agent linear quadratic regulatory problem, and the code can be customized for other applications. The code is available upon request. The approximate reinforcement learning solution features an impressive feature extraction ability and the study investigates this capability further. The approximate policy model and its underlying structure also raise several important research questions related to policy representation, induction principles, the role of correlations, credit assignment, option discovery, value function decomposition, gridded action spaces, state aggregation, cascaded architectures, hierarchical reinforcement learning, and the limits of generalization. The study has significant implications for the study of decision-making in complex, competitive, and dynamic systems, and it provides a suite of methods that can be applied to a wide range of multi-agent reinforcement learning problems. The most notable feature of this study is that it is accompanied by high-quality video recordings that can be viewed at the referenced arXiv page. The recordings showcase the agent's performance in various scenarios, including those with easy and challenging tasks, and they highlight the benefits of the approximate reinforcement learning solution, including quick adaptation and efficient decision-making. The recordings also demonstrate the prevalence of unexpected decision patterns that arise when the agent is placed in new situations, and they provide valuable insights into the complex interplay between value functions, policies, and the underlying dynamics of the system. The study is relevant to any research related to multi-agent reinforcement learning, approximate policy models, linear quadratic state-dependent controllers, computational neuroscience, complex systems, competition, cooperation, decision-making, generalization, gridded action spaces, hierarchical reinforcement learning, induction, option discovery, policy representation, state aggregation, and the value function decomposition of algorithms. This paper delves into the inherent vulnerabilities of privacy-preserving vertical federated learning (PFLL). Although current research on PFLL is burgeoning, existing studies have failed to scrutinize the security of these methods against curious and malicious data owners. Our investigation reveals that a comprehensive assessment of security in PFLL is both feasible and crucial. We probed the defenses of popular vertical federated learning protocols and uncovered distillation-based attacks on non-interlocking methods and data recovery attacks on methods that incorporate encryption. Furthermore, our findings showed that a sophisticated attack could compromise the privacy of both data owners and the server in interlocking protocols. We also developed a security framework for PFLL and proposed enhanced methods that incorporate negative sampling and multi-layer encryption to prevent privacy breaches. Empirical studies confirmed that our proposed methods can safeguard against the identified threats while achieving comparable performance to existing methods. Additionally, an in-depth analysis of the efficacy of negative sampling in preventing privacy breaches was conducted. To facilitate replication and advancement of our findings, we openly shared the code and datasets used in this study. Overall, our investigation emphasized the critical importance of security in PFLL and provided actionable insights for researchers and practitioners to ensure reliable adoption of these methods in real-world applications. This research will serve as a foundational benchmark for security assessments and developments in PFLL. Random Fourier Features (RFF) is an widely-adopted technique for efficiently reducing the dimensionality of kernels like the Gaussian kernel. Despite its success, RFF has a significant drawback: it requires a large number of dimensions to achieve optimal performance and often results in suboptimal predictions. In this study, we introduce Pseudo-Random Fourier Features, a novel approach that generates features with reduced dimensions, leading to improved performance. We demonstrate that PRFF outperforms RFF with lower dimensionality and achieve state-of-the-art results for polytime kernel methods, giving support to our framework through theoretical insights and empirical evidence. We also find that a straightforward application of our method can be improved by incorporating optimization techniques. Our method's clarity and effectiveness make it a valuable resource for the scientific community, and the code is available for replication at this link. 

This paper introduces Pseudo-Random Fourier Features (PRFF), a method that creates low-dimensional Fourier features with similar performance to Random Fourier Features (RFF). We show that using PRFF with lower dimensionality achieves better results than RFF and provide a theoretical analysis to support these findings. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in polynomial-time kernel methods and suggest that PRFF can be further improved with optimization techniques.

The concept of Cartesian Decomposition (CD) initially applied to solvable groups can be extended to the broader class of groups with regular actions and is equivalent to a diagonal group structure. This extension allows us to establish CD on groups with certain affine properties using their parabolic subgroups. Specifically, we demonstrate that CD on the wreath product $S_n \wr A$ is equivalent to its diagonal group structure, obtained from the product of the Cartan Decomposition of $S_n$ and the diagonal group structure of $A$. This extension of CD enables us to derive results on the bi-ordering of elements in groups with regular actions. For instance, in the symmetric group $S_n$, we show that an initial segment of the lexicographic order contains a randomly chosen element from the group. This can be extended to the general case of groups with regular actions, provided that their action induces a non-trivial permutation of the set. Furthermore, we prove that in the free group on two generators, any randomly chosen element is ordered with respect to the standard total order on the group. This result can be seen as an application of CD on the free group, established earlier by J. Lehnert. This further expands our understanding of the complex order structure of free groups. Lastly, we explore the interplay between the order structure induced by CD and the standard total order on a group, establishing a non-trivial relation between these orders when the group action is induced by a non-trivial permutation of the set. This relationship is demonstrated through the example of the symmetric group $S_n$, where the order structure induced by CD is shown to be equivalent to a segmented version of the lexicographic order. This reveals a fascinating mathematical connection between the bi-ordering of elements in these groups and their action structures. Consequently, our investigations provide novel insights into both the geometric and combinatorial aspects of these groups, their actions, and their elements' order structures. This research focuses on investigating the interplay between tiny-scale fluctuations and the gradual degradation of materials with varying compositions. To understand this interplay, our study is set within the context of a two-dimensional heterogeneous material composed of multiple components, where each component follows a different probability distribution. We represent the evolution of these fluctuations in a probabilistic sense, using a stochastic version of a well-known partial differential equation-based damage model. Specifically, our model includes a stochastic advection diffusion equation that accounts for fluctuation propagation, mean slope influence, and an upper bound on the material's deformation. We establish an important estimate that helps to overcome a significant technical hurdle in our analysis. Furthermore, we established an essential bound that enables us to control the fluctuations' impact on the material's degradation at a finite time. We also demonstrated that, under certain conditions, the material's degradation becomes progressively localized as time passes. Additionally, we established a crucial relationship between the largest possible probability distribution governing which component will eventually dominate the material's composition and the long-term behavior of the fluctuations. This relationship, coupled with the Kolmogorov-Arnold theorem, enables us to draw conclusions about the long-term behavior of the fluctuations and their impact on the material's composition. Ultimately, our findings highlight the complex interplay between small-scale fluctuations, material composition, and degradation in a way that is both precise and nuanced. This research investigates an energy-efficient, Generalized Antenna-Switching Technique (GEST) in a SWIPT-enabled wireless network. By considering various energy-harvesting protocols and antenna configurations, we develop an optimal GEST strategy that minimizes energy consumption while ensuring reliable communication. We then analyze the performance of this optimized approach and provide numerical results, showing significant energy gains for certain parameter combinations. Moreover, we find that a binary GEST scheme offers suboptimal performance, with results that align with theoretical findings. We also investigate the convergence properties of an associated stochastic process and identify conditions under which the optimal solution is achieved. Finally, we explore the impact of double-threshold protocols on GEST performance. Our study provides valuable insights into the design of energy-efficient SWIPT networks.

Approximating the distribution of extreme event tail probabilities is crucial in various contexts, including finance and engineering. Recently, researchers have focused on extending conditional tail probability assessments to a bivariate framework, incorporating information from multiple related variables. This study adapts the generalized Pareto distribution (GPD) to a bivariate domain and proposes several new estimators for its parameters. Initially, a non-polar estimator is suggested for the joint tail probability based on a single-domain GPD model, and its asymptotic properties are examined. Additionally, a polar estimator is introduced for estimating the upper tail probability in a bivariate extreme value distribution, and its performance is compared to that of a previously proposed estimator. Monte Carlo simulations were used to evaluate the efficacy of these estimators in finite samples. The results indicate that the new estimators can provide reliable approximations of the upper tail probability, and their efficiency is significantly influenced by the choice of domain. The proposed methods are illustrated through an empirical analysis of a financial dataset. This research is set within the framework of the recent studies on bivariate extreme value distributions, specifically that of Heffernan and Tawn (2004), which builds upon the concept of a bivariate generalized extreme value distribution. The work also explores the relationship between the estimated tail probabilities and the characteristics of a related copula model. The findings are applicable to various contexts, such as the assessment of financial institution default risks from a portfolio perspective or the estimation of extreme event loss probabilities in a multivariate insurance setting. Understanding language complexity is best assessed through analyzing how well a machine can grasp various aspects of language, including its syntax, semantics, pragmatics, and sound system, in different contexts and with exposure to different word forms. Prior studies have proposed numerous metrics to gauge these understandings but have largely focused on individual components of language and done so with limited consideration for context and word form effects. Furthermore, these studies have relied heavily on self-supervised models and been confined to the training settings of these models. In contrast, our work develops a comprehensive framework that simultaneously evaluates multiple language dimensions in context and across various word forms and proposes a novel neural model named the Context-Aware Multi-Dimensional Language Model (CAMLMM). This model is pre-trained on combined tasks that consider both context and word form and is designed to automatically determine the relevance of each aspect to the challenge being measured. In our experiments, we find that our proposed method not only outperforms existing state-of-the-art metrics but also provides valuable insights into the context and word form dependencies of these challenges. Additionally, we release multiple challenging, machine-language understanding tasks that are contextual and dependent on word form and sound system and make our model and related resources publicly available. With our work, we hope to establish a new paradigm for both studying the complexity of language and the performance of machines in understanding language. Despite significant advancements in recent years, machine learning models still struggle with complex tasks that involve both sequential organization and unordered instruction based on multiple input modalities. For example, arranging a group of photos without knowing the overall visual structure or an album layout without knowing the key theme. Currently, even the best-performing machine learning models under these conditions perform no better than 60% accuracy and have a significant performance gap (over 20%) compared to humans in a simple instruction-based task based on unordered text descriptions and visual cues. This research seeks to understand the underlying reasons for this significant performance disparity and presents a thorough theoretical and empirical machine learning framework analysis to identify key limitations within both linear sequence-to-sequence transformers and their conservative variations under strict instruction and structural uncertainty constraints. To overcome these challenges, we've developed a more flexible multi-modal memory-augmented transformer, a model that incorporates an external memory component that can be efficiently updated under both instruction and structural modifications with a simple yet efficient global attention mechanism, allowing for more flexible and spontaneous instruction following that can also accommodate complex input structures. Experimental results under both fully automatic and human-in-the-loop settings have shown substantial performance gains over machine learning baselines and near-human performance levels (over 90% accuracy) on multiple visual organization tasks based on unordered text descriptions and visual cues, solidifying the potential applications of this model in various creative and organizational tasks under complex instruction and structural uncertainty conditions. The developed dataset and code are available for public access under strict instruction protocols.

In complex networks, the distribution of cluster sizes following a random event like a single node failure can provide valuable insights into the underlying structure and the spread of influences within the network. To further understand and study near-critical, continuously changing networks, our research focuses on assigning probabilities to cluster sizes resulting from removing a single node. We establish and resolve the specific probability distributions for two extensively studied networks: the Erdős-Rényi network experiencing continuous and rapid changes, and a specialized variant of the Bradley-Terry network where edge strengths evolve independently. Interestingly, in these dynamic networks, the probability distributions of cluster sizes after removing a single node exhibit non-trivial patterns, often displaying power-law characteristics with an observable scaling relationship, and notable fragmentation thresholds exist, both reflecting critical properties of these rapidly evolving networks. Moreover, our theoretical analyses are validated through corresponding simulations. Furthermore, we discovered a crucial relationship between the sizes and locations of these clusters and the specific network parameters. In particular, in the Erdős-Rényi network, the probabilities of different cluster sizes are influenced by the threshold that separates large and small clusters, while in the Bradley-Terry network, the probabilities of different cluster sizes are influenced by the edge strengths generally, and also by a more intricate 'correlation decay' property. Consequently, our research offers a novel framework for studying influence spread and network dynamics, and can be expanded to examine more comprehensive and longer-lasting processes in these dynamic networks. Ultimately, our approach may be applied to broaden our understanding of various network phenomena, including the spread of rumors, viruses, and other types of influence. Additionally, this methodology can be used to examine multiple simultaneous node removals, and even extreme events like entire component or even network dismantling. This concept is particularly relevant to continuously changing networks that experience rapid and continuous changes, and may also be applicable to slower-changing networks experiencing significant events. This initial study paves the way for a more comprehensive investigation of complex network dynamics, and can provide insights into other processes occurring within these networks, and can be expanded to examine multiple simultaneous node removals, and even entire component or even network dismantling. This concept is particularly relevant to continuously changing networks that experience rapid and continuous changes, and may also be applicable to slower-changing networks experiencing significant events. This study paves the way for a more comprehensive investigation of these networks and their abilities to disseminate influences widely. This research also raises significant questions about the relationships between structure, dynamics, and influence spread within these dynamic networks, and could be expanded to examine other processes and network architectures,

Properties of the generalized sextic Freud and Cahn-Hilliard weights will be proven using a method that extends a technique previously used to analyze the generalized Airy weight. This method involves a discrete Painleve analysis and a discussion of steepest descent and stationary phase methods. As a result, we can demonstrate the existence of rational six-branch point singularities in random systems characterized by these weights. Similarly, we can show that these weights can be expressed using a universal determinant formula. In the case of the generalized sextic Freud weight, this expression differs from the generalized Airy weight by an additional factor that can be represented as a product of two discrete Painleve IV operators. Consequently, we can derive the precise form of the discrete KP equation and a higher-order analogue known as the "double six-line branch point DPKP" equation. We can then solve an associated algebraic curve problem and determine the critical behavior at six-branch point singularities for these equations. As a distinct achievement, our study introduces the generalized Cahn-Hilliard equation as an analogue of the Novikov equation. We can solve an algebraic curve problem for this new equation and determine the critical behavior at six-branch point singularities. We can then extend our results to a broader category of non-hermitian discrete Painleve equations and discuss the role of spectral symmetry in this context. We can specifically demonstrate the spectral symmetry of six-branch point singularities for discrete Painleve IV and a corresponding algebraic curve problem. As a broader implication, our study will provide a theoretical foundation for further mathematical analysis of random systems characterized by generalized Freud and Cahn-Hilliard weights. Furthermore, our research will explore possibilities for extending our results to additional weight functions and discuss the general principles governing the analytical properties of such systems. As an experimental approach, our study will investigate the potential of expressing these weights as universal determinant formulas and discuss the mathematical criteria for establishing analytical properties from corresponding discrete Painleve analysis. In this paper, we propose a new nonorthogonal uplink protocol, called NOVR-XL, which includes a randomized access phase to tackle the massive input sparsity in XL-MIMO systems. By leveraging an optimized signal processing technique and pilot sequence design, NOVR-XL significantly enhances random access performance. To validate our findings, simulations are conducted and the results reveal that NOVR-XL achieves substantial energy gains over an existing reference protocol. Additionally, by analyzing two scaling scenarios, we demonstrate the efficacy of NOVR-XL in both wideband, high-resolution scenarios and band-by-band scenarios, and explore various design flexibility considerations. Our study indicates that a key performance indicator, defined as the energy per bit, varies slightly from the benchmark deep learning-based technique and exhibits modest growth with an increase in antenna density. Furthermore, by examining NOVR-XL in relation to several key parameters, we identify potential research areas for further exploration. 

This work has been made available for sharing as the final manuscript is under review for consideration in IEEE Transactions on Information Theory. 

Please note that the code related to this study can be found on the following repository: https://github.com/lingyifeng/NOVR-XL 

In extension to our main paper, additional numerical results are presented, involving various sub-optimality levels, different resolution regimes and comparison with a widely used deep learning-based technique. Moreover, we have included an examination of design flexibility considerations, as well as an in-depth investigation of the energy per bit performance, in relation to several key parameters. These additional results are not part of the main manuscript under review.

In protoplanetary disks, small bodies like asteroids and planetary embryos form from
the transformation of solid particles due to gravitational and collidal forces. Researchers
have been studying the long-term evolution of forming solid bodies within protoplanetary
disks. Although the importance of ambient magnetic fields in this process has been
acknowledged, there is a lack of comprehensive studies that incorporate this factor.
Using ambipolar diffusion to model the interactions between gas, dust, and magnetic fields,
we presented a three-dimensional scheme for evaluating collisions between solid particles
and magnetic field lines. With this model, we simulated the growth of solid bodies from
millimeter-sized grains up to kilometer-sized planetary embryos. Our results show that
the presence of magnetic fields slows down the growth of solid bodies due to their ability
to link grains together and shape the evolution of dust layers. Without magnetic fields,
tightly coupled solid bodies would quickly become heavy enough to overcome the gravitational
binding to the ambient gas and sink toward the disk's center. In contrast, magnetic fields
would allow these objects to grow more rapidly, reaching planetary masses before sinking
deep into the disk. We found that magnetic fields divide solid bodies into two populations:
those that are closely coupled and sink toward the disk's center, and those that are free
and can grow into planetary mass objects. These results provide a new perspective on the
formation of exoplanets and clarify the role of magnetic fields in the early solar system. 
Further research is needed to validate our model's predictions by comparing them with
observational data and theoretical models of protoplanetary disks. 
Also, we propose that future high-resolution observations can test our findings by
studying the growth of solid bodies in action in actual protoplanetary disks. 
Our study paves the way for a deeper exploration of the complex interplay between
gas, dust, and magnetic fields in protoplanetary disks, a crucial area of research
in the study of planetary formation. 
Also, it highlights the necessity of developing multi-physics and multi-scale codes
that can simulate the development of solid bodies within protoplanetary disks by itself
and in conjunction with other disk processes. 
Such breakthroughs will become even more necessary in the near future as even more

The BigApple energy density functional, which is an empirical functional that can be modified, has been applied to various applications involving complex nuclear systems, including studies of single-particle properties, collective phenomena, and time-dependent states. This research aims to provide a comprehensive account of the BigApple's performance by investigating its self-consistent application to finite iron-group nuclei, specifically focusing on odd-systems. Employing the BIG2 code, developed by the research group led by Prof. H. Sagawa, self-consistent calculations were carried out using the BigApple parameter set based on the relativistic mean-field theory. Results from these calculations are compared to existing experimental data and previous predictions made by other relativistic mean-field models. Detailed analyses of low-energy states, magnetic moments, and B(E1) values are presented along with comparisons to observed values and theoretical predictions made by other relativistic mean-field models. This research demonstrates the BigApple's ability to replicate experimental data and underlying properties of odd nuclei, confirming its potential as a reliable tool for studying complex nuclear systems. Additionally, this work is expected to lay the groundwork for further investigations into time-reversal symmetry breaking phenomena in nuclei. We present a novel method combining configuration interaction and dynamical mean-field theory, allowing for correlated orbitals within the dynamical mean-field formalism. This methodology enables us to incorporate multiple orbitals with distinct energies and intertwined momentum-dependent spectral weights in our studies. We apply this approach to investigate SrMnO$_3$, a type of mott transition material, and find that considering two correlated orbitals thoroughly in our model yields a complex spectral structure reflecting the interplay between different electronic states at distinct momenta. Furthermore, our findings reveal a tendency toward localization or electron conduction based on whether these two correlated orbitals are filled with electrons or not. This phenomenon is consistent across all momenta, offering us a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms driving the mott transition in SrMnO$_3$. Ultimately, our studies suggest that considering the intricate relationships between different correlated orbitals with distinct energies is crucial for accurately modeling the spectral weights in complex materials. This breakthrough methodology of ours may also expand the range of materials that can be effectively modeled within the dynamical mean-field framework.

In this research, we analyze how different Molmer-Sorensen gate designs affect entanglement development in a chain of ions. Further, we propose a method to create frequency-resistant Molmer-Sorensen gates and demonstrate the usefulness of this technique in a quantum algorithm, specifically in entanglement accumulation, by showcasing a notable enhancement in success rates. Additionally, we examine the impact of varying laser power on the effectiveness of these gates and find that there is an optimal range in which the frequency robustness is most beneficial. Specifically, this optimal range arises due to the balanced effects of under- and over-dressed interactions at moderate laser powers. We also find that within this optimal range, the robustness against frequency errors allows for increased duration of the Molmer-Sorensen gates, thus further enhancing the success rate. However, it is essential to acknowledge that powerful lasers may cause adverse effects, such as ion crystalline structure alterations, which might impede the scalability of this quantum approach. Still, our study suggests that with careful calibration of laser and ion parameters, the Molmer-Sorensen gate could serve as a reliable and robust choice for quantum applications that involve multi-ion systems. We illustrate this potential by simulating the "Shor's algorithm" using a variety of ion chains and find that our robust Molmer-Sorensen gates maintain a high success rate throughout, while also exhibiting minimal error propagation. This, combined with an efficient phase estimation algorithm, allows us to achieve a notable decrease in error probabilities compared to other gate types. Ultimately, our findings suggest that frequency-robust Molmer-Sorensen gates hold significant potential for creating large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers based on ions. This potential is realized when the robustness against frequency errors is leveraged to develop highly reliable multi-ion algorithms, capable of managing high failure rates in individual ion qubits, thus enabling the development of scalable ion quantum computers. This advancement could be a crucial step towards the creation of practical quantum computers that can solve real-world problems.

Research on the structural characteristics of perovskites with varying equilibrium volumes and different cations is not complete without considering the effects of magnetic ordering and lattice distortions. To better understand the underlying principles, our comprehensive theoretical analysis will serve as a valuable reference for future studies, as it exhaustively examines the impact of volume and cation type on the position of B-cations within the lattice. Using a 45-atom cell, our high-resolution structure studies employed gradient-corrected functional and pseudo potentials to analyze a broad range of perovskites, including both metal and semimetal groups. The results show that increasing the equilibrium volume of a metal perovskite leads to a more pronounced movement of B-cations away from their central position, whereas this effect is minimized in semimetallic perovskites. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that B-cations exhibit significant movement away from their central position when the filler A cation has a large effective atomic radius, and that this movement is significantly reduced when the filler A cation has a small effective atomic radius. Interestingly, our results also indicate that B-cations tend to return to their central position when the filler A cation has an intermediate effective atomic radius. These findings provide a deeper understanding of the structural characteristics of perovskites and will pave the way for further related research. Additionally, our results may also shed light on the unusual magnetic properties and lattice distortions observed in certain perovskites, and could potentially serve as a framework for identifying potential candidates exhibiting magnetic ordering and lattice distortions. Candidates with filler A cations from the 5d series, specifically, are anticipated to exhibit notable lattice distortions, and could possibly exhibit magnetic ordering or lattice-related phenomena. As an example, our analysis reveals that Sr$_3$NiTaO$_6$ and Ca$_3$NiTaO$_6$ both exhibit significant movement of Ni$^{3+}$ ions away from their central position, and could thus be potential candidates for further study. Nonetheless, more advanced simulations are needed to determine their actual magnetic properties and lattice stability. Nonetheless, our results do provide a valuable starting point for identifying potential candidates, and could serve as a crucial reference for any related research. Our results have been published in Journal of Physics: Condensed Matter, Volume 28, Number 2 (2016).

The bimodal beta distribution proposed here addresses a common issue in data analysis - many datasets exhibit two primary patterns, yet existing models often fall short in capturing this key feature. Our new formulation achieves a bimodal design through a straightforward approach, where standard form parameters are modified to produce a notable double-hump effect. This is contrast to other proposed bimodal beta distributions, which introduce additional form parameters to achieve a similar outcome, often through complex methods. We detail the theoretical aspects of this new distribution, including its general form, properties, and key quantiles. Additionally, we provide an easy-to-use R function for implementing the distribution within broader statistical analysis tools. This function is demonstrated through a practical example involving real-world income data. We also explore the benefits of this new distribution in comparison to more established models, such as the beta and lognormal distributions, through a practical investigation using popular Bayesian clustering methods. This research offers a valuable contribution to the development of effective statistical analysis techniques for accurately modeling datasets with clear patterns. Our work in this area can serve as a foundation for future studies, where the bimodal beta distribution may be applied across a range of contexts, including medicine, economics, and engineering, among other fields. This new distribution is now available as part of the R package 'BimBeta' along with the R package'scIm.

We refute a conjecture made by F. Labastida and C. Viallet in 1989, which asserted that within a nilfibre - the intersection of a subgroup's action on a variety with a hyperplane defined by another subgroup - there exists no dense, open orbit. Instead, we demonstrate the existence of a dense, orbit created by repeatedly applying a nilpotent operator to a specific initial point. This counterexample is derived from a nilpotent operator found by H. Tsai in 2009, based on a simple quadratic singularity found by H. Ito in 1988. Notably, this counterexample has significant implications for the study of nilfibre's properties. By examining nilfibre's structure, we are able to identify various subvarieties and determine their roles within the larger geometric context. In particular, we define a new invariant called the nilindex, which measures the number of times a nilpotent operator must be applied to return to the original point, and we establish its fundamental properties. Furthermore, we explore the concept of a subnilfibre - a nilfibre created by limiting the action of a nilpotent operator to a subset of the original variety - and we establish the existence of a subnilfibre with a dense, open orbit. Additionally, we define the dual of a subnilfibre and demonstrate its equivalence to another geometric context. Lastly, we introduce an algebraic operator Yang-Baxter equation and show that its solutions can be represented as the dual of a subnilfibre. If the subnilfibre contains a dense, open orbit, then this yields a new class of set-theoretic solutions to this equation. Notably, this includes a dense, open orbit itself, which can be viewed as a generalization of many well-known solutions found in the literature. Moreover, we observe that this new class of solutions has significant connections to various established mathematical frameworks such as the representation theory of the borbose algebra and the study of birational geometry throughout the complex tori. Lastly, we propose a more extensive conjecture regarding the properties of nilfibre's structure and suggest that this conjecture has important implications for our current understanding of these complex geometric contexts. Our study delves into an alternative configuration where a neural language model is used in an encoder-decoder setup, with the substitution of the internal decoder's neural components with $N$-gram models. We theoretically illustrate that this hybrid approach leverages the advantages of both models, specifically the preservation of contextual information by the neural components and the compact representation of probabilistic distributions by the $N$-gram models. We also provide empirical evidence from experiments conducted on the tasks of machine translation, text classification, and summarization, using both publicly and privately sourced data. These results demonstrate that this straightforward hybridization method yields performance improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, with improvements ranging from a 0.73 absolute improvement in BLEU score to a 15.59 absolute improvement in ROUGE-1 score. As governments invest heavily in low-carbon energy and storage technologies, optimizing the performance of these resources is becoming increasingly important.  Storage units, designed to mitigate volatility and ensure reliability in the energy system, can sometimes store clean energy and delay non-clean energy delivery to only after and unless there is high demand.  Therefore, storage resources behave risk-ously and it is essential to incorporate this behavior in models used to evaluate the very long-term performance of these technologies.  To this end, we develop a first-of-its-kind storage performance model, based on a technique called expectation maximization, that learns optimal storage and generation policies from scratch by utilizing machine learning to analyze data from simulated simulations.  This model outperforms industry-standard models and matches the performance of more advanced computer simulation tools used to study energy systems for up to 10,000 hours.  When applied to actual energy data, it shows a similar performance.  When used to make policy recommendations, it suggests a combination of policies that can increase the performance of these technologies to at least 10% better than current methods used to evaluate their performance.  It also identifies specific storage technologies that can perform better than current standards and indicates how often different generation units should operate to maximize performance.  This indicates that storage technologies like lithium-ion and pumped hydro can perform better than current standards and that generation units like gas and coal should operate full-time, except in instances where there are high demands and it makes sense to delay their delivery until then.  It also shows that solar and wind should operate about 90% of the time, except in instances where there are high demands and it makes sense to delay their delivery until then.  It indicates that energy storage technologies can cover at least 50% of the energy generation gap by 2050 and that a combination of policies that include pricing incentives, capacity payments, and contract pooling can increase its performance to at least 20% better than current standards.  It showcases its results in the form of a long-term performance chart that compares the performance of different energy technologies and storage resources, providing valuable insights for policymakers and industry stakeholders.  It highlights the potential of machine learning to create value from existing data in the energy industry and paves the way for the development of more advanced models that can capture even more intricate behavior in these technologies.  It employs a method called reinforcement learning to analyze data from simulated simulations, a technique that is useful when there is a large amount of data available but it is difficult to develop models that can perform well in these situations.

Our study offers new insights into the atmospheric circulation patterns on Mars, specifically in its mid-latitudes, by simulating a baroclinic storm similar to those found on Earth. To achieve this, we created a simplified computer model that mimics the Martian atmosphere, using realistic conditions and measurements to do so. In doing so, we were able to successfully reproduce the characteristic vortice patterns seen in Martian circulation, and even replicate the atmospheric circulation patterns common in Earth-like atmospheres. Notably, our model revealed that the swirling storms on Mars share a common thread with hispanic circulation patterns - they are both products of the interaction between atmospheric waves and the shape of the planet's surface. Furthermore, we found that these Martian storms are governed by the same rules that apply to Earth's storms, and are even sensitive to the same factors, such as the amount of carbon dioxide and the planet's rotational rate. Perhaps most intriguingly, our model suggested that the Martian atmosphere may harbor a type of persistent weather pattern, one that forms over wide areas and is driven by the movement of cold air. If this theory holds water, it could have significant implications for our understanding of the Martian climate system. Lastly, we found that the CO2 polar caps on Mars may actually be composed of three-component mixtures, rather than the two previously assumed. In this scenario, the mid-latitude atmospheric circulation plays a key role in transporting CO2 between the poles and the rest of the planet. In our final analysis, we compared our findings to other computer models and studies. In doing so, we found that our model reproduced the circulation patterns seen in other simulations, and that these patterns share a common feature - they all rely on the friction between the atmosphere and the Martian surface to function. Lastly, we proposed a set of observations and experiments that could help confirm our findings. If carried out, these experiments could provide crucial insights into the Martian atmosphere's circulation patterns, as well as the planet's climate system as a whole. In the end, our study serves as a starting point for a broader investigation into the Martian atmosphere's circulation patterns, and the fundamental processes that govern the planet's climate system. In doing so, it may one day help make the case for the Red Planet as a viable location for life beyond Earth. In this regard, our model raises important questions about the feasibility of life on Mars, and what steps must be taken to confirm the existence of life there.

In thick quantum wells with high scattering rates, resistance oscillations near the zeroth Landau level can be intense and well-defined. These oscillations, observed in macroscopic samples, are influenced by the interaction between electrons and the non-magnetic random potential, which creates a well-defined energy spectrum. In contrast, in thin, low-scattering quantum wells, the resistance around the zeroth Landau level becomes poorly defined due to the breakdown of single-electron behavior and the emergence of a collective, edge-state spectrum. This work focuses on the latter case. It is shown that, within a single-Landau-level picture, the oscillations in magnetic-field-dependent resistance can be understood using a simplified model, which takes into account the energy separation between adjacent edge states at the magnetic field where the resistance peaks. The peak resistance and the associated activation energy in this model are determined by the local electron concentration and the inter-edge-state scattering rate. This paper presents an innovative adaptive cooperative protocol based on Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (NOMA) called AC2-NOMA, targeted at improving the outage probability in downlink cellular systems. By dynamically allocating a cooperative user to serve an outaged cell and switching between cooperative and non-cooperative modes at the base station, AC2-NOMA significantly reduces the outage probability. Our analysis shows that the outage probability of AC2-NOMA decreases exponentially with a large rate and exceeds twice the performance gain of the best existing protocol in simulations. Moreover, AC2-NOMA achieves this performance improvement with minimal additional communication and computation overhead. Numerical results confirm the efficacy of AC2-NOMA in a simulated meta-scenario that mimics real-world scenarios.

To accelerate progress, we propose a method for synthetically generating complex road networks that interact with these automated systems, specifically focused on lane keeping. We've designed a flexible, multi-lane road generator that utilizes a combination of spatial relationship rules and mathematical formulas to create highly detailed, interactive 3D scenes, encompassing various challenging scenarios, such as curved roads, intersecting roads, and missing lane markers. This tool enables rapid creation of engaging scenarios for lane keeping system testing and validation, allowing for the exploration of design choices and user experience assessments. We've incorporated our road generator into a pioneering approach that leverages scene graph data structures, incorporating multiple lane levels and parsing capabilities. Our investigation introduces a breakthrough linearized stochastic hydrodynamic method for quantum hydrodynamics, a semi-empirical quantum theory. We break down the algorithm into two novel sub-protocols to linearize both quantum hydrodynamics and their corresponding boundary conditions. The proposed method achieves significant enhancements in simulating out-of-equilibrium quantum correlations when compared to conventional methods, with the main difference being the inclusion of quantum stress tensor correlations. A demonstration of this approach is in the form of simulations of a quantum shock wave scenarios, where our results show the importance of stress tensor correlations in properly modeling correlation functions across the front of the shock wave. The proposed algorithm represents an important advancement in feasible simulations of quantum systems with substantial deviations from equilibrium conditions. The challenge of the algorithm remains the identification of a suitable Wigner function initial condition, particularly for complex systems, where the hydrodynamic description is more established, as seen in the discussion surrounding the hydrodynamic description of helium. The new algorithm is set to become an essential tool for the simulation of quantum shock waves, a phenomenon that has the potential to be studied using next-generation electron storage rings with the ability to produce high-field, short-wavelength light. The ability to simulate these quantum shocks will not only provide valuable theoretical insights but will also offer the potential to design and carry out theoretical simulations that can be directly compared with ongoing and future experimental research. The potential applications of this research also extend to the development of new quantum hydrodynamic equations that can be applicable to systems interacting with photons and other weak probes. The new algorithm is especially relevant for the study of quantum systems with long mean free paths, where quantum hydrodynamics is expected to emerge as a powerful theoretical framework that can be used to study a wide range of systems, from superconducting circuits to quantum fluids and electrons in transition metals. Recent action proposal generation methods primarily focus on using deep convolutional neural networks with additional auxiliary tasks to represent combined spatial and temporal proposals. In contrast, we suggest that proposals should be described using local and global contexts found within the bounded video frame, rather than relying on costly context extraction from the entire video. Based on this context-based representation, we introduce the Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN), a straightforward yet effective action proposal generation model that incorporates context aggregation modules at both the individual frame and proposal level. By incorporating context from both the local frame and the proposal's extent, DCAN increases the accuracy of proposal quality and reduces the overlap between proposals. Our experiments demonstrate that DCAN performs exceptionally well on benchmark datasets, achieving the highest average proposal quality and average overlap among currently competing methods. Moreover, DCAN surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving a high mean average precision of 54.8% at an overlap threshold of 0.5 in Valence and Actionforce datasets. The code for DCAN is openly available at https://github.com/cg1177/DCAN.
