For linear Majorana fermions in one-dimensional space, an external linear potential modifies their behavior and calculates the resulting change in entropy according to Shannon's formula, considering both infinite and confined conditions. Infinite conditions lead to a constant entropy value, while confined conditions produce an unregularized form of entropy that varies linearly with the Fermi energy. Introducing a finite coupling to a nearby reservoir causes the entropy to take on a typical quadratic form, closely related to the energy of these modes. Additionally, we investigate the interplay between these two scenarios and determine the conditions under which each case applies. Our study provides a theoretical basis for understanding the thermal properties of Majorana fermions in one-dimensional settings. Furthermore, we propose two possible setups to experimentally realize and manipulate the zero-energy Majorana modes in different environments. Lastly, our discussion on stability considerations highlights the importance of both electrical and mechanical stability in solid-state systems that host zero-energy Majorana modes. Such stability ensures that these modes remain unchanged in the presence of mechanical stress or electrical bias. We also examine the impact of linear and parabolic potentials on the entropy of these Majorana fermions and propose a protocol for switching the fusion pattern of these modes through an external linear potential. This potential also influences the zero-voltage conductance properties of these systems, providing a means to control their electronic transport characteristics. Ultimately, reliable manipulation of these zero-energy Majorana modes is crucial for the development of topological fault-tolerant logic operations. Our analysis starts with a specific quantum system - a string of one-dimensional bosonic sites arranged in a specific linear configuration, where atoms and molecules undergo reciprocal transformations. We establish that, due to their similar timescales, atom-molecule interaction dynamics can be effectively represented by a non-rigid pendulum model, which encompasses multiple harmonic oscillators connected by springs. This model facilitates comprehension of the emergence of instability and atom-molecule conversion dynamics at its edges. Notably, it reveals that the onset of instability near the molecule edge is caused by an unstable molecule-atom conversion, whereas the stable molecule edge results from a stable atom-molecule conversion. Furthermore, we identify that the edge spin dynamics in this system can be described using a non-rigid pendulum model reduced to a single harmonic oscillator. This can be achieved by applying a suitable unitary transformation at each edge site. Due to its interacting nature, this model surpasses the limitations of existing edge spin dynamics theories, which are confined to isolated and non-interacting edge spins. Additionally, we propose a possible experimental implementation of this model's dynamics using laser probes. Our study showcases that even the most complex quantum systems can be simplified using effective models, which can be derived from microscopic descriptions and demonstrated through experimental observations. This, in turn, may pave the way for us to better understand other complex quantum systems. In DNA data storage, the limited number of possible base identities restricts data density. This study investigates how read errors impact DNA storage efficiency and proposes an innovative approach, error-correcting primer design, to mitigate the effect of errors. By developing a new algorithm that prioritizes storage space utilization, we introduce a new method for primer design. Additionally, we examine the influence of error propagation on DNA storage and present an analytical model to estimate error propagation's impact on error-correcting primer design, incorporating both cyclic and linear error-correcting codes. Our experiments demonstrate substantial increases in storage density and overall system performance when using error-correcting primer designs. Furthermore, our results show that highly efficient DNA storage systems can be achieved with relatively low additional computational overhead. We also showcase the applicability of our approach to various storage systems and investigate the potential for further improvements in storage efficiency through more advanced coding techniques. Our findings are accompanied by an open-source implementation on GitHub, along with a publicly accessible DNA storage simulator on SciDB. We are seeking community feedback and suggestions for further development.

Our discovery of a non-basal nodal line in Mn$_4$N-based monopnictides starts from theoretical predictions, ends with experimental confirmation, and differentiates the state from other topological phenomena. Computational models predict a one-dimensional nodal line in the electron pocket of Mn, situated on a crystallographic mirror plane, which is corroborated by angular resolved photoemission and momentum microscopy. The exceptional nature of this finding lies in its uniqueness within the topological materials family – nodal lines are isolated in independent momentum spaces, contrasting with intertwined arcs in Ta$_2$NiO$_4$ and disconnected pockets in Mn$_4$N-based monopnictides. Additionally, this non-basal nodal line exhibits a notable sensitivity to long-range antiferromagnetic ordering, manifesting as a nodal semimetal state and magnetic topological phase that may be distinguished by distinct electronic signs on opposite sides of the nodal line. This study provides direct evidence for a nodal line and combines it with magnetic topology in a single material, Mn$_4$N. This approach leveraged adversarial training and domain misclassification constraints to achieve accurate results despite limited labeled data. The method demonstrated the potential to reduce the need for labeled data in future medical image analysis tasks. This approach was also applied to a different medical image analysis task, namely retinal blood vessel segmentation, and the corresponding code is available for public use.

This paper introduces a novel technique for approximate shadow computation in 3D computer graphics, based on spatial analysis rather than ray tracing. To achieve this, we leverage machine learning to derive compact, analytical representations of object surfaces from rendered images. By comparing these surface representations with those of light sources, we determine areas of an scene that would be in shadow. To demonstrate the feasibility of this approach, we developed a system that uses a neural network to extract surface representations from images, applied this to shadow computation, and showed improved results compared to traditional methods. While our method shows promising performance, it has limitations, including an excessive computational requirement for the neural network and inaccurate predictions on complex surfaces. To address these issues, we identify the potential benefits of incorporating multiview information into the neural network. Furthermore, we explore possible variations of this approach, applying similar techniques to compute ambient occlusion and volumetric rendering. Additionally, we summarize the existing literature on computer graphics techniques that utilize machine learning. To facilitate further research, we will make the code and data associated with this project publicly available.

We propose a novel method using finite element geostatistics to estimate riverbed topography from direct velocity observations.  First, we establish a parametric model that connects velocity measurements to the topography using the finite element method. Then, we employ stochastic simulation to process this model and accommodate uncertain direct velocity observations.  Specifically, we leverage the benefits of spatial decomposition to build a detailed, high-resolution topographic estimate.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to synthetic data sets and one real-world data set, showing that it yields accurate results.  An advantage of this method is that it can handle complex riverbed topographies and produce detailed, high-resolution estimates.  We also compare our method to an alternative approach, combining finite element simulation with Gaussian processes.  Overall, our method offers a flexible and efficient way to estimate riverbed topography from direct velocity observations.  An implementation of the PCGA algorithm is available online. Creating High Dynamic Range (HDR) images involves combining multiple exposures of a scene to capture its full range of brightness. Advances in image processing have led to developing automatic exposure setting selection (AE) algorithms that can choose the optimal exposure settings to produce high-quality HDR images. Initially, these algorithms were limited by HDR reconstruction methods that could only handle small ranges of contrasts. Recent advancements in deep learning and inverse tone mapping have enabled the production of realistic HDR images from single HDR images. In this research, we introduce a novel approach that uses a convolutional neural network to directly select the optimal exposure settings from a set of randomly generated HDR images, simulating real-world capture conditions. By training and refining this network with the help of inverse tone mapping techniques, we created a model that can choose the optimal exposure settings to produce not just technically excellent, but also aesthetically pleasing HDR images. This is achieved by training the network with both technical and artistic quality metrics, allowing it to balance contrast and composition. The results demonstrate that our approach surpasses existing AE algorithms and produces HDR images of unparalleled quality. Additionally, we experimented with training the network to respond to global adjustments, such as brightness and contrast, and the potential it holds for future research. The project's code and data are available online.

The long-term accurate measurement of temperature in nuclear reactors is crucial for ensuring safe and efficient operation. The proton resonance frequency shift in water, resulting from its interaction with nearby nuclei, provides a reliable and self-consistent temperature indicator. However, achieving acceptable measurement times demands a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms and additional factors influencing the proton resonance frequency, including how much they contribute to noise in the measurement signal. In this study, we conducted a comprehensive theoretical and experimental analysis of how much the proton resonance frequency in water is affected by nearby nuclei and the resulting proton resonance frequency noise. We developed a noise model that takes into account different neutron-induced recoil processes and found that these processes contribute significantly to the measurement noise, especially at typical reactor operating temperatures, where the largest contribution to noise comes from 33K neutrons inducing a water molecule to change its proton resonance frequency. We also found that the noise in this process is highly correlated with other noise sources in the reactor's cooling system and that there is potential for further reducing measurement noise through careful design of the reactor's cooling system. Finally, we developed a method for determining the accuracy of temperature measurements based on measurement time and the reactor's operating conditions and found that the maximum achievable accuracy is around 0.1 K. In future work, we plan to investigate ways of further reducing measurement noise in addition to exploring the applicability of this measurement technique to other water-based nuclear reactors. In order to validate our model, we conducted a series of experiments using a neutron beam and water samples and found that our model predicts the observed frequency shifts and noise levels accurately. In particular, we found that our model predicts that the maximum frequency shift relative to a calibration point will increase by about 0.16 ppm per degree Celsius increase in temperature, which is consistent with our experimental findings. We also developed a data analysis method that allows for accurate determination of temperature from the measured frequency shift, excluding any systematic errors, and achieved an accuracy of about 0.01 K when the measurement time was around 100 seconds. The Madsen-Weiss theorem is an influential result that bridges the b-principle and stable maps in topology. Initially published in 2005, the theorem has been a driving force in expanding the Madsen-Weiss structure theorem to its current form over the past eighteen years. Researchers are now extending the original result to include the Madsen-Weiss structure theorem for oriented manifolds of arbitrary dimension. This paper confirms the existence of a limiting spectral distribution for symmetric square matrices with independent entries, under either joint or marginal asymptotic independence conditions, provided the matrix dimensions scale in a certain way. We also obtain an accurate description of the resulting spectral distribution. Additionally, we demonstrate that a broad class of matrix models, including those related to random graphs and various stochastic processes, can be analyzed using these techniques, often yielding more detailed information about the spectral distribution than previously available. In particular, near the spectral edge, we are able to convey significant amount of information about the spectral distribution's characteristics using the large-dimensional matrix version of the Widom's formula. We further illustrate this understanding with specific examples from the given study. One such example involves the edge-spectral distribution of a matrix whose entries are defined by a product of two independent, independently asymptotic, variables, a scenario previously considered in 2012 by Johnstone and Paul. Another example involves the design of an extreme eigenvalue optimizing problem, where the objective is to find the minimum or maximum mean-variance portfolio efficiency threshold under which all portfolios achieve the best variance given by the top eigenvalue of a large-dimensional covariance matrix. We show this efficiency threshold actually scales in a very simple way and is non-rigorously confirmed to be roughly on the order of the square root of the number of assets, a finding that has been supported by various simulations. We also establish that any portfolio whose variance is less than this threshold will asymptotically converge to a distribution that is the result of multiplying the standard normal distribution by the square root of the number of assets. This thesis also explores new methods for estimating the unknown parameters of a signal-plus-noise communication model, where the signal and noise have varying asymptotic independence properties, a scenario that is also applicable to the design of an extreme eigenvalue optimizing problem mentioned above. We develop non-asymptotic formulas for measuring estimation performance, as well as a new matrix estimation approach that is based on a specific ordering of the matrix rows, an idea that was initially conceived as a part of the research on the design of an extreme eigenvalue optimizing problem mentioned above. This new approach produces the best known to date negative minimum diagram for the spectral edge of a broad class of matrix models, a finding that is also confirmed by Monte Carlo simulations. We also establish that any matrix model that has independent entries will converge to the same limiting spectral distribution, provided the model is properly scaled, which is a result that was previously only confirmed for models that have marginal asymptotic independence. However, creating a built-in emotional response through music requires a deep understanding of the intended emotional impact on the viewer and the video's content. Our innovative approach involves developing a cutting-edge AI system capable of generating original music in response to various viewer emotions and video content. We've experimented with several advanced algorithms and tested our results against traditional entertainment music, demonstrating that our findings hold significant potential to shape music recommendations based on emotional intelligence and individual preferences. While there are opportunities for further improvement, our current approach proves effective in designing music to elicit a specific emotional response from viewers watching videos on social media. Our research focuses on two particular emotions - disgust and fear - and incorporates publicly accessible intelligence and music composition tools to craft music that can be played alongside video clips available on YouTube. Our analysis reveals that music generated using our AI system can effectively predict the intended emotional response in 70-80% of cases, as validated by crowdsourced feedback from 200 participants. Moreover, our approach highlights the potential for similar techniques to be applied to various other multimedia applications, such as film soundtracks, video games, and virtual reality experiences, offering a more personalized and engaging experience for viewers. Ultimately, our research has the potential to establish a new connection between music composition, emotional intelligence, and viewer experience. Various studies have demonstrated that gradient masking, a defense mechanism employed by certain neural networks, can be circumvented by tailored attacks. To facilitate comparisons among these models, this study introduces a metric called quantified gradient masking (QGM) to numerically measure the effectiveness of gradient masking. In addition, this metric allows for the evaluation of defense strategies across different models, network architectures, and scenarios. Furthermore, QGM is utilized to analyze the efficacy of gradient masking in diverse neural networks and attack scenarios, which can serve as a reference for future research in this area. Additionally, this study explores alternative frameworks for measuring the occurrence of gradient masking and provides specific examples involving quantified bias transmission. In the context of preventing gradient masking, the properties of QGM are investigated in relation to neural network training configurations and architectures. Ultimately, this study proposes a new concept called the quantified transmission barrier (QTB) to quantify the ability of neural networks to prevent gradient masking and bias transmission. The effectiveness of QTB is illustrated through an example involving a modified training approach. The underlying theory suggests that this new approach might yield neural networks with intrinsic resistance to gradient masking and bias transmission. Researchers aiming to fabricate acoustic metamaterials at the microscopic level face challenges when scaling down their design due to the significant impact of thermoviscous phenomena, such as boundary layer resistance and viscous dissipation, on subwavelength propagation. To address this issue, scientists have proposed using rapid acoustic flows in two-dimensional, microscopic resonators. However, designing these resonators involves overcoming the difficulties of optical acoustic field manipulation. This study leverages a nanoscale acoustic filter device consisting of an array of $450\text{ nm}$-diameter holes to investigate how thermoviscous effects influence flow dynamics across different resonance modes and demonstrate the ability to selectively suppress certain modes through temperature and flow velocity manipulation. The findings of this study are underpinned by numerical simulations that account for both continuum and quantum phenomena and reveal the possibility of optimizing design parameters for improved mode selection, demonstrating the potential for precise manipulation of acoustic fields on the nanoscale. This research may pave the way for innovative applications of acoustic metamaterials, including enhanced sensing capabilities. Furthermore, this study introduces a framework for evaluating the performance of subwavelength acoustic devices, addressing a critical shortcoming in the field. This framework's utility in evaluating device efficiency is demonstrated via the analysis of a microscopic acoustic diode. This research, which combines experimental technique development and rigorous theoretical analysis, provides a crucial step towards overcoming the limitations imposed by thermoviscous phenomena when designing microscopic acoustic metamaterials and their devices. This advance has the potential to empower innovative quantum technology applications that rely on acoustic phenomena. This research has also highlighted the value of combining numerical simulations with experimental evidence, showcasing the importance of a holistic approach that integrates both theoretical and experimental studies. This approach can yield greater insights and understandings of complex quantum phenomena and provide a framework for further research in this field. This research has also created opportunities for cross-disciplinary training and may pave the way for the development of new quantum acoustic sensing technologies, offering potential solutions to real-world problems. This work has also been made possible by the unique capabilities of the ion beam finishing facility, which enabled the fabrication of complex acoustic metastructures with subwavelength features. This facility's expertise may be of interest to other researchers working on the development of quantum technologies and involving the fabrication of intricate nanostructures. In a loop resonator, the interaction between two counterpropagating modes can either greatly enhance cross-phase and self-phase modulation or cause them to become equivalent. In this study, a loop setup consisting of two identical optical fibers is analyzed, with the focus on four-wave mixing interactions within this configuration. In one scenario, two modes in the same direction are examined, with their phase shifts due to cross- and self-phase modulation shown to differ significantly. In the case of counterpropagating modes, however, the distinction disappears, with both experiencing identical cross- and self-phase modulation. A proposed application for this equal cross- and self-phase modulation involves a simple loop configuration to generate phase-randomizing effects useful for various techniques, including blind amplitude noise multiplication and randomized spectral broadening. In this context, a method involving a counterpropagating four-wave mixing process is described to efficiently broaden a laser's spectral profile without introducing spectral phase distortions. In the case of a 10-Gb/s RZ signal, for example, a 20-Gb/s optical signal with an unchanged spectral profile can be generated. In addition, in a loop setup consisting of two different photosensitive fibers, the difference in photosensitivity and optical loss in these fibers can lead to an up to 20-dB advantage in the generation of four-wave mixing effects. This advantage can be applied to efficiently deploy existing short-haul optical connections and provide reliable data transmission in sensing applications, particularly those involving in-fiber Bragg reflectors. In one instance, in an up to 20-km long fiber loop, reliable data transmission from a distant server was achieved over a 10-Gb/s optical link. In another application, a method involving a counterpropagating four-wave mixing process in a loop resonator is described to efficiently generate phase-randomizing effects, including blind amplitude noise multiplication and randomized spectral broadening, without the need for an external modulator or coherent detection. This study explores the dynamic behavior of control systems that permit unbounded control inputs within certain constraints. Researchers have previously demonstrated that, in systems characterized by Lipschitz-continuous drift dynamics and bounded control inputs, trajectories are drawn to a singular set consisting of asymptotically stable periodic orbits within a neighborhood of the origin. However, the current investigation reveals that in systems enabling unbounded control inputs, trajectories along singular trajectories can exhibit chaotic behavior, and the singular set's stability is significantly impacted as a result of an infinite number of heteroclinic connections forming in the neighborhood of the origin. Moreover, the study shows that the topology of this stability structure is extensively influenced by the dynamics of an associated system defined by time-one maps of the system's solutions, and that this associated system possesses a infinite-dimensional topological complexity. Finally, the investigation provides an analysis of an aircraft control system in the presence of obstacles demonstrating the aforementioned stability structure and the occurrence of an infinite number of heteroclinic connections. The findings are verified through actual experiments conducted on an aircraft equipped with a flight control system capable of enabling trajectories to move between these chaotic orbits. The ability to achieve these complex behaviors is made possible by the use of high-speed actuators in the aircraft's flight control system, and the development of a control strategy utilizing bounded control inputs within extremely narrow time intervals. The resulting system is a nonautonomous control system requiring the application of nonlinear, high-speed controls, and the first known example of a system of this kind exhibiting an infinite number of heteroclinic connections in a neighborhood of the origin in three-dimensional space. The discovery of this complex stability structure is attributed to the development of an innovative Lyapunov function, and the application of nonlinear spectral decomposition. The associated system defined by time-one maps of the system's solutions is a subject of ongoing research, but it is believed that this system could provide valuable insights into the understanding of chaotic behavior in higher-dimensional spaces, and the study of strange attractors in systems characterized by unbounded controls. The possibility of homoclinic connections occurring in systems characterized by unbounded controls, and the potential for trajectories to exhibit chaotic behavior along singular trajectories in systems characterized by continuously differentiable drift dynamics and unbounded controls are the key subjects that are yet to be fully researched. Nonetheless, this study offers an unparalleled look at the most complex stability structure in a system characterized by unbounded controls, and it is the first known example of an infinite number of heteroclinic connections forming in a neighborhood of the origin in three-dimensional

This study involves enhancing super-resolution GAN models using multiscale resolution sampling, adapting techniques from turbulent flow simulation. The investigation employs the exact same model architecture for all experiments. The findings show that the model excels at replicating turbulent flows at Reynolds numbers similar to those used in training. The most impressive results are obtained in flows with constant viscosity conditions. The introduction of variance terms in sampling procedures further boosts the model's performance, especially when replicating turbulent flows at higher Reynolds numbers. The research also involves comparing the original and sampled residual vectors in an attempt to better comprehend how the model generates coherent, turbulent flows. The investigation includes a summary of the dataset, explanation of the training process, evaluation metrics, and detailed analysis of turbulent flow replicas at different scale levels. The work also compares replica results with actual data flow at various Reynolds numbers. The research reveals that while the model excels at replicating turbulent flows at similar Reynolds numbers to those used in training, it struggles with flows at significantly different Reynolds numbers even with the enhanced sampling technique. The most impressive results from using variance terms in sampling procedures hold significant potential for future research in coherent, turbulent flows. The work also lays the groundwork for applying similar techniques to improve other coherent, turbulent flow simulations like boundary layer separation and turbulent round jets. The study's findings have the potential to contribute to a deeper comprehension of turbulent flow dynamics, especially if combined with analytical models and other simulation tools. This research can serve as a starting point for several potential areas of investigation, like enhancing the model with a better discriminator architecture or using neural operator-based methods to improve flow simulations. The study's results also suggest that training the model with data from pre-turbulent flow conditions may lead to better performance when facing unknown initial conditions. The research provides preliminary analysis of several promising extensions, such as using variance terms in sampling procedures and comparing original and sampled residual vectors. Deep neural network classifiers have revolutionized the field of computer science, particularly in image recognition and object detection, due to their exceptional performance and efficiency. Nonetheless, these networks suffer from a significant flaw: they are incapable of providing accurate confidence levels for their predictions. This major shortfall stems from the way the networks are typically trained on labeled data, as the loss functions used in training only focus on predicting the correct output labels rather than the model's confidence in those predictions. To tackle this issue, researchers have proposed various alternative training objectives that aim to simultaneously produce accurate predictions and associated confidence levels. One such objective is the minimum amount of reliable distributional change (MRC) that has shown promising results in multiple tasks and scenarios. However, MRC is computationally expensive and has a tendency to produce overly cautious predictions. To address this limitation, this paper introduces an enhanced model training objective called the maximum reliable distributional gain (MRG), which builds upon MRC by incorporating three key components: a noise-based data augmentation technique, a generalized expected loss function, and a customized learning rate schedule. Experimental results across four distinct visual classification tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of MRG, as it outperforms MRC and other baseline methods in terms of performance and prediction confidence. The code for this paper is available on GitHub at the specified URL. With MRG, models trained on visual domains can serve as a starting point or benchmark for other research in reliable deep neural networks.

To fairly assess reinforcement learning algorithms, we propose a method using a variable curriculum. This approach involves adjusting the curriculum in a predetermined manner to test each algorithm multiple times, thus providing a comprehensive evaluation. We introduce a metric called the optimal cumulative return under the original curriculum settings as the performance benchmark. Then, we establish a statistical test to compare the performance of different algorithms based on the observed data. To enhance the reliability of our results, we suggest implementing multiple independent evaluations. Finally, we illustrate the usability of our method by applying it to a set of simple causal models. Moreover, we suggest a new method to generate diverse curricula, which can also be utilized to create more complex causal structures by filling in missing transition probabilities. This technique allows us to explore the boundaries of our variable curriculum framework. Ultimately, we outline future research paths to explore other methods for generating curricula and testing reinforcement learning algorithms. The code is available online.

Time-dependent process changes pose challenges for existing approaches in process mining, which typically focus on static processes. A recent method called Dynamic Conformance Checking uses sequence data to analyze and identify deviations from known processes, even in the presence of temporal changes. Although it can handle dynamic processes, the Dynamic Conformance Checking method is only applicable to closed loops of processes and requires additional information about process behavior from past observations. A new algorithm called DCReplay is designed to address these limitations by enabling the detection of process changes and conformance checking using only current sequence data and established reference processes. Like process conformance checking methods, Dynamic Conformance Checking relies on graph-based models that compare actual and expected process paths. However, previous implementations of these methods were prone to errors caused by similar paths with different meanings due to a lack of context, leading to inaccurate process change detections. To overcome this limitation, a new method called Dynamic Conformance Checking on Context-dependent graphs is proposed. This method involves building context-dependent models from closed-loop process data and using these models to analyze process changes and conformance checking. Since this approach requires building models from data, their quality depends on the quantity and relevance of the underlying data. A novel method called DCReplay is presented as an alternative to these context-dependent models. This method enables process change detection and conformance checking without building process models from data. Instead, it uses established reference processes to forecast expected process paths and compare them with actual sequences. Since this approach is based on individual process paths rather than overall process contexts, it is susceptible to errors caused by similar but contextually distinct process paths. A new graph-based approach called Dynamic Conformance Checking on Dependability graphs is proposed as an alternative to these methods. This approach focuses on process changes and conformance checking from a dependability perspective, using graph models that take into account the context, similarity, and relevance of process paths. Dependability graphs represent relationships between process steps and their contextual dependencies and can be constructed from closed-loop process data containing information about process behavior, data relevance, and graph context. A novel algorithm called Dependability Conformance Checking is designed to analyze these graphs in order to identify process changes and deviations from expected paths. This approach can also handle multiple types of process paths by building separate dependability graphs for each type. In quasiperiodic lattices, certain conditions can cause a reentrant shift between the localization and delocalization of light as the transmission strength varies. This study employs an optical waveguide network based on the Octagonal Fibonacci quasiperiodic arrangement to experimentally and numerically investigate this phenomenon. Our findings show that near the critical point of this reentrant transition, a minor change in the transmission strength can switch between fully delocalized and localized states, with the potential for observing dynamical phenomena like hysteresis and memory effects. This research provides an example of how quasiperiodic arrangements can give rise to intricate and multifaceted phenomena that may lay the groundwork for the discovery of new principles underlying non-linear, non-equilibrium phenomena in these structures. Even though neural models can produce high-quality program code on their own, they often rely on feedback from other sources, including program analyzers that can be time-consuming to develop and run. This leads to a significant bottleneck in large-scale program-generation systems, which can't utilize these models at scale. This paper introduces an innovative approach that leverages weak supervision from a simple, fast, and easy-to-develop static program analyzer to significantly improve the performance of neural models in generating programs. This technique, called guided program iteration, allows a neural model to iteratively refine its program suggestions based on static analyzer feedback, without requiring any additional training parameters. This approach was tested on two challenging program-generation tasks, namely generating API function implementations in Java and refining the HTML user interface of web applications. The evaluation showed that guided program iteration can produce accurate and usable programs, surpassing the capabilities of the underlying neural model when trained without any additional training, including programs generated through reinforcement learning. Notably, this approach achieved particular success in addressing one of the primary drawbacks of neural program synthesis methods, which often produce programs that are difficult to understand and poorly perform their intended function. In comparison to more advanced program analyzers, this method demonstrated a notable trade-off between its analysis precision and its speed, with the ability to scale to large programs and help future neural models that can outperform it. This paper's innovative approach to combining neural models and program analysis also paves the way for other applications, such as refining existing programs. This could have a big impact on the industry, as there is now a viable solution for developers who struggle with complex program-generation tasks, such as building entire operating system components or the entire front-end of a web application, with minimal human input. This method should also be of interest to the broader machine-learning community, as it shows that a simple, fast, and easy-to-develop analyzer can leverage the underlying structure of neural networks, exploiting the patterns extracted by the neural model during training, with the potential to transfer this technique to other code-related tasks that involve generating or refining existing code. This approach can be further improved by using more precise analyzers, refining the static analyzer's feedback to the neural model, and exploring other guidance mechanisms. Notably, we present the first examples of publicly-key encryption schemes capable of withstanding authoritarian coercion mechanisms for data recovery, encryption, and multi-user settings. Our solutions showcase innovative applications of classic problems such as key-exchange protocols and identity-based encryption. Additionally, we propose a publicly-key encryption scheme capable of withstanding coercion for a single user, but our research highlights the inherent limitations when extending this to a multi-user setting. Our research contributes to both theoretical research and practical applications, and holds significant potential for further exploration. By doing this for several operators with varying properties, we gather sufficient information to estimate the impact of these transitions on the accuracy of direct determinations of the charm quark mass. Our results indicate that if the charm quark mass is calculated under the conditions applicable to the bottom to charm transition, it would be overestimated by about 10 MegaeV. Additionally, our work provides a method for evaluating the theoretical uncertainty associated with such calculations, and it highlights the significance of such approaches in understanding the fundamental properties of the charm quark. Our study also introduces a new approach for analyzing how the mass of a heavier quark is influenced by the properties of the medium in which it exists, and it demonstrates that even a small difference in such conditions can lead to noticeable discrepancies in the mass of the charm quark. Nonetheless, our findings suggest that if the mass of the charm quark is accurately measured under the right conditions, it may be determined to a precision of no more than 5 MegaeV. Deep learning models excel at image processing and recognition, and are frequently applied in healthcare and security fields. Nonetheless, the lack of transparency in these models regarding their decision-making process hinders their adoption in high-stakes situations. This study initiates a comprehensive investigation into making artificial intelligence (AI) more explainable. We consolidate various XAI techniques and methods derived from neural networks' training and inference stages. Specifically, we examine four popular training methods and 13 inference methods, before presenting a representative neural network designed for efficient performance. This efficient network is then used as a baseline to test the effectiveness of each inference method in enhancing the network's performance, both with clean and manipulated data. The results reveal that different methods yield superior outcomes depending on specific criteria, and that some methods surprisingly outperform others, even those closely related. Additionally, we observed significant variability in methods' performance across clean and manipulated data sets. We hope this study's findings will serve as a guide for researchers seeking to develop new XAI techniques, and contribute to the development of open-source AI tools. All code and datasets employed in this study are available for replication at the address stated in the references.

We investigated the influence of the Koster-Cronenberger ladder on the Heisenberg spin exchange interaction in a silicon crystal lattice, specifically for substitutional and interstitial dopants along the $<100>$ direction. Our study suggests that a precise control over the position of dopants is crucial for optimizing the exchange interaction in quantum devices, such as spin-based logic gates and quantum processors, built on silicon platforms. Additionally, our work highlights the importance of incorporating the exchange interaction in tight-binding models used for theoretical simulations of silicon-based quantum devices. As the field continues to evolve, we anticipate that our framework will become an essential tool for designing and understanding the physics behind various silicon-based quantum devices.

Notably, our findings show that in certain three-partite codes based on the Mermin-Holder box operator, the quantum nonlocality arises solely from a single pair of parties, illustrating the interplay between quantum nonlocality and entanglement in code units. Furthermore, our study shows that certain four-partite code contexts exhibit profound quantum nonlocality, exhibited through an unavoidable context in one of the parties. This phenomenon cannot be explained by studying fewer parties and demonstrates the genuine multi-partite nature of this quantum nonlocality. In addition, our analysis identifies the minimal number of qubits required in each party to achieve this level of quantum nonlocality. We also propose a novel, robust four-partite context, based on the Pauli-X gates, that exhibits this complex quantum nonlocality. This finding is accompanied by a detailed analysis of the properties and functionality of this new context. This new context can be realized using ion trap technology and may provide a suitable paradigm for investigating multi-partite quantum nonlocality in quantum systems. Ion trap simulations of this context suggest that this level of quantum nonlocality cannot be achieved through near-term, shallow quantum experiments. This phenomenon underlines the complexity that can arise in multi-partite quantum systems and the challenges associated with studying these systems one party at a time. This study is intended to spark a comprehensive investigation of robust quantum nonlocality in exceptional product codes, encompassing various contexts and applications. As massive spectroscopic surveys are increasingly conducted with astrobots, ensuring safe and efficient trajectories is crucial. To tackle this challenge, a novel framework combines formal verification and optimization techniques to design collision-free and time-optimal trajectories. By leveraging a bounded subscription model and solving a finite-state reachability problem, the framework identifies the safest trajectory subset. Then, it employs iterative linear programming to find the most efficient option within this subset, minimizing energy consumption and observing time. To verify and evaluate this approach, we develop a case study centered on the K2 galaxy cluster and featuring astrobots powered by three different propulsion methods. Computer simulations demonstrate that our method outperforms both a simple recursive algorithm and a hypothetical optimal solution obtained through exhaustive search. The framework's astrobot trajectory performance is also compared to that of human-operated spacecraft, revealing a significant gap in efficiency. To address this disparity, we propose a strategy to gradually transition observational time on these galaxy clusters to astrobots. This proposal is based on the premise that astrobots will play a crucial role in the future of extensive spectroscopic surveys, enabling the study of rare cosmic objects and facilitating the development of a universal galaxy formation theory. To this end, we outline a roadmap for verifying and efficient astrobot trajectories and advocate for the adoption of formal verification techniques in astrobotics, which can also benefit other space missions. Lastly, we suggest that researchers collaborate with space agencies and industrial partners to develop more sophisticated verification frameworks, taking into account the capabilities and limitations of these agencies and industries. This collaborative effort is essential to successfully implement formal verification methods for astrobots in future massive spectroscopic surveys. Moreover, we anticipate that the development of these methods will lead to other significant contributions to the field of astrobotics, which will be critical for the success of these surveys in the years to come. Ultimately, this research has the potential to shape the future of astrobotics and the direction of galaxy cluster observations from space, with far-reaching implications for both the field of astrobotics and the study of these cosmic structures. By applying an inversion formula, we are able to establish a direct connection between these series and certain Fourier coefficients, achieving a precise, explicit expression as a result. Consequently, this method enables us to create mock Eisenstein series, even when the underlying space is highly non-trivial. Moreover, this framework also reveals a connection between certain multiple Dirichlet L-series and a specific class of mock modular forms. Our proposed solution involves training a dialogue system using a type of regularization called adversarial training, which enables it to produce more precise results even when confronted with unreliable role descriptions. The method involves training two models simultaneously – one model produces a role description, while the other model strives to contradict it. The goal of this approach is to train the dialogue system to pay close attention to the role descriptions, even when they are inconsistent, which helps the system perform better in natural conversations. We put the adversarial training method to the test on two different large-scale datasets and found that it consistently produces a 10% improvement in user relevance when evaluating the system's interactions with real users. Effective decision-making methods are crucial for managing diseases that affect agricultural productivity and profitability, often involving complex relationships between variables. In the case of strawberry management, a key disease control issue is the fungus Verticillium, which can lead to significant yield and profit losses if not properly addressed. Given the challenges of collecting timely and reliable data, agricultural practitioners face difficulties in making informed, data-driven decisions to optimize yields and profits while minimizing control costs. To tackle this problem, a novel approach is proposed, combining a computational biology method for parsing laboratory data with a machine learning technique to build a predictive model that quantifies the economic impact of disease pressure on strawberry management practices. Specifically, this proposed framework utilizes genetic algorithm-based feature selection to identify key variables, which are then used to build an optimal quantitative regression model. The performance of this proposed approach was evaluated using historical data from a strawberry farm, comparing it to a standard linear regression model. Results showed that the new approach yielded more accurate predictions, demonstrating its effectiveness as a practical solution for addressing disease management challenges in the agricultural industry. Furthermore, this method's scalability and flexibility make it applicable to other similar problems in computational biology. The code developed for this research has been made publicly accessible, enabling others to build upon and expand this work. Additionally, the framework may be adapted for other quantitative regression scenarios. For more information, please visit https://github.com/leowei1120/Disease-Economic-Impact-Model. For instance, it could be applied to modeling the economic effects of antibiotic resistance development in livestock by identifying key variables and optimal quantitative models that quantify profitability and productivity losses due to resistance. This research provides a crucial foundation for developing decision-making tools that leverage computational biology methods, facilitating collaboration between computer scientists and biologists and paving the way for addressing more complex problems at the intersection of these disciplines. In our research, we propose a multi-task learning approach, grounded in the concept that video subtitle information can be used to view the video environment and understand its semantic content. The empirical evaluations conducted across four distinct datasets demonstrate notable improvements in mean average precision scores, with particularly notable gains observed in scenes featuring complex backgrounds. We consider the Airy particle in a random energy landscape and examine the location of the first degenerate point, denoted as $\lambda_1$, as we move the surface according to its stationary version. By employing a combination of Taylor-based analysis and canonical surfaces, we significantly expand our understanding of this point and find that it marks the sudden onset of a new, faster decay in the variance of the normalized particle position at large times. This new decay rate is found to be extremely precise, with an accuracy of at least $O(N^{-2})$ for any $d \geq 4$. Moreover, we provide more detailed information about the first nondegenerate point, obtaining an accurate expression for the location $\lambda_1$ in terms of determinants. These findings, particularly the precise decay rate, are notable for being the fastest known decay of this type in any system of interacting Brownian motions. As an additional contribution, we establish that the point $\lambda_1$ is associated with the onset of asymptotically vanishing correlations between the particle and a hypothetical'mirror' particle moving in the same random landscape, and that these correlations become negative for larger displacements. As we move the surface more quickly, we are able to follow the evolution of $\lambda_1$ as it breaks into multiple distinct points. As the surface is moved even faster still, these points move even further apart and coalesce with other, previously distinct points, providing a complete picture of the spectral structure of the Laplacian on this family of canonical surfaces. This understanding is then utilized to create a highly precise analysis of the decoupling phenomenon in these systems. As a result, we are able to establish a significantly expanded definition of optimal decoupling, as well as a precise expression for the location of this new boundary in terms of logarithmic determinants. As an additional contribution, we establish that this new boundary is associated with the onset of asymptotically vanishing correlations between different components of the particle's motion. As we move the surface more quickly still, these components become negatively correlated over longer distances. As an even broader contribution, as an even broader contribution, we are able to establish that this phenomenon of growing negative correlations holds not just for these particular systems, but for any system of interacting Brownian motions in a random energy landscape, provided that the interactions are strong enough. These measurements are obtained through a differential acceleration method, involving the sudden interruption of data transmission between the CME's host station and the space laboratory. Such unexpected interruptions are classified as glitches and have a substantial impact on measurement outcomes, often distorting the predicted values by more than 10%. We have formulated a variant of the shortest path cover problem, specifically the k-strongest shortest path union cover problem, where the goal is to combine the k shortest paths between all pairs of nodes using a minimum number of unions. We have demonstrated that this problem has NP-Hard classification and that an approximate solution can be found using a polynomial-time algorithm with a logarithmic probability of error. Additionally, we have developed exact algorithms for limited input parameters, such as when k is 1 (the shortest path cover problem) or when the input graph consists of only two nodes. We have also established upper and lower bounds for k equal to 2 and 3, respectively. The graph resulting from combining the k shortest paths between all pairs of nodes has a specific property that may be of independent interest. We have termed this property the k-strongest shortest path intersection graph and have established that it shares a classification with the k-strongest shortest path union cover problem. Like the k-strongest shortest path union cover problem, the k-strongest shortest path intersection graph also has a classification of NP-Hard. Additionally, we have established that determining the minimum number of components in the k-strongest shortest path intersection graph has a classification of P. We have also established that the minimum number of components in the k-strongest shortest path union cover graph has a classification of NP-Hard. Two new algorithms were developed to address specific applications of the k-strongest shortest path cover problem. The first application involves identifying the minimum number of components needed to combine the k shortest paths in a graph that contains all possible paths between all pairs of nodes. The second application involves tracking the minimum number of components needed to combine the k shortest paths in a graph that contains only the k shortest paths between all pairs of nodes. Both of these algorithms were developed using a method known as parameterized approximation, but they differ in their ability to track the minimum number of components. The first algorithm was able to track the minimum number of components, but the second algorithm was not. The reason for this difference is because the graph that contains all possible paths between all pairs of nodes has a property known as a complete multigraph property. This property is significant because it was used to establish the classification of the k-strongest shortest path union cover problem and the k-strongest shortest path intersection graph. The graph that contains only the k shortest paths between all pairs of nodes does not have this property. The reason for this difference is because the k strongest shortest paths in this graph are not guaranteed to combine into a component.

In this study, a novel type of magnetophotonic crystal is analyzed, made from a thin metal film with a periodic array of holes, arranged in an airysquare configuration. When light with a specific wavelength and incident angle interacts with this metal film, a surface plasmon and a Rayleigh anomaly from the surrounding air interfere, resulting in the formation of a magnetic field that reverses direction every half wavelength. This interaction also creates additional optical features related to the magnetization of the film that can be adjusted by altering the thickness of the metal layer. When this layer is thin enough, the film's magnetization causes a noticeable shift in the long-wavelength branch of these features, resulting in a spectral range with negative permeability. Conversely, the film's magnetization can induce an enantiomeric morphological inversion at the point of zero wavelength, leading to the creation of left-handed surface plasmon modes. This unique functionality makes this magnetophotonic crystal suitable for the design of magnetically controlled left-handed waveguides and filters. Furthermore, the interplay between the surface plasmon and Rayleigh anomaly leads to polarization-dependent diffraction in this film, resulting in the creation of magnetic photonic crystals without magnetic fillings. These findings also demonstrate the potential of this system for the development of magnetically controlled optical filters and waveguides capable of separating left- and right-handed waves. Such technology could play a significant role in the creation of advanced optical communication systems. Additionally, researchers may employ this metal film's unique magnetic field properties to improve the sensitivity of magnetophotonic biosensors. Lastly, the unique optical features of this film provide a foundation for understanding the fundamental physics underlying surface plasmon phenomena. Consequently, this study is expected to contribute substantially to the advancement of magnetophotonic research and its potential applications. In recent years, knowledge distillation has proven an effective method for black-box model compression. This compression technique involves training a smaller student model on labeled output distributions from a pre-trained, high-performance teacher model. A new, cutting-edge approach to knowledge distillation is gaining traction - decision-based black-box knowledge distillation (DB3). In DB3, the student and teacher models make decisions based on input instances, with the student then being trained on output distributions from the teacher model. This compression technique yields superior performance when compared to conventional knowledge distillation methods. However, a significant drawback of DB3 is the large amount of labeled data required from the teacher model. This limitation stems from the fact that DB3 relies on decision outputs from the teacher model that are highly accurate, a requirement that is difficult to satisfy in many real-world scenarios. This paper investigates new DB3 approaches that leverage noisy data from the teacher model, with one proposed method involving the selection of top predicted classes by incorporating an uncertainty quantification technique. Another approach involves the application of a non-linear transformation to map low-quality outputs to more accurate output distributions. Experimental results have demonstrated the efficacy of these approaches in allowing DB3 to utilize noisy data, with a further finding highlighting the relationship between data quality and loss functions. Various factors that influence the performance of DB3 in scenarios with noisy data are explored and evaluated across different scenarios, with the paper's proposals showing superior performance when compared to conventional knowledge distillation methods. This research's findings have the potential to make a significant contribution to the compression of deep neural networks via knowledge distillation. 

This work is distinct from conventional knowledge distillation methods, with which it differs in the following key ways. Firstly, in DB3, the student and teacher models make decisions on input instances, with the student then being trained on output distributions from the teacher model. Secondly, DB3 leverages decision outputs from the teacher model. Thirdly, DB3 can be used with noisy data from the teacher model. 

We begin by outlining two proposed DB3 approaches. In the first scenario, where there are multiple classes, we investigated the top predicted class in each sample. We developed a technique involving uncertainty quantification, with the application of a specific loss function resulting in the best performance. In the second scenario, with a single class, we explored the use of a non-linear transformation to map low-quality outputs to more accurate output distributions, with an evaluation across different transfer functions. 

Our research's findings have a range of potential extensions and variations, with topics for further exploration

Additionally, we explore the relationship between the strong geodetic number and the minimum geodetic number in S, and establish an upper limit of (|S|+1) for the strong geodetic number when compared to the minimum geodetic number in S. We also examine the concept of strong geodetic subsets and the unique geodetic subset in a graph, and present an example of a graph that has a unique strong geodetic subset that is not a strong geodetic subset itself. Even though imitation learning can efficiently learn tasks from limited labeled data, it still relies on a large pool of unlabelled demonstration data. This problem becomes severe in resource-constrained settings where labeled samples have significant value. To tackle this issue, this study proposes a novel algorithm called TRAIL that leverages unlabeled demonstrations within the same order of sample efficiency as regular imitation learning. By establishing a game-theoretic framework and utilizing the least squares method, TRAIL accurately estimates the optimal policy parameter and achieves significantly better sample efficiency. Experimental results validate the performance of TRAIL, revealing it achieves comparable or better outcomes than standard imitation learning methods while using only a small fraction of the unlabeled data. Furthermore, this study analyzes the optimal sample complexity of TRAIL and provides an intuitive explanation for its efficient use of data through the visualization of a simple case. TRAIL's code is available at https://github.com/hanghi88/TRAIL.

Co-Imitation Learning is the first method for imitating both experts and random players, allowing multiple-nation learning where you can learn from interactions with players from various optimization objectives. This approach addresses the limitation of conventional imitation learning, which only allows you to learn from labeled demonstrations. Our algorithmic framework includes two key components: (1) a two-layer model that effectively combines diverse optimization targets and (2) an optimized training procedure with incremental model updates. We demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of Co-Imitation Learning by showing that it can learn from interactions with an expert and a random player, resulting in performance surpassing that of both the expert and the random player. Our results show that Co-Imitation Learning can learn policies that outperform those learned through conventional imitation and reinforcement learning, as well as learn multiple optimal policies simultaneously. Additionally, we explore the method's application to learning multiple kitchen manipulation tasks and a self-driving car track. In reinforcement learning-based machine translation, the primary challenge lies in designing an optimal action space for the models to learn from. While previous methods simply treat each word's vocabulary as the action space, our innovative approach proposes a dynamic action space structured around sentence structures and phrasal semantics. We demonstrate that leveraging this optimized action space, derived from strong parser and semantic role labeling tools, enhances the performance of reinforcement learning models, leading to better overall performance and more robust learning dynamics. Our results show significant improvements over state-of-the-art translation systems, with scores of 37.57 for BLEU in the full test set of the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task. Moreover, our models achieve substantial gains in both parallel and sparse reward settings, with performance consistently better than that of an state-of-the-art strong baseline model. We also find that models learning in this optimized action space exhibit distinct learning patterns, with action dependence varying greatly as they progress through training. This phenomenon is particularly evident when comparing models trained on subdomains, which show marked action distribution shifts at the start of training, with a more gradual dependence on previous actions as they progress. Our work represents a pioneering exploration into the possibilities of structured action spaces for reinforcement learning-based machine translation, with numerous opportunities for further research and development. The code and models developed during this project are openly accessible online. 

Keywords: reinforcement learning, machine translation, structured action spaces, semantic role labeling, parser tools.

A new method has been developed that uses a camera to take multiple images at the same time it calculates the end-effector's position. This method estimates and removes any movement caused by the robot's position changes and its built-in vibrations, as well as any natural blurring, allowing it to accurately calculate the end-effector's position even when the robot is moving its arms quickly. The Web's impact on the spread of misinformation and political polarization is a pressing concern, with clear effects on society. However, the ease of accessing news articles, social media, and online forums has made it difficult to study users' browsing habits dynamically. To address this challenge, we introduce a theoretical framework that allows us to dynamically observe users' browsing habits and measure the influence of their online interactions within a social network. By applying this framework to a dataset of users' browsing habits from Wikipedia, we demonstrate that the spread of misinformation and political polarization among users is primarily driven by their browsing habits rather than the structure of the Web graph. Additionally, we found that a dynamic ranking system, which considers the frequency of users' transitions between articles, can identify and rank the spread of polarization and misinformation more effectively than traditional static ranking methods. Furthermore, we developed a method to estimate the influence of users' online interactions within a social network and verified its applicability to real-world networks by conducting experiments on Wikipedia's dynamic subgraphs. Lastly, we propose a technique to monitor the spread of polarization and misinformation over time by utilizing Wikipedia's edit history and term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) analysis. Our study's framework and approach can be adapted to study the spread of polarization and misinformation on other dynamic networks, such as Twitter. By exploring alternative dynamic ranking methods, we also look forward to gaining insights into the effectiveness of various algorithms within this new framework. All of our code is available at https://github.com/linwoodfeng/DynamicRank.

Our research reveals that in quantum mechanics, an open system can engage in a two-way information exchange with its surroundings, contrary to popular belief that there's only forward information flow. We demonstrate this conceptually through a scenario involving a single photon interacting with a highly entangled two-partite system; it's shown that the system's state remains fully correlated with the environment, exhibiting non-local properties even when separated by vast distances. Furthermore, even if the system's state becomes imperfect due to various factors such as spontaneous emission, scattering, or darkening, its continued connection to the environment allows for precise reconstruction of the system's original state. These findings form the basis of a new quantum communication protocol, enabling the reliable transmission of quantum information between two locations without the need for a direct quantum connection. This protocol leverages the non-local properties of the system's state to efficiently handle tasks like quantum teleportation and entanglement swapping. Notably, this approach surpasses existing quantum communication techniques and has potential applications in the development of robust and efficient quantum networks. Additionally, this work indicates possibilities for the exploration of new phenomena related to non-locality and information manipulation. This could be particularly relevant in the realm of quantum mechanics, where there's still much to be understood about the intricate relationships between systems and their environments. We've proposed an idea to combine the $a$ anomaly and the QCD axion while incorporating the dilaton, linking the axion field to the SU(3)$_{L}\times\)SU(2)$_{L}\times\)U(1)$_{Y}$ symmetry via a non-linear realization. This concept, referred to as the '$a$u$MSM$, builds upon the'vector triplet axion' model proposed by Ji and Lee. The $a$u$MSM$ successfully resolves the strong CP paradox and fortifies the electroweak vacuum's stability. Moreover, this model anticipates the existence of axion-like particles with masses spanning from below 1 eV to over the Higgs mass, their couplings to both matter and other axion-like particles being highly sensitive to the dilaton's properties. The $a$u$MSM$ also encompasses the Peccei-Quinn symmetry, leading to the axion's near vanishing gluon coupling, leaving it slightly greater than $10^{-3}$. The model's predictions can be empirically validated or disproved by means of: direct or indirect detection of the axion, its relatives, or the axion's triplet partner; determination of the axion's gluon coupling via $K^+$ decay width means; discovery of the dilaton, with mass spanning from over 1 GeV to below 1 eV, along with its specific couplings systematized in the paper's appendix. The $a$u$MSM$ model offers novel, testable answers to three fundamental questions of particle physics. This model offers the most comprehensive framework to date for interpreting the anomalous $U$-meson decay within the context of the Peccei-Quinn axion models. Moreover, it provides the most compelling explanation for the absence of any significant direct or indirect evidence for the dilaton, a phenomenon that, given the axion's proximity to its "weakness" threshold, is inevitable within the $a$u$MSM$. The $a$u$MSM$ model's additional feature is its incorporation of the axion-like particles, rendering it the most comprehensive and all-encompassing theoretical framework for the benefit of both high-energy and low-energy particle physics research communities. constructed from 1.4 million spectroscopic observations. Of these candidates, 34,000
were identified as potential interacting doubles with irregular light curves. This paper
describes the methodology used to build this large dataset of binaries. It reports the
success rates of follow-up observations in the Local Volume, the distribution of orbital
periods, and the types of spectroscopic classifications obtained. The majority of the

hidden by their companion stars and 2,623 candidates with unusual binary configurations. MongoDB's current implementation of multi-document atomicity is based on four variants of snapshot isolation: strict, conservative, snapshot, and semi. Our research involves evaluating the concurrency control methods used in MongoDB's distributed system, specifically looking at the SHARDED CLUSTER deployment. We examine three popular MongoDB deployments - WIREDTIGER, REPLICASET, and SHARDED CLUSTER - and find that only two of the four isolation levels are followed in the first two deployments, and only find evidence of one concurrency control method in the third deployment. Our findings also show that the three deployments do not follow the recommended strong consistency model, and that the SHARDED CLUSTER deployment's concurrency control method may not adhere to the strict, conservative, and semi isolation levels. Our research includes testing various workloads and find that the WIREDTIGER and REPLICASET deployments may not follow the strong consistency model, and that the SHARDED CLUSTER deployment may not follow the strict, conservative, and semi isolation levels in all workload scenarios. Our research's implications suggest that applications relying on MongoDB for data management should review the database's concurrency control methods to ensure they align with required isolation levels. Our research is ongoing with plans to extend it to other NoSQL distributed databases. Our research is unique as it is the first to evaluate the concurrency control methods used in a popular distributed database, and is the first to examine MongoDB's concurrency control methods. Our research is also accompanied by evidence and includes a detailed analysis of the methods used in the database. The success of all deep learning models relies on high-quality, bias-free datasets.  However, since datasets are often implicit in biases, the models developed from them will likely suffer from decreased generalizability in real-world applications, including medical image analysis.  One possible solution to this problem is dataset enhancement, which involves using multiple datasets to combine their distinct strengths.  Even though research has been done in this area, there are still several roadblocks that prevent the generalization of such methods to various tasks and modalities in medical image analysis, such as enhancing datasets for different imaging modalities rather than enhancing datasets for specific tasks.  In order to overcome these limitations and improve the generalizability of models in medical image analysis, a new simple yet effective method called Coarse-to-Fine Domain Generalization Synthesis is proposed.  This method works by first using a dataset that is similar in appearance to the target dataset and is derived from a coarser modality, and then using another dataset that is derived from a more detailed modality and contains more meaningful biases.  Even though the method is straightforward, the way that samples are weighted during the training process makes it difficult to achieve optimal results.  In order to address this challenge, a new weighting strategy called the Generalized Cross-Entropy method is proposed.  This method works by iteratively updating the weights of each dataset based on the performance of the model, and has the benefit of easily integrating new datasets with minimal training time.  In order to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method, several experiments were conducted on enhancing datasets for different imaging modalities, such as enhancing MRI datasets that are similar in appearance to CT scans, and enhancing datasets for specific tasks, such as enhancing datasets for breast tumor segmentation.  The results of these experiments showed that the method works well on various datasets, including public and private datasets, and outperformed several state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin.  In order to facilitate the advancement of this research, the proposed method is open-sourced and available on GitHub.  In addition to the method, the code used to conduct the experiments, the datasets used, and the model weights are also available online.  It is hoped that this research will contribute to the development of medical image analysis models that can generalize well across different datasets and imaging modalities, and ultimately improve the accuracy of these models in real-world applications.  In order to achieve this goal, the author would like to invite researchers to join in the discussion and try out the proposed method on their own datasets
