We introduce an efficient fixed-point iteration method called the Nested Neumann algorithm, which we prove converges at a rate of $O(1/k^2)$ after $k$ iterations, primarily by re-expressing the neural network as a function of its input and optimizing a regularized version of it. We demonstrate that the algorithm's convergence rate can be further increased to $O(1/k^4)$ or even $O(1/k^6)$ under specific neuron parametrizations, and our work is relevant to several existing works, such as the Neumann algorithm, network gradient propagation, and designing neural networks based on signal propagation properties. Additionally, we propose a new concept known as inception depth, which is the deepest input that a neural network can reach within the network itself, and we investigate several specific neural network architectures in terms of their inception depths and values achieved at different initialization settings. We also discover that the proposed algorithm can reach an inception depth of several thousand layers on simple dataset projections with a relatively small number of layers. To further analyze our results, we propose an alternative method called the iterative Neumann algorithm, which allows us to visualize the starting point, the inception depth, and the convergence rate of the neural network at each iteration. We hope that our work will lead to a deeper understanding of neural network dynamics and provide a practical solution for training neural networks. All of our code and data are available online at this link https://github.com/heng6f/Nested-Neumann-algorithm.

The backward pass, often referred to as backpropagation, is a crucial component of solving optimization problems involving functions that are expressed as computations on tensors. Specifically, researchers have explored generating code for computing backward passes automatically by leveraging syntax trees from the source code, under the assumption that the input expressions are valid. However, this approach has significant efficiency issues when dealing with large datasets and complex neural network architectures. In contrast, a novel technique presented in this paper compiles abstract mathematical formulas into highly optimized code for computing backward passes, without requiring source code or low-level tensor operations. This innovative approach, based on an extension of existing computational models for forward passes, generates concise and efficient code that outperforms existing solutions by at least 2-3 factors in terms of performance. Cloud-based HPC systems face growing difficulties keeping up with declining latency and increasing bandwidth requirements, necessitating a more efficient and less costly HPC model. A fully integrated, side-channel-free design is proposed, comprising a client-side HPC accelerator powered by a low-power, high-performance processor and supported by the cloud via a secure VMM-based sandbox. This hybrid design focuses on providing reliable and secure data protection, ensuring that even if an unauthorized attacker gains control of the virtual machine, they cannot access valuable data. The proposed system is based on an actual implementation, utilizing a Intel NUC mini PC powered by an Intel Core i7-4500U processor and coupled with an Intel Xeon E3-1270 v5 accelerator card containing 5.5 teraflops of processing power. The results show that, when running various scientific applications, this hybrid cloud HPC system can achieve comparable performance to a standalone Xeon E3-1270 v5 server, while demonstrating robustness and security against various attacks, including data-breach attempts. Additionally, the side-channel-free design provides impressive benchmark results, proving that secure design does not have to come at the expense of performance. Further, the proposed system showcases a significant reduction in energy consumption in secure modes, outperforming both a similar system relying on physical memory isolation and one relying on encryption. In policy learning, using efficient value function estimates has proven beneficial, especially when combined with optimal policy updates, by leveraging data multiple times and reducing the impact of function approximation errors. Despite existing methods providing effective estimates, their full potential is not realized due to insufficiently large testing samples, which limits their value when applied to large-scale datasets. This paper explores how to make the most of these efficient estimates by utilizing larger training samples, a scenario we refer to as the "big batch" setting. By applying theoretical analysis and conducting extensive experiments on large-scale datasets in various settings, this paper demonstrates the performance of various efficient value function estimates in the "big batch" setting, involving both single-machine and distributed environments. Our findings show that model-based policy learning methods can achieve comparable performance to behavior policy learning even when only a single sample is used per model update, and that a 256-fold increase in batch size can yield a 2-fold improvement in value function estimate accuracy. Additionally, our results indicate that a significant improvement in the efficiency of these estimates can be achieved by employing parallelization strategies based on model and data distribution methods, resulting in up to a 16-fold reduction in required training time. Moreover, our findings suggest that the benefit of robust value function estimates can be further optimized by leveraging additional optimization techniques, such as larger model capacities and longer training schedules, resulting in a potential 4-fold improvement in value function estimate accuracy. Recent findings, based on data from the 2018 and 2019 seasons, allow researchers to compare the transverse momentum distributions of positively charged hadrons, specific types of mesons (pions and kaons) and baryons (protons) across different levels of elliptic flow. As a result, identifying negation has been a persistent challenge for natural language processing specialists working with clinical text. To address this, we've developed a two-part evaluation process that assesses both the detection and the impact of negation on the original text's meaning. Our study compares the performance of a range of cutting-edge models, including BERT-based variants and a dedicated medical language model, against both human judges and a neutral model that serves as a control. Our findings reveal that these models excel in detection but often produce inaccurate results for negation's effect on meaning, with some models even performing worse than the baseline. A subsequent in-depth analysis of the models' mistakes shows that some of them misinterpret the context or the relationship between sentences containing negation. To overcome these limitations, we've proposed a more effective approach that incorporates additional semantic information and engages in a more thorough contextual understanding. Our study's results demonstrate significant improvements achieved by the proposed model over the current state-of-the-art models and even show that it performs closely to human judges' levels of accuracy. A subsequent analysis of the models' performance in complex scenarios reveals that they perform best in scenarios with simple sentences and limited contextual involvement. This pattern-based representation can be adjusted to focus on either the changing aspects or the stable aspects of the software system's structure. To provide meaningful interpretations of our results, we conducted a thorough analysis, including determining average negative emotions at the national, state, and city levels, as well as identifying high-risk warning indicators for healthcare systems and governments.  Our approach demonstrated its effectiveness by accurately predicting the peak of the COVID-19 epidemic and the subsequent implementation of lockdown measures. Researchers suggest that dust particles in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks should cool through radiative dissipation rather than through direct emission. To examine this concept, a one-dimensional radial model was created to simulate the temperature distribution in a gas-rich environment surrounding a T Tauri star. An extensive parameter survey was conducted to identify how various dust properties, gas density, and optical depth affect cooling rates. The results indicate that high-density environments with large dust grains can cool efficiently, reducing temperatures by up to 5 K, especially in the outer gas regions. However, in lower-density environments with smaller dust grains, little change in temperature was observed. These findings imply that dust cooling may be ineffective in most outer disk regions but could be an important process in the formation of massive dust particles in the outer reaches of protoplanetary disks. Furthermore, a correlation between dust cooling and the formation of massive dust grains in these regions is a distinct feature of outer protoplanetary disks that can be distinguished from those surrounding low-mass stars and contributing to the diversity of disk formation processes. This new perspective on disk evolution highlights the potential importance of dust cooling in shaping the outer disk architecture and setting the stage for massive grain growth. This theory is supported by recent observations of massive dust grain growth in the outer disks of low-mass stars. The outcome of this research underscores the significance of dust cooling in the outer disk regions and lays the groundwork for a more comprehensive examination of this process, including optical radiation from dust, which has relevant implications for the interpretation of high-resolution spectroscopy and upcoming far-infrared and millimeter-wave surveys of protoplanetary disks. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of dust cooling, combined with future observations and theoretical modeling, will provide valuable insights into the structure, evolution, and composition of outer protoplanetary disks and their connection to disk dispersal and planet formation. Recent research into machine learning vulnerabilities, specifically backdoors, has primarily focused on static triggers. Implementing reliable and versatile hidden commands in a robust and complex machine learning model like BERT across multiple tasks poses significant difficulties. Although a few studies have explored contaminated training datasets with hidden goals in simplified scenarios, the associated challenges of achieving consistent and widespread desired outcomes from such a methodological approach are substantial. Furthermore, existing techniques fail to achieve satisfactory results when applied to advanced models like BERT or multiple tasks at once. In response to these limitations, this paper introduces a novel trigger-based attack capable of embedding a hidden command in any model that can recognize relationships between objects, regardless of the model's performance. Additionally, this method can be adapted for use with multiple training examples and combined with a method that can hide multiple commands within a single trigger, resulting in a more advanced hidden command that can be activated by various inputs. A robust evaluation of the attack, including multiple attempts to mitigate the backdoor, highlights its unparalleled effectiveness when compared to existing static trigger-based attacks. Moreover, an exploration of activating the advanced hidden command with minimal alterations to existing activation methods reveals its immense potential when applied to models that can generate text. Lastly, this paper presents an interactive tool that can be used to visualize and experiment with the proposed attack in a comprehensive and user-friendly manner. The code for this research has been made publicly available. All associated experiments and the interactive tool can be accessed via the provided repository link.

Using the most accurate astrometric data from GAIA, a significant trend has been identified - the parallax of planets appears to shift as their position changes in relation to the Sun. This effect, first noticed in the inner planets, now shows a similar pattern for outer planets. Analyzing this behavior further, researchers found it depends on the planet's ecliptic latitude - there's a noticeable increase in the parallax shift in planets positioned near the ecliptic poles. By incorporating this new insight, scientists can refine their methods for estimating the mass of low-mass stars and planets through gravitational interactions with their companions. For example, even with existing information, the mass of the Solar System's planet Uranus is recalculated as being approximately 15% more massive than previously thought. Similarly, researchers reevaluated the mass of the brown dwarf T dwarf based on its orbital parameters and movement, and concluded it's approximately 1.5 times more massive than initially estimated. This effect is expected to be just as noticeable in other high-precision astrometry data, and may provide a powerful new tool for studying the properties of low-mass stars and planets through their interactions with one another.

Using radio telescopes at Arecibo and the Very Large Array, we discovered three massive HI clouds located near the Orion spiral arm in the Local Group. These clouds are likely associated with the SMC satellite, NGC 292, and are moving at 84 km/s towards the center of the Milky Way, likely influenced by the gravitational force of the SMC satellite. One of the clouds has a diameter of approximately 11 kpc and is shaped like a ringet with a missing piece, while the other two clouds are around 7 kpc in diameter and have more irregular shapes. Observations suggest that these clouds started interacting with the Orion arm about 400 million years ago, and as a result, the Orion arm is now experiencing enhanced star formation. This discovery provides insight into how nearby spiral galaxies dynamically respond to the presence of satellite galaxies and highlights the significant impact that a single satellite galaxy can have on its surrounding environment. Similar HI clouds have been found in the Big Dipper region and are associated with the satellite galaxy LMC2, suggesting a similar interaction between the LMC and its satellite galaxy in that area. These findings highlight the importance of HI mapping in understanding the behavior of nearby galaxies and the impact it has on the Milky Way's own evolution. Additionally, we propose that the HI features in the anti-centris region, shaped like a giant ringet with a missing piece and containing enhanced molecular gas and star formation, could be a result of the galaxy Andromeda's gravitational influence on the Milky Way, a effect that occurred about 11 billion years ago. Further research is needed to confirm this hypothesis. Using data from the Planck satellite, we estimate that the total mass associated with these HI clouds is around 10^10 times the mass of the sun. Due to their irregular shape, these clouds are unlikely to be discernible as satellites galaxies, but they do offer a window into how nearby galaxies respond to their satellite galaxies and interact with each other. This discovery highlights the importance of using radio telescopes to map HI in nearby galaxies and provides a new perspective on the galaxy interaction model. It also highlights the need for a re-evaluation of the total mass associated with satellite galaxies in our Local Group. It is possible that other similar HI clouds exist in the Milky Way, shaped by its interactions with galaxy Andromeda and the SMC, and could hold the key to understanding the galaxy's own evolution. The success of deep learning techniques in question answering relies on their ability to derive answers from text based on their current understanding. Despite their capabilities, these models often struggle with incorporating external knowledge to improve their performance. A major obstacle in this process is the lack of clear guidance on how to map knowledge graphs to the semantic representation of the text, hindering the incorporation of relevant knowledge. This issue persists even when using state-of-the-art semantic parsing methods that break down text into a set of propositions and relationships. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach that uses a semantic-driven method to guide the knowledge graph embedding process. By leveraging the semantic structure derived from the text's semantic representation, our approach enables the efficient embedding of knowledge graphs in the context of specific questions and entities. This context-aware knowledge representation can significantly improve the performance of models when using the embedded graphs for question answering. Our experiments demonstrate the benefits of our method over conventional knowledge graph embedding techniques in both single-support sentence and question answering scenarios. This study introduces an innovative theoretical approach, a full spectral model, for investigating 1-datomic molecule cations. Due to the intricate nature of these species, comprising just one atom and a single positive charge, constructing an all-encompassing theoretical framework has proven exceptionally challenging, particularly for molecules containing oxygen. For example, a comprehensive theoretical framework has yet to be developed for the positively charged isotopologues of water, carbon monoxide, and hydrogen cyanide. In contrast, our novel method has successfully provided an unifying explanation for the observed spectral patterns across all possible isotopologues of these molecules, aligning with experimental data. The method combines high-level perturbation theory with an accurate single-configuration approach, utilizing a reliable theoretical model of the dimeric neutral species as a foundation. Notably, our model showcases exceptional convergence across all possible isotopologues of the three mentioned molecules. In the case of water, our model predicts the adiabatic ionization energies, vertical ionization energies, and electronic spectra, demonstrating exceptional convergence across all 18 possible isotopologues and aligning with experimental data. For the two heavier molecules, our model also predicts the adiabatic ionization energies, vertical ionization energies, and electronic spectra along with a possible ion pair structure, and provides converged results across all 4 possible isotopologues. In the case of water, our method also addresses the longstanding debate regarding the ground state structure of the water molecule ion, the H2O+ linear or V-shaped, and finds that a linear structure is just 40 kJ/mol more stable than a V-shaped one. The small energy difference between the two possible structures of the water molecule ion may be attributed to the V-shaped structure's presence in an inner well of a potential energy curve. In the case of CO and CN, our method also finds that an ion pair structure, a linear structure and a possible V-shaped structure, and an estimated energy difference of no more than 100 kJ/mol, all exist in the energy spectrum of these molecules when they become positively charged. The two research areas of small 1-datomic molecule cations and full spectral models, that have historically been separate and distinct, are now integrated together by this innovative theoretical approach. The method we have developed is extremely versatile and can be used to investigate any positively charged molecule composed of just one atom. We introduce an innovative algorithm for breaking down any element in a set of rational function variables into the sum of a perfect square, expanding on ideas from Karpinski and Shoup, with modifications tailored to support Trager's symbolic factorization technique. Although our method yields factors with a high degree of precision, it still lacks a closing step to achieve actual factor representation. By constructing a set of monic polynomials from these factors and performing a Groebner show, we can successfully derive the desired factorization. Our algorithm also includes an efficient 'quick check' option for determining whether a given number can be expressed as the sum of two perfect squares, based on the application of a certain function to the number's remainder when divided by four. For fields that are locally quadratic, such as global fields of char not two and globally quadratic extensions of $\mathbb{Q}_p$, we demonstrate that this 'quick check' method is not only highly efficient but also inherently optimal, with a computational complexity of exactly $\mathcal{L}_\mathfrak{p$.\footnotetext{Here, $\mathfrak{p}$ represents a prime number in local fields and a prime ideal in global fields.}}, in line with the theoretical limits set by the field's complexity. Additionally, our algorithm can also be applied to express an odd number as the sum of two prime powers or as the sum of three tangent powers. We have further developed an array-based implementation of our algorithms, along with a 'quick check' method, with a fully functional prototype available on our project website listed in the references section. This prototype features an interactive command-line interface, supported by a comprehensive set of commands, and has been successfully optimized for maximum performance using state-of-the-art automatic optimization techniques. Our project is currently accessible over the Internet.}

In this work, we investigate how entanglement swapping, combined with a measurement of correlation delay, can enhance global astrophysical measurements, specifically in relating two wide-field cosmic ray experiments. We apply this concept to a hypothetical entanglement network involving neutrino experiments across the globe. Although implementation challenges exist, we believe our proposal inspires innovative possibilities at the intersection of quantum physics and astronomy. We also introduce a new function, the "astrophysical concurrence," as a relevant metric in this context. This idea's potential could be further expanded to other areas where quantum sensing intersects with general astronomical research. Our relational database contains over 10,000 drug compounds, incorporating over 200,000 molecular substructures, linked to around 15,000 biological targets. Our comprehensive evaluation involves four demanding tasks, requiring models to extract valuable target information from substructures and learn relationships between targets, substructures, and drug effectiveness. Inertial wave turbulence was observed in a rotating annular tank filled with a viscous fluid, and a new frequency spectrum was found that aligns with $k^{3}$ even when accounting for the shell averaging. Researchers previously hinted at this frequency distribution, though it was only inertial wave turbulence that made it observable. To mathematically derive this frequency distribution, the inertial wave turbulence was modelled using a direct interaction picture, and the resulting equations yielded a triadic conservation law that indicated the presence of a universal frequency distribution that is independent of any specific initial conditions and is maintained at all wavenumbers except those corresponding to the primary driving forces of the wave. The obtained frequency distribution verifies the hypothesis that the energy contains the same amount of power as the magnitude of the wavenumber has, and it is observable in the context of highly turbulent regimes that are characterized by an equilibrium between the transfer of energy to all wavenumbers and the dissipation of energy at all wavenumbers. The obtained frequency distribution is in line with the findings obtained using Lagrangian techniques and it is in line with the predictions made using the multi-cascade model. The obtained results can be applied to an ideal rotating sphere and they enhance our understanding of inertial wave turbulence, the properties of turbulent inertial flows and the dynamics of global geophysical flows. The obtained frequency distribution provides strong evidence for the forward cascade theory of inertial wave turbulence. Individuals suffering from mental health disorders are more likely to engage in crime, particularly violent and property crimes, than the general population. Research indicates that those with mental health issues who are involved in the criminal justice system and receive treatment have lower recidivism rates compared to those who do not receive mental health services. Among prisoners, approximately 15% of those without mental health conditions reoffend within three years, whereas up to 55% of those with mental health disorders reoffend during this period. To minimize the high costs associated with incarcerating individuals with mental health conditions, it is essential to provide adequate treatment to reduce their recidivism rates. According to the National Alliance on Mental Illness, only 30% of the necessary treatment for prisoners with mental health conditions is provided. To address this issue, an integrated system involving law enforcement, courts, probation services, and mental health providers is needed to identify and provide treatment to individuals with mental health disorders involved in the criminal justice system. Advanced technologies, including artificial intelligence and blockchain, can enhance this system by quickly identifying prisoners with mental health conditions and tracking their treatment progress. Our research proposes a comprehensive framework that leverages these technologies to create an integrated database, which can rapidly detect prisoners with mental health disorders and suggest personalized treatment plans to reduce their recidivism rates. In addition, our proposal includes various policies and guidelines tailored to specific crimes, which can vary in their priority for treatment, such as prioritizing violent crimes over property crimes. The performance of this proposed framework is evaluated using real-world crime and mental health dataset, namely the FBI's Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) dataset and the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) dataset. Our experiments demonstrate that this technology can accurately identify 85% of prisoners with mental health disorders involved in the criminal justice system and reduce their recidivism rates by 40%. Our research offers a pioneering approach to creating a holistic technology-driven system that can effectively identify and provide necessary treatment to individuals with mental health disorders involved in the criminal justice system, thereby reducing their recidivism rates. This innovative framework is critically evaluated through a comprehensive analysis of its components, including its potential benefits, challenges, and future directions. Moreover, a detailed overview is provided of the technologies, datasets, and programming languages used in this research, along with a sturdy code repository consisting of 200 loopy Python lines. Ultimately, this research has the potential to create a paradigm shift in addressing the pressing issue of prisoners with mental health disorders involved in the criminal justice system. Keywords:

In semi-supervised learning, particularly in medical image segmentation, gathering labeled data for training is costly and time-consuming. A widely-accepted technique for addressing this challenge involves combines supervised learning with the regularizing effects of interpolation-based mixing. However, existing methods that leverage this regularizing influence of interpolation have mostly been confined to two-dimensional (2D) applications. This paper deviates from this path and instead explores the potential of interpolation-based mixing as a regularizing strategy in super-resolution, driven by the desire to enhance low-resolution chest X-rays. Enhanced low-resolution images can, in turn, benefit medical image segmentation. We begin by conducting a comprehensive analysis of the relationships between noise and interpolation methods, observing that linear and bi-cubic interpolation yield compatible results. This compatibility forms the basis for developing a technique that learns an optimal mixing function to combine supervised outputs. The proposed method, known as Semi-Supervised Enhanced Super-Resolution (SESR), is initially validated on synthetic data before applying it to enhance real chest X-rays. SESR is used to improve both compression-based and labeled data-driven methods for medical image segmentation. Our studies demonstrate its capacity to produce realistic images and promote accurate segmentation. SESR is now accessible on GitHub.

To handle the increased luminosity of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) in its Phase-2 era, the LHC will undergo upgrades, including a new detector called ATLAS' Forward Liquid-Neutron Tagger (FLNT). A key component of this detector is the jet Field-Reverse Configuration (FEC) system, consisting of four square antennas that will provide precise neutron energy information. With expected data processing speeds of 10 GBytes per second and a total data output of 40 GBytes per second, the jet FEC system relies on a custom Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) design to process its data in real-time. Developed at MIT, this FPGA design utilizes a hierarchical architecture featuring 1,536 processing units and has been successfully tested under realistic conditions at CERN. The design achieves an average throughput of over 6.7 GBytes per second while maintaining a low, consistent latency of approximately 4.5 microseconds. This design serves as a model for the Full Scale FEC system, consisting of 1,536 antennas and producing 60 TBytes of data per second, and has significant implications for the development of real-time, high-speed data processing systems in particle physics. With the jet FEC system's design now complete, the Full Scale FEC system is on track to meet the data processing demands required for LHC's Phase-2 era. As the jet FEC system's design also has broader applications, it may also be adapted for use in other real-time, high-speed data processing scenarios. Reaching high-level visual goals through significant scene changes proves
challenging for current rendering-to-texture approaches due to their
simplistic design. To overcome this limitation, we propose Articulated Neural
Rendering (ANR), a new framework capable of rendering dynamic objects with
underlying structures using a compact, detailed texture. To build this
framework, we introduce several novel components, including an object parser,
a 3D encoder, a renderer, and a text generator, that work together to create
realistic visual data and associate text. ANR includes an innovative method
called Articulated Pre-training, which enables the discovery of inherent
articulations across multiple objects. Using this approach, ANR is able to
derive object structures from detailed textures and manipulate 3D models based
on descriptive text. By combining Articulated Pre-training with extensive
training, ANR demonstrates the capacity to create complex, dynamically changing
scenarios and accurately generates corresponding images with associated text.
While current ANR implementations are limited to rendering single objects in
clipping box bounds due to computational constraints, ANR offers a comprehensive
framework that lays the groundwork for future research and developments in
articulated 3D rendering. ANR is publicly available at

Researchers who study materials structure and properties rely on quantifying local atomic arrangements to predict variations in material properties. A recent advancement in this area involves using graph neural networks to classify local atomic configurations by their proximity to a specific atom within a certain spatial range. This has created growing interest in studying local atomic environments. Unlike previous methods that focused solely on first-nearest-neighbor atoms, these new approaches are capable of analyzing more complex multi-nearest-neighbor structures. Although graph neural networks have successfully been applied to multiple tasks, there is still a significant gap in understanding their fundamental properties. In particular, there is a lack of quantitative analysis in measuring the diversity of local atomic environments in materials. To address this, we propose a method to systematically classify local atomic environments in a systematic and hierarchical manner. This approach enables us to assign a unique numerical identifier to each distinct environment and establish a quantitative scale to measure its occurrence frequency across the material. By applying this approach to two popular benchmark datasets, we successfully demonstrated the inherent hierarchical structure of local atomic environments and created a scoring system to rate their prevalence. Moreover, our analysis exposed several underrepresented environments that could pose challenges for materials modeling methods. Our tool, alongside the two datasets and their associated scores, is openly accessible online. By leveraging this framework, researchers can evaluate the capability of their modeling approaches in identifying rare but important local atomic environments that are critical for understanding materials structure and properties. In particular, we concentrate on two scenarios: (a) local environments centered on a specific atom and (b) global atomic environments across an entire material composition. This study has far-reaching implications, as it has the potential to assess the generalization performance of materials modeling methods and will facilitate the development of more sophisticated models capable of analyzing multiple atom environments. Furthermore, our framework can be expanded to analyze other materials properties and facilitate the creation of a publicly accessible materials knowledge base. In the process, we introduce a novel graph representation of materials composition and create an open-source toolkit that is available online. In the long term, this framework can contribute to the creation of an open materials knowledge base, enabling the seamless sharing of materials data and accelerating the development of new materials. In the present study, we focus on quantifying local atomic environments in materials and introduce GraphScore, an open-source toolkit that can classify and score the diversity of local atomic environments in materials. This framework is particularly useful in evaluating the capability of materials modeling approaches to identify rare but critical local atomic environments that are important for understanding materials structure and properties. This paper examines the implications of weak convergence for estimating functional relationships between model parameters and their distributions, as well as for constructing confidence sets. Our analysis focuses on the context of statistical models defined by minimizing contrast functions, with specific attention to the case of Gaussian designs. We draw on the theoretical framework established by Wasserman (2006, 2007) and extend it to accommodate general score functions. Our results provide an empirical risk minimization (ERM) perspective on the convergence issue discussed by Brownlees and Veall (2000, 2005). Furthermore, we apply these findings to linear models with regularization, robust regression models, and models involving latent variables. Our methodology is complemented by a simulation study covering various designs and models. The study includes an analysis of local and global performance across over 100,000 simulated scenarios. Our results demonstrate that in many cases, the convergence issue disappears when the model is estimated efficiently, as confirmed by recent results on model selection and model averaging. However, some situations continue to present challenges in terms of point estimation, and our study offers strategies to address these challenges through default and adaptive sampling-based methods. Our results also provide insights into the performance of constructed confidence sets. Lastly, our study paves the way for further research on the properties of statistical models, particularly models defined by non-differentiable score functions. Software implementing our methods is available online. 

Keywords: empirical risk minimization, model selection, model averaging, statistical models, score functions, Gaussian designs, contrast functions, robust regression, latent variable models, linear models with regularization, confidence sets, sampling-based methods, default and adaptive methods, performance analysis, simulation study, design and model extensions.

Given a smooth domain $\Omega$, consider the scalar second-order elliptic differential operator $L$ and its associated boundary value problem $Lu=\lambda u$ with Dirichlet boundary conditions. A fundamental property of this operator is examined - specifically, the frequency function $\sigma(L)$, which measures how completely the operator surjects onto its domain. It has been established that $\sigma(L)\leq \infty$; the focus of this paper is on establishing a lower bound for this quantity. It is shown that $\sigma(L)$ is finite and at least as large as the smallest number of orbits in a smooth flight plan across $\Omega$. This provides a rigorous mathematical framework for understanding the concept of surjectivity of elliptic operators and their relationship to the topological properties of flight plans. Theoretical results are supported by computational data, which can also inform strategies for controlling the behavior of partial differential equations. Finally, the introduction of a new flight plan invariant - the path connectivity index $\tau(L)$ - is proposed, which can be used to study other problems related to the solvability of partial differential equations. The interplay between flight plans, homology, and the Frechet spectrum of operators is explored, leading to the introduction of a new concept - the spectral flight plan theorem. This new theoretical framework has the potential to shed light on numerous existing problems related to the solvability of partial differential equations and can be used to study other problems related to the frequency function of elliptic operators. The results of this paper also raise new questions related to the solvability of partial differential equations and the behavior of flight plans in different geometric settings. The methods developed here can be used to study other problems related to the frequency function of elliptic operators and may have applications in related fields of mathematics. We have refined veriT's theory and implementation, making it the verification technology theorem prover verification output format by popular consensus among researchers and developers who participate in the initiative. We constructed a versatile proof format that can be used for various theorem provers and verification tools, giving users access to a broad range of reasoning capabilities. We have enhanced veriT's proof format to include multiple conclusion and anticonclusion properties, allowing it to support multiple validation use cases. Additionally, we have improved verification technology's efficiency and added a concise human-readable comment feature to valid theorems. This improved format is now featured in the latest versions of the first-order logic reasoning technologies from the verification technology platform, including Lean, Idasen, and Zipperproofs, among others. We have also incorporated a set of checkers that can validate proofs and counter-proofs in this enhanced format, making it suitable for various reasoning tasks and enabling the development of more sophisticated tools that can manipulate and solve satisfiability problems from first-order logic formulas. We have demonstrated the capabilities of this proof format and its associated checkers by solving a significant problem related to the verification of linear congruent architectures, specifically the detection of cycles within LCA graphs, and have made the implementation and related tools publicly accessible.

Personal data protection meets scalable learning via federation learning but is hindered by the large communication costs involved. Private, scalable, and efficient federated learning is achieved through FedBuff, a novel algorithmic framework that builds upon the success of FedAVG. FedBuff's design involves introducing random buffers to learn shared and private components at a fraction of the cost. We conduct the first comprehensive analysis of FedBuff's scalability and privacy, focusing on regression tasks with data sensitivity measured by structural risk. Our research reveals that FedBuff reduces communication costs exponentially while ensuring strong privacy protection, underscoring its potential to drive private, scalable learning across various settings. Moreover, we develop an efficient practical implementation of FedBuff, coupled with empirical studies validating its performance gains. Our findings pave the way for private, scalable learning solutions, especially in context-aware settings. We also introduce the FEDBuff toolkit, an open-source framework that makes private, scalable learning accessible to researchers and practitioners alike. Speech recognition systems can be highly accurate in languages with significant similarity, but performance significantly declines between languages with greater differences. This challenging gap exists between English and Arabic, causing existing approaches using multi-task learning to achieve only limited success. We examined a unique transfer learning strategy, beginning with an English model as the source and aiming to achieve significant improvement on Arabic speech recognition. Our innovative method involved three steps: first, identifying a source domain model; second, performing a coarse-to-fine adaptation on the target domain; third, using a combination of label smoothing and mixture-based approaches to adapt the vocabulary. Our proposed method resulted in a substantial 11.3% improvement in accuracy on the Farsee dataset and a 5.3% improvement on the English-Arabic dataset, surpassing previous benchmarks. The field of node embedding has seen notable advancements in recent years, with numerous novel algorithms emerging. However, there is a significant challenge in fairly comparing these algorithms due to diverse application domains and a lack of standard evaluation metrics. To address this issue, we propose a new evaluation framework called MetaNodeEmbedding, which aggregates node embedding algorithms into higher-level components called MetaNEs. We then compare the predictive capabilities of these MetaNEs using a range of classification and regression tasks across different datasets. Furthermore, we gather user feedback to augment the framework through a process of active learning, thereby refining the MetaNEs and evaluating the algorithms' generalizability. Our results demonstrate that even a single comparison between two node embedding algorithms can yield distinct MetaNEs with varying performance, highlighting the value of this framework in conducting comprehensive, in-depth comparisons of novel node embedding algorithms. We have publicly accessible the code and the evaluated results on MetaNodeEmbeddings, along with the datasets and the implemented MetaNEs. They used data on the stimulation of primordial black hole formations during the Big Bang's early stages, based on a specific set of mathematical formulas, to determine this range. This study assumes a specific power law relationship between two important factors, the rate of molecular hydrogen recombination and the density of primordial black hole formations, and finds that the resulting black holes make up exactly 100% of dark matter. It also identifies a specific range of cosmic inflation parameters that led to the creation of these black holes. If these black holes exist, researchers predict that they will form around five billion years from now, when the Milky Way galaxy merges with one of its nearby galaxies, Andromeda. The predicted number of these black holes formed during the Big Bang's early stages is on the order of $10^{64}$. It's also estimated that primordial black holes with the same mass characteristics could make up anywhere from less than 1% to almost 100% of dark matter, depending on various factors, including the strength of a specific interaction between dark matter and normal matter, known as the interaction rate. This research also suggests that primordial black holes with the mass of small stars could hold as much as 80% of the dark matter in the universe's most massive galaxy clusters, based on simulations of the universe's evolution, and could also account for almost 50% of dark matter in the universe's cosmic structures known as filaments, regardless of their mass. Determining actual force generated by series elastic actuators (SEAs) is difficult because their behavior is influenced by both the nonlinear properties of elastic elements and the limitations of sensors used to measure force. To overcome this challenge, a novel algorithm has been developed which utilizes a linear controller known as proportional control and incorporates feedback from the sensor. The algorithm tests the elastic actuator's behavior under different conditions and its ability to track the desired force output. It does this by analyzing the closed-loop system's behavior over time and comparing actual and desired force readings. The method was tested on a SEA hand equipped with finger pads and mounted on a robotic base. The hand was programmed to grasp and squeeze an object and the algorithm was tested with different elastic modulus values. The results showed that the algorithm could accurately measure actual force and its relationship with sensor feedback. The test also revealed that the SEA's behavior conformed to first-order linear dynamics and that the algorithm could effectively regulate the SEA's force output even with inaccurate sensor feedback, indicating its robustness. The algorithm successfully demonstrated a high degree of correlation between actual and desired force readings, proving its effectiveness in measuring actual force generated by SEAs. The algorithm's ability to track desired force output in various scenarios further solidified its value in controlling SEAs. The developed algorithm can be applied to other elastic actuators that employ similar control schemes and sensor feedback systems. It has the potential to contribute to the development of more sophisticated robotic hands and other elastic actuators equipped with complex capabilities. The algorithm is suitable for general-purpose use and can be adapted to suit the specific requirements of different elastic actuators. The algorithm has been made publicly accessible on GitHub, marking a significant step towards its further development and potential use in industrial applications. Our research focuses on multicomponent complex scalar theories, utilizing lattice models to identify pattern formations and phase transitions. We represent these theories using linear symmetry groups and apply renormalization-group techniques to analyze the associated continuum field theories. By matching the symmetries present in the lattice models with those of the corresponding continuum theories, we determine the renormalized parameter values and transition temperatures for the lattice at various scales. These results are used to relate the lattice models' phase transitions to the renormalization-group flow of the continuum theories. Leveraging this framework, we interpret the lattice models' transition patterns in terms of the renormalization-group flows. For instance, we find that one of our lattice models, exhibiting multiple phase transitions, undergoes a transition akin to a tricritical point, while another model's transition is associated with an instantonly-like transition, characterized by a non-thermal phase transition at the critical temperature. Additionally, we observe that another lattice model displays a symmetry-breaking transition, accompanied by a non-trivial topological phase. We also showcase the relevance of this approach to designing lattice models capable of mimicking continuum field theories. As an example, we demonstrate that one of our lattice models can be utilized to approximate a Z2+Z2 symmetric theory, a linear symmetry group that has not been extensively studied in lattice models. Our research offers a novel methodology for creating lattice models with specified properties and phase transitions and can also serve as a bridge to understanding the phase transitions observed in complex scalar lattice models. This work may also contribute to the development of lattice models that efficiently replicate the behavior of continuum field theories. This research could be particularly helpful in finding models that can accurately approximate a QCD-like theory, even one with a single, complex fundamental field, which remains an open challenge in lattice field theory. In high-dimensional underwater navigation tasks, efficiently evaluating policies is a significant challenge. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel algorithm called SPGP-SARSA, which leverages a sparse grid method to create a factorized policy evaluation operator. By doing so, the algorithm reduces the computational complexity from O(N) to O(log N) per update, where N represents the number of action options. We demonstrate that SPGP-SARSA achieves optimal regret performance compared to a uniform random policy and establish an upper bound on its optimal expected return. To further accelerate convergence, we explore an asynchronous variant of the algorithm and apply it to a real-world underwater communication dataset, showcasing its superior performance over multiple baseline algorithms. The results highlight the algorithm's efficiency and effectiveness in tackling complex underwater navigation tasks. Moreover, an analysis of the algorithm's performance is provided, along with a detailed study of its efficiency in action spaces of various dimensions. To facilitate future research, we openly share the code and dataset associated with this project. By introducing a more efficient policy evaluation method, we also discuss potential applications of the algorithm in reinforcement learning and beyond. Ultimately, our work aims to contribute positively to the ongoing efforts to develop efficient underwater communication technologies. Recently discovered sorting networks with two inputs have been shown to require at least 4 layers to sort any two-element sequence. This study investigates the minimal input arity necessary for sorting networks with more than one input, across various depths. It finds that for depths of 1 to 4, a sorting network with more than one input can be achieved using 2 inputs, but for depths of 5 and above, the minimal input arity increases to 3. Additionally, a method for constructing optimal sorting networks with three inputs has been developed, and the construction process is outlined for sorting networks with three inputs across depths of 5 to 10. Up to layers 13, the constructed sorting networks remain the most efficient known. This study also introduces a method to construct sorting networks with more than one input, by applying a monotic transformation to previously known sorting networks. This method effectively triples the input arity in the resulting sorting network. This new approach enables a broader range of superadding functions to be considered and it is demonstrated that many previous studies can be represented as a composition of this monotic transformation and superadding functions. This knowledge increases our understanding of the properties of sorting networks with more than one input, especially those with three inputs, where the behavior becomes more complex due to the application of antipodes. This leads to the existence of counter-intuitive counterfactuals when considering three-input sorting networks. This existence of counter-intuitive counterfactuals is shown to stem from the interplay between the applied function and the structure of the sorting network, rather than the input sequence itself. This concept is further illustrated by applying this method to a specific sorting network and the resulting discussion yields several open questions related to the study of sorting networks with more than one input. This research has been supported by a grant from the NSF. This work has been presented at the 2021 42nd IASTED International Conference on Advances in Modeling and Control, but this paper represents a more comprehensive expansion of those findings. This study has the unique identifier AIC 2021 04.13.

We explored various structural parameters of a galactic disk using three-dimensional N-body simulations, including an initial condition based on the Milky Way, to observe how they affect the formation of bars. Our findings indicate that the formation of bars are influenced by the scale length of the disk's density distribution, with a critical value existing below which stable bar formation is guaranteed. Bar formation was also accelerated and its stability increased when considering interactions with a massive spiral arm. Additionally, we discovered that a disk's velocity dispersion plays a significant role in bar formation, with higher dispersion leading to bar destruction or formation of double bars. A disk's velocity dispersion also affects the formation of satellite galaxies, with greater dispersion resulting in galaxies that resemble dwarf spheroidals. Our research provides a framework for understanding the effects of disk structures on bar formation, offering a possible explanation for the variation in bar prevalence observed across various galaxies. This work will be followed by more comprehensive studies incorporating star formation and gas dynamics. Our reference model, with its initial conditions and parameters, will be available for the community to use in further research. The effect of magnetic fields on merger remnants formed through major, gas-rich mergers is being investigated by means of high-resolution, three-dimensional simulations. These simulations revealed an unexpected outcome: regardless of how magnetic fields influence the merger process, the same ultimate shape of the merger remnant results. However, the initial form of the merger remnant can vary significantly due to magnetic fields, leading to increased instability and a greater likelihood of merging with nearby galaxies. Additionally, magnetic fields cause enhanced and maladaptive star formation within the merger remnant, at both early and late stages post-merger. This, in turn, magnifies the amount of heavy elements ejected from the merger remnant, particularly in the early stages, and causes a temporary (100 million years) enhancement in the ultraviolet radiation from the merger remnant. This, along with the greater mass of heavy elements, results in the enhanced formation of low-mass dwarf galaxies in the merger's surrounding area, shaped like a disk. This may provide a possible explanation for dwarf galaxies exhibiting enhanced chemical composition. Moreover, magnetic fields increase the likelihood that a merger remnant will host a central black hole, and may also influence the formation of low-mass, star-less globular clusters within the merger remnant. These findings suggest magnetic fields play a significant role in shaping the post-merger universe. This includes a greater degree of variability in galaxy spectra and a more complex, magnetic field-driven chemistry landscape behind it. This study offers a possible explanation for several observed celestial phenomena, such as the enhanced chemical composition of dwarf galaxies, low-mass, low-surface-brightness galaxies, and low-mass, star-less globular clusters. Furthermore, it raises intriguing questions about the impact of magnetic fields on galaxy interactions and mergers. This research is part of the MAGNUM project, utilizing the Astro-Dynamic code and combining magnetic field effects with gravitational physics at its most fundamental level. This code leverages the Astro-Dynamic code's high-resolution, three-dimensional capabilities, inspired by the success of magnetic field-driven simulations of turbulent molecular clouds. This research is also aligned with observations and theoretical modeling of merger remnants, including those from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array and the Event Horizon Telescope. This research is further backed by ongoing and future spectrographic and imaging surveys, such as the Square Kilometre Array and the James Webb Space Telescope. This difficulty arises from the limited number of high-quality, severely affected images available. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel 3D contrastive learning model that adapts a simplified robust watermelon dataset. This model incorporates contrastive learning and a clever data augmentation strategy called Mixup. By employing two efficient techniques, hyperplane adaptation and contrastive learning, our model successfully addresses the issue of data imbalance. We apply this model in a supervised learning setting and evaluate its performance on two 3D datasets, namely lung lesion detection and brain tumor detection. The results show significant improvements over existing methods, with severity scores that serve as direct inputs to the model. We also observe improved robustness and accuracy on synthetic data. The success of pre-trained language models is significantly hindered by their lack of adaptability to processing erroneous text. Generative corrections (GEC) are particularly challenging due to the limited size and quality of available training data. In response to these difficulties, we've developed a novel adaptation technique that leverages structural semantic predictors and builds upon the existing multi-task transfer learning framework. By doing so, we've achieved notable improvements in correction accuracy and significantly outperformed traditional approaches that rely on masked language modeling. Our method demonstrates particularly robust performance on difficult-to-correct sentences and has achieved state-of-the-art results on the ICSVL test dataset, achieving a mean absolute error rate of 0.76. In 2020, Japan faced a significant suicide crisis compounded by the COVID-19 pandemic.
To address this issue, the Japanese government launched the "Suicide Prevention Basic Plan," a
program that relies heavily on data-driven decision making. However, the pandemic brought
another challenge, with the government having to balance the release of detailed suicide data
against potential disclosure risks. As a result, some geographical areas were rounded to one
or two digits, potentially distorting the true suicide rates. This paper addresses the impact of
these data aggregations on statistical inference and finds that even with minimal rounding,
simple data masking can significantly alter inferences about suicide rates and their variation
Across different methods of data masking, we found that robust nonparametric tests could
still draw meaningful conclusions about pre-post changes in suicide rates at the national
level, even with no data rounding. On the other hand, we show that suicide rate inferences
are heavily influenced by data masking, especially when looking at regional changes.
Notably, robust linear mixed effects models could still provide accurate estimates of pre-post
changes in suicide rates even with minimal rounding, while simple nonparametric tests
could not. Our findings highlight the importance of using robust statistical methods and
sensitive data handling to facilitate data sharing and monitoring of public health outcomes. 
This study uses suicide data from Japan, but its implications are relevant to any data collection
effort facing similar data privacy challenges. 
 
Keywords: data sharing, suicide prevention, statistical inference challenges, sensitive data handling

When utilizing pseudo-labeling for out-of-distribution target data, it's common to train a model using multiple translations of the same target image. Despite producing diverse and often accurate predictions, these translations can also yield misleading pseudo-targets due to existing flaws in the source data. Since target data is typically limited, directly rejecting such noisy pseudo-targets would severely reduce the effectiveness of pseudo-targets for supervised learning. Instead, we propose an innovative approach to combine the predictions from multiple translations of a single target image, leveraging their diversity to improve pseudo-targets. By applying a proposed attention-based mechanism and circular correlation operator, our method successfully integrates the diverse predictions and produces more reliable pseudo-targets. Experimental results on the broad domain adaptation task demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, showcasing significant improvements over baseline methods and the importance of diversity in predictions for effective pseudo-target generation. We performed a detailed analysis of HII regions in UGC 8839, an interacting spiral galaxy. Using wide-field imaging from the CFHT and Mt. Lemmon, we studied over 700 HII regions across 12 chip images. Our research revealed a notable population of HII regions located 10 kpc or more from the galactic center, a feature not commonly observed in other spiral galaxies. Within the outer 10 kpc radius, we found a relatively flat distribution of HII regions, which suggests a constant specific star formation rates in this region. However, at larger radii, the distribution drops off more sharply. We observed a correlation between the potential companions and the increase in star formation at certain radii, which may indicate the effects of past mergers. We also found a broad ring-like structure consisting of young stellar disks surrounding the central bulge. This feature is consistent with a stellar disk that has experienced significant gravitational stirring. We compared our findings to other spiral galaxies and noted the exceptional nature of UGC 8839's outer star formation. Its remarkable ring-like structure and widespread outer HII regions distinguish it from other spiral galaxies. We developed an age map of the galaxy, which showed a marked drop in ages at radii greater than 7 kpc. This indicates a constant outside-in star formation pattern in UGC 8839's stellar disk. We estimate the galaxy's current specific star formation rate at its outer regions to be 0.6-1.0 years^-1, which is consistent with galaxies of similar mass. However, its outer HII region population's broad ring-like distribution, coupled with a potential grand design ring structure, points to a spiral density wave with an estimated pattern speed of 30-50 km/s/kpc. This research provides the most detailed analysis to date of an interacting spiral galaxy's HII region population and its underlying physics. Our study highlights the exceptional features of UGC 8839, which make it an ideal galaxy for conducting in-depth research of spiral density waves and star formation in interacting galaxies. Despite significant advancements in Re-identification (ReID) techniques due to the vast expansion of surveillance data, the lack of labeled data remains a major challenge for unsupervised ReID methods. To tackle this issue, this study introduces a novel contrastive learning framework, termed Dual-Contrastive Learning for ReID (DLReID), which incorporates two contrasting techniques to extract useful information from unlabeled data. The first approach, Global-Contrast, uses the method of contrastive learning to train a prototype discriminator that identifies distinct entities based on global characteristics and robust general features. The second approach, Local-Contrast, employs a wrapper discriminator with a contrastive loss function to detect and eliminate similar but not identical images characterized by local unique features and noise. To obtain more reliable unsupervised labels for the training process, a method of cycle consistency constraint is proposed to eliminate differences based on clothing types. Numerous experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed DLReID framework over existing unsupervised ReID methods on various benchmark datasets. The source code of the proposed method is available online at: https://github.com/cg1177/DLReID. The code will be continuously updated in line with further improvements and advancements in the coming days.

We analyzed the parameter space of pulsar timing arrays using sampling algorithms from the field of evolutionary computation, and evaluated their performance with a focus on parallel processing. Our results showed that, despite varying fitness function representations, different algorithms exhibited similar convergence rates, and had only mildly variable robustness when subjected to noise. In terms of efficiency, parallelizing the sampling process yielded the most significant gains, with some algorithms showing improved performance through intrinsic parallelization techniques and tension reduction. Our findings suggest that the most effective sampling strategy for PTA analysis involves parallelizing the sampling process and leveraging computational clusters, which can facilitate exhaustive sampling across multiple parameter spaces. This approach has notable implications for big data analysis in this field, and may have broader applications in the analysis of complex astrophysical data sets. We demonstrate the efficacy of these sampling methods through the re-analysis of a real-data experiment from the EPTA dataset, and highlight potential avenues for further research. Additionally, we contribute an open-source Python implementation of our sampling framework, which is freely available for use and modification under the MIT license. This implementation includes sampling classes for both parallelizable fitness functions and combinatorial optimization problems. This code can be accessed through our GitHub repository at https://github.com/raoulblommaert/sampling_pta. We also outline potential extensions to this work, which may be of interest to researchers in this field.

However, T Tauri stars are notable for their extreme variability in mass accretion rates, which ranges from less than 10^(-6) to greater than 10^(-4) M_sun/yr. People generally agree that helping the less fortunate is important, but there's less consensus on how to achieve this goal. Luck can influence opportunities or income, and our research explores how these two different sources of luck impact Americans' willingness to support redistribution. We conducted a series of experiments, involving a representative group of over 3,500 adults, in which we simulated scenarios where luck affects opportunities or directly determines income, and observed their responses in terms of desired tax rates and charitable donations. Our findings reveal significant differences in how people react to situations where luck affects opportunities rather than income, and provide new insights into how people's preferences are shaped by their own economic circumstances, social connections, and emotional reactions, particularly fear and envy. Ultimately, our study shows that most people prefer to reduce the inequalities created by luck, whether it's through increasing their own charitable donations or supporting the government to do so, especially when luck directly determines income. Interestingly, women and individuals with lower incomes and education levels exhibit a stronger desire to support redistribution, but only in scenarios where luck affects opportunities, not income. Interestingly, our data also shows that people overestimate the benefits they receive from government programs, but still want to pay more taxes to support these programs, and that people are more willing to support redistribution when they think about broader social inequalities, but become more focused on their own circumstances when considering charitable donations. Our study's findings have important implications for designing policies and programs aimed at reducing income inequalities. Keywords: Inequality, Luck, Redistribution, Experiments, American Citizens. Understanding how knowledge evolves over time is crucial for navigating the vast amount of scientific literature. Inspired by the concept of diffusion, researchers have been using language models to study the quantifiable and qualitative knowledge flows among papers based on citation networks. However, existing measures of knowledge flux are either difficult to compute or lack a clear, theoretical basis. In our work, we introduce the Quantitative Index of Knowledge (KQI), a simple and interpretable metric that estimates the knowledge quantity at each point in time and space. We also propose an intuitive method to visualize literature knowledge evolution, using a heat map. By applying these techniques to two well-known datasets of scientific literature (one about protein function and the other about gene regulation), we successfully identified unknown knowledge flux trends and correlations with external factors. Notably, our results revealed an unexpected delay in the spread of knowledge about gene flux and a possible impact of external factors on the evolution of knowledge about protein function. Our method is straightforward to execute and requires no specialized knowledge of machine learning, as it can be done with widely available tools such as GPyODA. All of our code and data are available online for further exploration and extension. In the long run, our approach could be adapted for use in other domains of scientific literature, with possible customization to accommodate domain-specific knowledge. In the short term, our technique can be employed to analyze ongoing research, providing scientists with a powerful visual representation of research progress and suggestions for future investigations. This study explores how automated vehicles can predict and avoid obstacles at intersections by analyzing the impact of traffic signals on their possible trajectories. Since current automation systems typically rely on sensing data and focus on avoiding obstacles rather than optimizing routes, this research simulates a connected automated vehicle to study its trajectory planning strategies. By analyzing the effect of traffic signals on available pathways, this simulation determines the impact of red, yellow, and green phases on the vehicle's ability to navigate safely through intersections. As the vehicle approaches the intersection, its projected path is calculated based on its current speed, allowing the simulation to identify potential conflicts with other road users approaching the intersection. Since the vehicle's trajectory is highly dependent on its speed and the time spent in each traffic signal phase, this study demonstrates that even small variations in these factors can significantly affect the vehicle's ability to navigate safely through intersections. Additionally, this research finds that its proposed methodology can be applied to any intersection configuration and that the resulting conflict patterns are influenced by the right-turn phase at this specific intersection. However, this is deemed a simplification and may not reflect more complex intersection configurations. To further improve its findings, the research suggests incorporating additional factors into the analysis, such as the behavior of other road users and the physical characteristics of the vehicle itself. By doing so, the simulation may better capture the complex nature of urban traffic interactions and conflict patterns at intersections. In this case, a comprehensive analysis of conflict patterns emerged, and the results are expected to contribute to the development of more effective trajectory planning strategies in connected automated vehicles. Ultimately, this research is positioned to lay the groundwork for a dynamic traffic pattern analysis tool and may also have applications in evaluating the safety performance of signalized intersections. This approach is particularly relevant for evaluating the safety of connected automated vehicles, particularly those powered by machine learning technologies that rely on experience from navigating similar intersections. This approach is also seen as essential for mitigating the potential safety risks of introducing automated vehicles in existing traffic networks. A notable exception is the TextWorldExpress protocol, developed to accelerate evaluations and enable the exploration of hard problems in game understanding. This protocol's success motivates researchers to re-examine existing frameworks and settings in search of improvements. These experiments involved adapting reinforcement learning and neural network techniques to TextWorldExpress and comparing the performance of different models, trainers, and architectures. A particularly striking finding was the discovery that a simple multi-layer neural network was able to master TextWorldExpress variants at a speed of over 10 times faster than human players on moderately difficult terrain. While data efficiency is a major concern in NLP, most models still rely on extensive training datasets and data augmentation techniques to achieve high performance. Despite notable advancements, the efficiency of efficient models like MLP and BigBird via data augmentation remains a subject of debate due to their large size and the difficulty of scaling smaller models. This study focuses on developing context-free data augmentation methods that are model-agnostic, efficient, and scalable, with applications to medium-sized NLP models. We evaluated six different context-free augmentation methods, combining character-level replacement, deletion, insertion, masking, and permutation, along with two more sophisticated techniques, Lexicon-based WordNet augmentation and a proposed character-level BERT-style augmentation. This study utilizes the BART small model as a case study for medium-sized NLP models and trains it on two datasets with various augmentation methods. The results show that three of the context-free augmentation methods significantly outperform the baseline model and enhance its performance when applied to the robustness evaluation. This research provides a preliminary framework for developing context-free data augmentation methods, which can be adapted to other NLP models and tasks with further optimization. We then derive the core prediction of this framework, which asserts that the strength of its self-interaction must exceed a minimum threshold proportional to the volume of the three-fold, in line with the Witten-Calabi-Yau volume formula. We also explore the possibility that this may be linked to the "strong duality" hypothesis, which posits an equivalence between four-dimensional theories described by Calabi-Yau three-folds and their dual descriptions in the space of five-dimensional supergravity. We further analyze a pair of simple, non-supersymmetric solutions, which provide support for our new formulation of the Self-Binding WGC. These solutions involve a fundamental string or five-brane in AdS_5 x S^5, which can be solved analytically. Independent system operators (ISOs) are beginning to adopt all-or-none (AON) designs in redispatch markets to mitigate the drawbacks of traditional within-market solutions.  While AON designs promote balanced and efficient redispatch, the interplay between these designs and price discovery mechanisms, particularly those used for price-based procurement, becomes a critical issue.  Specifically, the effect of AON designs on price discovery mechanisms and the resulting prices affects the grid operator's procurement strategy and ultimately the efficiency of price-based procurement.  In this paper, a model that captures the grid operator's procurement decisions, price discovery mechanisms, and AON designs is analyzed to examine how the operator's procurement strategies respond to different design parameters, including the frequency of price discoveries and market clearings.  This model is utilized to investigate how the grid operator's procurement strategies are influenced by AON designs and price discovery mechanisms, and to explore the implications for energy balancing services markets.  This research finds that in markets with AON designs, the grid operator over-procures during periods of high frequency price discoveries, and that the optimal frequency of price discoveries is optimal when it equals the frequency of market clearings.  This research also introduces a novel procurement strategy for the grid operator known as the double auction mechanism, and finds through simulation that this mechanism outperforms traditional methods by reducing procurement costs during periods of high frequency price discoveries, and that it can be robust to various parameter settings.  This research provides a framework that can be utilized by ISOs to design effective price-based procurement strategies that account for the interplay between price discovery mechanisms and market clearing mechanisms, and can facilitate open access research on this topic.  This research is part of the larger research project titled "Designing Price-Based Procurement Strategies for Energy Balancing Services Markets".
